items.title: OPAL Tutorials
items.text: OPAL — Orbitals, Plotting, Analysis and Layout — is a set of browser tools for OpenMolcas. They run offline from a single HTML file each.

items.title: What OPAL is
items.text:
OPAL is a suite of eight tools and a launcher that opens them. The tools build a molecule, show it, read the results that OpenMolcas writes, and help you prepare the next input:

  • MolBuild draws a molecule and gives it a 3D geometry.
  • MolViz shows a geometry as balls and sticks.
  • CSFsCalc counts the configuration state functions of a RASSCF active space.
  • OrbViz shows orbitals, electron densities and density differences.
  • RassiViz shows transition densities, transition dipole moments and the absorption spectrum from a RASSI calculation.
  • GeoDiff compares two structures.
  • IntCoords writes the block of internal coordinates that SLAPAF needs for a transition-state search.
  • PathVibViz follows optimisations, reaction paths, conical intersections and vibrations.

Each tool is one file. You open it in a browser: nothing is installed, no server is needed, and your files are not sent anywhere. The launcher, the first page of the suite, puts the tools side by side. OPAL is part of OpenMolcas and shares its licence; see About.

items.title: Two ways in
items.text:
• By tool. Each tool has a folder of short pages, one per feature: Tools.
  • By story. A case study, the photoisomerization of azobenzene, walks through a typical project from an empty screen to publication figures: Case study.

items.title: How to use these tutorials
items.text:
• A feature page is short and has the same parts every time: What it does, How (numbered steps), one image, Tips and pitfalls and Related. Interface names are written in bold, as they appear on the screen.
  • Things that all the tools do in the same way, such as opening a file, the side panels, the theme button, or saving an image, are explained once on the pages of Common to all tools. A tool's pages link to them.
  • The files used by the case study are on the page Example files. You can follow every tool page with a file of your own.
  • A small calculation can be run without installing anything: Running OpenMolcas in Colab. It uses a small molecule of its own; the azobenzene calculations of the case study are too large for it and are supplied as ready results.
  • A page marked Draft at the top is not finished: it has not yet been read and tried in the tool by its author. A page describes the version of the tool it was checked against, and the tool may have changed since.
  • On the published site, a link such as Open MolViz on a tool's overview page opens the tool itself.

items.title: How to cite
items.text:
If you use OPAL in published work, please cite the OPAL article and the OpenMolcas paper that presents OPAL. At the time of writing neither reference is published, so there is none to give here yet; the reference will be added when it exists.

Every tool and the launcher have a button, ⓘ, at the right end of the toolbar. It opens a small window with the current references, with a button to copy each of them, and with a link to the tutorial of that tool. The launcher also shows the references in a section called How to cite. When a reference is published, those places show it, and the tools can add it to the comment lines of the files they export.

items.text:

Each file belongs to the geometry the calculation used for it, and the geometries differ: the SCF and the first RAS step (9/0/7) were run on the MolBuild structure of trans-azobenzene, while the second RAS step (5/⅚) and the RASSI file were run at the trans ground-state minimum. The inputs name their structure and orbital files as they were called when the calculations ran, so rename those names in the Coord and FileOrb lines before rerunning one. items.title: The question
items.text: Why does light switch azobenzene between trans and cis? What do we need to compute?

items.title: What you do
items.text:
No feature page: this chapter sets the plan. You read it, and you decide what you want from the calculations of the next chapters.

Azobenzene is two phenyl rings joined by an N=N double bond. It exists in two forms, trans (the rings on opposite sides of the double bond) and cis (the rings on the same side). Light of a suitable colour turns one into the other, and the molecule is the standard example of a photoswitch. To say anything about how this happens you need four things, and each one is a chapter:

What you need Where A structure of each isomer, and a check that it is sensible Chapter 2, chapter 3 A method that can describe the ground and the excited states, which means a multiconfigurational one, and an active space small enough to run Chapter 4, chapter 5, chapter 6 The excited states themselves: which are dark and which are bright Chapter 7 The paths: the minima, how they differ, the way back in the dark and the funnel in the light Chapter 8, chapter 9, chapter 10, chapter 11

The last chapter, chapter 12, turns the results into pictures and animations for a paper or a talk.

Every tool of the suite has a place in this story, and the calculations are real OpenMolcas runs whose result files you can download from the Example files page. You can follow the story from the first chapter to the last, or take a chapter on its own: each one says which files it needs.

items.title: What it tells you
items.text:
The question has a chemical half and a practical half. The chemical half is what the light does: it lifts the molecule to an excited state, and from there the molecule finds its way back down to the ground state, either as trans or as cis. The practical half is that the way down passes through places where two electronic states come close or meet, and an ordinary single-reference method cannot describe them. That is why the calculations use a state-averaged RASSCF wave function, and why you will spend a chapter on the choice of the active space.

The method, the active space and the basis set were chosen so that the calculations run quickly. The results are for tutorial purposes; they may differ from published values, including the authors' own.

items.text: None.

items.title: The question
items.text: Get reasonable trans and cis starting structures.

items.title: What you do
items.text:
You make both isomers in MolBuild, one after the other, with the same four steps. A force field gives a geometry in seconds. It is not a quantum-chemical result, but it is a good place to start the calculations from.

  1. SMILES. Type the molecule as text in the section SMILES. The two isomers differ only in two characters. The slashes tell MolBuild on which side of the double bond each ring lies: for trans, type c1ccccc1/N=N/c1ccccc1; for cis, type c1ccccc1/N=N\c1ccccc1. After each import, read the formula in the status bar and check it is C₁₂H₁₀N₂ with 24 atoms, as the page on SMILES advises.
  2. Stereochemistry. Azobenzene has no stereocentre, so you draw no wedge and no dash: the two isomers differ about a double bond, and the slashes of step 1 are what set it. The page is the place to see how MolBuild marks the other kind of stereochemistry, if a later molecule of yours has one.
  3. Optimise in 3D. Click ⚡ Optimise and wait for Optimised ✓. Do this for each isomer before you export.
  4. Export XYZ. Click ⬇ XYZ and save the structure, for example as azobenzene_trans_start.xyz and azobenzene_cis_start.xyz. Read the comment line of the file: it must say UFF-optimised.

items.title: What you should see
items.text: After each optimisation the 3D pane shows a structure with the two rings joined through the N=N bond. In the trans isomer the two rings lie on opposite sides of that bond and the molecule is flat and elongated. In the cis isomer they lie on the same side and the molecule is folded. The example files carry the comment line MolBuild v0.78 | UFF-optimised; the comment line of the cis file adds that the optimisation moved the atoms by up to 1.967 Å from the geometry before it: for a folded molecule the optimisation does real work.

items.title: What it tells you
items.text: You now have a starting geometry for each isomer, and nothing more. The force field knows nothing about the excited states and does not treat the N=N double bond as a quantum chemist would. Later chapters relax both geometries with the method of the tutorial, and you will see by how much they change. The next chapter checks that these two structures are sensible before you spend calculation time on them.

items.text:

  • azobenzene_cis_start.xyz: cis-azobenzene, force-field structure. Present; see Example files.

items.title: The question
items.text: Are the geometries sensible? N=N length, CNNC dihedral.

items.title: What you do
items.text:
You open each structure in MolViz and measure the three numbers that tell the two isomers apart: the N=N distance, the C–N=N angles and the C–N=N–C dihedral.

  1. Open a file. Load azobenzene_trans_start.xyz. The message at the bottom of the view says how many atoms and bonds were found: 24 atoms.
  2. Navigate the 3D view. Turn the molecule until you look at it from the side and from above: the first view tells you whether it is flat, the second whether the rings are on opposite sides.
  3. Atom labels. Tick Permanent labels. The number of an atom is its position in the file: the N=N group is N1 and N2, and the carbons they bind are C4 (on N1) and C3 (on N2).
  4. Measure distances and angles. With Distance, click N1 and N2. With Angle, click C4, N1, N2 (the vertex is the second atom). With Dihedral, click C4, N1, N2 and C3 in that order.

Then repeat the four steps with azobenzene_cis_start.xyz; its atoms are numbered in the same way.

items.title: What you should see
items.text:
The coordinates of the two files, worked out by a script outside MolViz, give these values. MolViz shows the distance with three decimals and the angles with two, so expect the same numbers to the precision of the table:

trans cis N=N distance (Å) 1.251 1.269 C–N distances (Å) 1.434 and 1.434 1.436 and 1.436 C–N=N angles (°) 114.6 and 114.7 119.5 and 119.5 C–N=N–C dihedral, size (°) 180.0 1.3

The sign of a dihedral depends on the order in which you pick the atoms, and MolViz gives it the sign that SLAPAF prints; the size is what matters here.

items.title: What it tells you
items.text:
Both structures are what an N=N double bond should give. The N=N distance is short, close to 1.25 Å in both, the C–N bonds are longer, and the C–N=N angles are near 120°, which is the angle of a double bond. The dihedral separates the isomers: the trans structure is flat, with the dihedral at 180°, and the cis structure has the two carbons on the same side, with the dihedral near 0°.

Two things to keep in mind. The force field decides all these numbers, and the quantum-chemical optimisations of chapter 8 and chapter 9 will move them, so these values are a check of the construction, not a result. And a dihedral of 1.3° across the N=N bond does not say that the cis molecule is flat: the rings can still be twisted about the C–N bonds, which is why you looked at the molecule from more than one side in step 2.

items.title: The question
items.text: The full π system plus the nitrogen lone pairs is 18 electrons in 16 orbitals: is a complete active space affordable, and how does a RAS partition cut it down?

items.title: What you do
items.text:
You do not need a molecule file for this chapter. CSFsCalc counts the configuration state functions (CSFs) of an active space from three numbers of orbitals, two numbers of electrons and two limits, and it does so as you type.

  1. Set the RAS orbitals. For a complete active space put all 16 orbitals in RAS2 Orbitals and 0 in RAS1 Orbitals and RAS3 Orbitals.
  2. Set the electrons and the spin. Type 9 in Alpha Electrons and 9 in Beta Electrons: 18 electrons, a singlet.
  3. Limit holes and excitations. With everything in RAS2 the two limits do not matter. Now split the space: put 9 orbitals in RAS1 and 7 in RAS3, none in RAS2, and set both limits to 2. Then try 5, 5 and 6 orbitals with both limits at 2.
  4. Read the results. Read Configuration State Functions each time, and the string at the foot of the panel: RAS(18, 2, 2; 5, 5, 6) for the last one.
  5. Show the CSF distribution. Click Show CSF Distribution Details with 5, 5 and 6, and read how the CSFs share among the ways of distributing the electrons.

items.title: What you should see
items.text:
The counts below were produced by running the counting code of CSFsCalc itself on these inputs, outside the page.

Active space Orbitals RAS1 / RAS2 / RAS3 Limits (holes / electrons) CSFs Complete (CAS) 0 / 16 / 0 not used 27 810 640 First RAS step 9 / 0 / 7 2 / 2 2 080 Second RAS step 5 / 5 / 6 2 / 2 24 295

For the last row the box of the distribution has nine lines. The largest is (N1=8, N2=8, N3=2) with 12 825 CSFs, then (N1=9, N2=7, N3=2) with 7 950 CSFs; the smallest, (N1=8, N2=10, N3=0), has 15. The nine lines add up to the 24 295 of the table. N1, N2 and N3 are the numbers of electrons in RAS1, RAS2 and RAS3: N1=8 means two holes in RAS1 (it holds ten electrons when full), and N3=2 two electrons in RAS3.

items.title: What it tells you
items.text:
A complete active space of 18 electrons in 16 orbitals has about 28 million CSFs. That is far too many for a calculation that has to be repeated at every step of a geometry optimisation. The RAS partition cuts the space by a factor larger than a thousand: the electrons of RAS1 may lose at most two, and RAS3 may receive at most two, so only excitations up to a certain level remain.

The two RAS rows are the two steps of the calculations of the following chapters. The first, with an empty RAS2, is cheap (2 080 CSFs) and is used to obtain good orbitals. The second, with five orbitals in RAS2 meant to carry the low-lying states, is the one that is used for the states and for the optimisations. Its 24 295 CSFs are about twelve times more than the first step and still a tiny fraction of the complete space. The choice of 5, 5 and 6 is a choice for a tutorial: it is not a recommendation, and a different partition or different limits would give other numbers and, possibly, other energies. The counts depend only on the numbers you type, not on the number of states you ask for, so the five states of chapter 7 do not change them.

Chapter 6 shows how to get the orbitals into the three spaces.

items.title: The question
items.text: Which orbitals are n and π? Which go to RAS1, RAS2, RAS3?

items.title: What you do
items.text:
RASSCF takes its active orbitals from the file you give it, in the positions they have there. The orbitals of an SCF calculation are not in the positions the active space needs, so you tell RASSCF which pairs to exchange. OrbViz works out that instruction for you. The campaign did it in two steps, and so do you.

Step one: from the SCF orbitals to a first RAS calculation.

  1. Open a file. Load azobenzene_trans_scf.h5. The molecule appears with its 24 atoms, and the section Molecule gives the number of basis functions, which is also the number of orbitals.
  2. The orbital list. Read the section Molecular Orbitals: the occupied orbitals come first, with an occupation of 2. Scroll towards the highest occupied orbitals and the lowest empty ones: the active space is made from these.
  3. Show an orbital isosurface. Click rows near the border between occupied and empty, and look at each orbital. An orbital with lobes above and below the plane of the molecule, with a nodal plane in it, is a π orbital. An orbital with lobes in the plane, on a nitrogen atom and away from the N=N bond, is a lone pair, an n orbital. Note the numbers of the orbitals you want in the active space.
  4. Choose the active space (ALTEr). Fold out Active Space · ALTEr, tick Select the active space, and type 9 in RAS1 orbitals, 0 in RAS2 orbitals, 7 in RAS3 orbitals, 18 in Active electrons and 0 in Molecular charge. The tool computes the inactive and the secondary orbitals; use Move to in the list to put the orbitals you chose in the spaces until every row of the table shows a tick. Copy the block into the input.

The input of this first step is azobenzene_trans_ras_9_0_7.input. Its own block of exchanges has 15 pairs, below the limit of 16 pairs that RASSCF accepts. If a choice of yours would need more than 16, OrbViz refuses it and says what to do: run RASSCF with the exchanges first, then open the new orbitals and exchange again.

Step two: reorder, then the second calculation.

  1. Reorder by occupation. Open azobenzene_trans_ras_9_0_7.h5, the result of the first step. Fold out Orbital Order · ALTEr and tick Reorder by occupation. OrbViz writes the block that sorts all orbitals by decreasing occupation. The second input, azobenzene_trans_ras_5_5_6.input, puts 5, 5 and 6 orbitals in the three spaces and starts from the orbitals of its own first step. Its own block of exchanges has 4 pairs.

items.title: What you should see
items.text:
Numbers read from the example files with a script outside OrbViz:

  • The molecule has 246 orbitals and 96 electrons. In the SCF file the 48 lowest orbitals are occupied, with an occupation of 2.
  • In the result of the first step the orbitals fall into 39 inactive, 9 in RAS1 (positions 40 to 48), 7 in RAS3 (49 to 55) and 191 secondary. The occupations in RAS1 run from 1.988 to 1.678 and the first orbital of RAS3 has 0.641.
  • Not all of them are in decreasing order: orbital 44 has 1.810 and sits before orbitals 45, 46 and 47, which have 1.916, 1.849 and 1.848. This is why a reordering is useful.
  • In the result of the second step, 39 are inactive, 5 are in RAS1 (positions 40 to 44), 5 in RAS2 (45 to 49), 6 in RAS3 (50 to 55) and 191 are secondary. The occupations in RAS1 are 1.991 to 1.924; in RAS2 they are 1.785, 1.785, 1.807, 1.689 and 0.783; in RAS3 they are between 0.082 and 0.024.

The occupations are the averages over the five states of the calculation, as OrbViz shows them.

items.title: What it tells you
items.text:
Four orbitals of RAS2 are nearly full (between 1.689 and 1.807) and the fifth (position 49, with an occupation of 0.783) is partly empty. That is the orbital that gives and takes electrons most easily, and the one to look at first when you ask what the excited states are made of. RAS1 holds orbitals that stay almost full, and RAS3 orbitals that stay almost empty, and the limits of two holes and two electrons let a few electrons move between the three spaces. The partition is a teaching choice and not a recommendation: you could choose differently, and the next chapter shows what the five states look like with this one.

Whether a particular orbital is n or π is something you decide by looking at it. The numbers above only tell you where the orbitals sit.

items.title: The question
items.text: Which state is dark (nπ*), which is bright (ππ*)?

items.title: What you do
items.text:
The calculation of the previous chapter gives five singlet states at the ground-state minimum of trans-azobenzene, and the RASSI module computes what links them. You open the result in RassiViz.

  1. Open a file. Load azobenzene_trans_rassi.h5. The status text gives 24 atoms and 5 states, and the file bar says OpenMolcas HDF5 (RASSI). RassiViz starts computing the density of the first transition by itself.
  2. States and transition-dipole vectors. Read the table of states: for each transition from S₀ the energy ΔE/eV, the wavelength λ/nm and the oscillator strength f. Show the arrow of each transition with the box in the column Vis; an arrow is missing for a transition whose strength is zero.
  3. The spectrum. Press Spectrum. Switch Sticks on and read where the lines are and how tall.
  4. Electron density. Fold out Electron Density, choose a transition and Δρ (difference), and press Compute. Do it for the lowest transition and for the one with the largest oscillator strength.
  5. Density isosurface. Move Isovalue until the surface shows the places where the density changes, and look at where the blue (gain) and the red (loss) are.

items.title: What you should see
items.text:
Planned image: chapter-07.png; RassiViz with the RASSI file of trans-azobenzene: the table of states, the window Absorption Spectrum with sticks, and the difference density of the bright transition on the molecule.

The table has four transitions. These values were calculated from the energies and the dipole moments stored in the file, with a script outside RassiViz; they agree with the ones the campaign recorded.

State ΔE (eV) λ (nm) f S₁ 3.464 358 0.000 S₂ 5.487 226 0.179 S₃ 5.507 225 0.000 S₄ 5.750 216 0.985

These are the energies of the state-averaged RASSCF calculation, without the correction of perturbation theory. RassiViz names the states S₁ to S₄ in order of energy; in the numbering of the calculation they are roots 2 to 5. In the spectrum, the line of S₁ lies far below the others, at 3.46 eV, with no height. The other three lie at 5.49, 5.51 and 5.75 eV: the middle one has no height either, the first is small and the last is by far the tallest.

items.title: What it tells you
items.text:
The lowest excited state, S₁, has an oscillator strength of zero: light does not take the molecule there from the ground state. This is the dark state, the one described as nπ*, in which an electron moves from a nitrogen lone pair to the π* orbital of the N=N bond. The tall line at 5.75 eV, S₄, is the bright state, described as ππ*: it is the one that absorbs strongly. The difference density is what lets you check the labels yourself: for an nπ* state the density is lost in the plane of the molecule, on the nitrogen atoms, and gained in the π* region above and below it; for a ππ* state it moves within the π system. Look at the two surfaces and decide whether you agree.

Two cautions. The numbers are those of a small RAS partition and a modest basis set, at the RASSCF level: they are good for learning the tools and not for comparing with an experiment. And S₂ and S₃, 0.02 eV apart, are close enough that their order and their strengths may change with the method.

The bright state is also the one that the optimisation of the next chapter follows: the files azobenzene_trans_bright_min.slapaf.h5, azobenzene_trans_bright_min.geo.molden and azobenzene_trans_bright_min.xyz hold the minimum of that state, and chapters 8 and 9 open them.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The OPAL suite shows the results of OpenMolcas calculations. To run a calculation without installing anything, OPAL offers a notebook for Google Colab. You open it in your browser, write an OpenMolcas input, run it and read the energies and the orbitals in the same page. It is meant for teaching and for a first try, and it suits small molecules: a free Colab session is a modest machine. The case study uses a small molecule of its own here, trans-diazene (HN=NH), and returns to azobenzene in the chapters that follow.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the launcher, press Open on the card OpenMolcas on Colab. The notebook opens in a new tab. You need a network connection and a Google account.
  2. Connect to a runtime with the button at the top right of Colab.
  3. Run the Setup cell. It downloads a prebuilt OpenMolcas and installs what it needs. This takes about half a minute.
  4. In Configuration, give the job a name. The notebook refuses a name with characters it does not allow.
  5. In Input file, write or paste the OpenMolcas input. The editor starts with a water example. For the case study, use the input of trans-diazene, diazene_trans.input (see Example files).
  6. Run the Run cell, then read the Output file and the Results cells. The results cell picks the SCF, CASSCF and CASPT2 energies and the dipole moment out of the output.
  7. Look at the molecule in the Geometry viewer cell, and at the orbitals in the Orbital viewer cell, which is OrbViz inside the notebook.
  8. Run the last cell, Download, to get your files as one ZIP. Colab forgets them when the session ends.
Planned image: colab-notebook.png; the companion notebook with the diazene input loaded.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What the example does

The input of diazene_trans.input is for trans-diazene with the ANO-S-VDZP basis set and no symmetry. It runs an SCF, a state-averaged CASSCF over five singlet states with six electrons in four orbitals, a CASPT2 calculation on all five states and a RASSI calculation. In the test made for this tutorial it ran in 11 seconds.

Any method of OpenMolcas

The notebook builds OpenMolcas with HDF5 support, so the SCF, RASSCF, CASPT2, MP2, RASSI, ALASKA and SLAPAF modules can be used. The run writes both .h5 files and Molden files, which the OPAL tools read.

A session does not keep your files

When the Colab session ends, the files on it are gone. Use Download before you close the tab. The notebook opens read-only from GitHub: to keep changes to the notebook itself, use File, Save a copy in Drive.

Small systems only

Azobenzene with its 18 electrons in 16 orbitals is too large for a free session to treat in a lesson. That is why the azobenzene files of the later chapters are supplied as ready results on the Example files page.

The notebook can stop working after a Google update

The prebuilt OpenMolcas belongs to the version of Ubuntu that Colab runs. If Google changes it, the Setup cell may fail until a new build is made. If it fails, say so to the author.

items.title: Parts of a tool page: sections that fold
items.text:
Several tools group their controls in sections, each with a title. In those tools a click on the title folds the section, and another click opens it again. The small arrow at the right of the title shows the state: it points down when the section is open and to the right when it is folded. Its shape differs a little from tool to tool (▾ and ▸, ▼ and ►, or one arrow that turns). Folding only hides the fields. It does not change any value, and whatever the tool computes keeps following the fields. A feature page that tells you to find a section does not repeat this: if the section is folded, open it first.

A title with no arrow does not fold.

items.title: Shared features
items.text:
These features work in the same way in several tools. Each page says what is the same and has a note for every tool that differs.

  • Navigate the 3D view: turn, move and zoom with the mouse or with your fingers, and bring the view back.
  • Spin and Tilt: let the molecule turn or swing by itself (MolViz, OrbViz and RassiViz).
  • Export images (PNG and SVG): save the 3D view as a picture, in pixels or as a vector drawing.
  • Export an animated GIF: record a movie of the 3D view.

items.title: Exceptions
items.text:
Two differences are on purpose and are not defects:

  • MolBuild has no drag and drop of files. It builds a molecule from nothing, and its Load button opens a file only to change it. See Opening files.
  • CSFsCalc has no side panels, and no 3D view, so the pages on the 3D view, on Spin and Tilt, on images and on the animated GIF do not apply to it. See Side panels.

IntCoords and MolBuild cannot record a GIF, and IntCoords cannot save a PNG; the pages on images and on the animated GIF say which tool has what.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Every tool has a button labelled OPAL at the left end of its toolbar. It takes you back to the launcher, the page with one card for each tool. You use it to move from one tool to another without typing an address.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press OPAL, the first button of the toolbar.
  2. The launcher opens in the same browser tab.
  3. Press Launch on the card of the next tool.

If you had switched to the light theme, the launcher opens in the light theme as well, and so does the next tool.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
It needs the launcher beside the tool

The button is a plain link to the file index.html in the same folder as the tool. On the OPAL site, and in a folder where you keep all the OPAL files together, it works. If you saved a tool alone, or moved it, the link finds no launcher and the browser shows an error page. Use the browser's own back button, or open the launcher by its address.

The launcher has no such button

The launcher is where the button leads, so it does not carry it.

Your work is not saved

Leaving a tool closes what you had loaded in it. Save an image, a file or a state first if you want to keep it. See What is stored in your browser.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The OPAL tools run in an ordinary web browser, on a computer, a tablet or a phone. Nothing is installed. This page says what the browser needs, and what you see when it does not have it.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Use a browser from the last few years: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Opera or Edge, on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iPhone or iPad.
  2. Keep JavaScript switched on. Every tool is a page of JavaScript and shows nothing without it.
  3. For the tools that draw molecules in 3D, make sure the browser can use WebGL. This is on by default in every browser named above, as long as the graphics driver is working. The 3D tools are GeoDiff, MolBuild, MolViz, OrbViz, PathVibViz and RassiViz.
  4. IntCoords and CSFsCalc are different: CSFsCalc draws no 3D view, and IntCoords can do everything except the 3D view without WebGL.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
An old browser can show a blank page

The tools are written for browsers of about 2017 and later, with a floor in the style sheets at Safari 14.1. In an older browser a tool can fail to start and show an empty page, with no message. The same holds for an old copy of Safari on an old iPad. Updating the browser is the remedy.

No WebGL in IntCoords

When WebGL cannot start, IntCoords says The 3D view is not available in this browser (WebGL could not start). and keeps the atom table on the left working, so you can still build the block for SLAPAF. The other 3D tools have no such message: with no WebGL, their view stays empty.

A phone or a tablet

The tools are written to be used on a phone or a tablet too. Panels fold away behind handles; see Side panels. Files open through the file picker; see Open a file. On an iPhone or an iPad, saving a file works differently; see Save files on iPhone and iPad.

The exact minimum was not measured

"About 2017 and later" and "Safari 14.1" come from the rules the code is written to, not from tests on old browsers. No table of the oldest working version of each browser exists yet.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The tool records a short movie of the 3D view as an animated GIF: the molecule turns once around an axis (Spin 360°), or swings once to each side and back (Tilt ±). The file plays in a web page or a slide with no program of its own. In PathVibViz the movie shows one swing of the vibrational mode you have chosen instead.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Turn the molecule to the view you want. The movie starts from the present orientation, and whatever is on show, such as an orbital or a density, is part of it.
  2. Open the recording controls of your tool. They are described in the notes below.
  3. Choose the motion, Spin 360° or Tilt ± (the label is Motion type in the window of MolViz, OrbViz and RassiViz, and Motion in GeoDiff), and the Axis (Y — Vertical, X — Horizontal or Z — Depth; GeoDiff writes them in lower case after the dash). For a tilt, set the amplitude, from 5° to 90° (20° at the start).
  4. Set Frames (18 to 120, 48 at the start), Frame delay in ms (20 to 200, 50 at the start) and the width in pixels (200 to 1200, 600 at the start; Output width in the window of MolViz, OrbViz and RassiViz, Width elsewhere). More frames make a smoother movie and a larger file. The delay sets the speed of playing.
  5. Choose the options: Transparent background and Crop to content, ticked at the start, and the supersampling box (Supersample ×2 in GeoDiff, 2× supersampling in MolViz, OrbViz, RassiViz and PathVibViz), which is slower and uses more memory but gives smoother edges.
  6. Press the button that records (Record & Download, or ● Record GIF in GeoDiff). The tool draws the frames, then encodes them; a message shows its progress. On a computer the file is saved when the encoding ends. On an iPhone or iPad the tool waits for one more tap; see the tip below.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
On an iPhone or iPad a second tap saves the file

Encoding takes longer than the tap that started it, and the system then refuses to open the sharing sheet. The tool therefore keeps the finished GIF and shows a button Save GIF with Discard. Press Save GIF to choose where to keep the file. See Saving files on iPhone and iPad.

A transparent GIF cannot be partly see-through

In a GIF each pixel is either transparent or solid. A translucent surface comes out solid, or disappears, when Transparent background is ticked. OrbViz, RassiViz and PathVibViz (for a ghost centre) show a note when this applies. Untick the box to keep the see-through look; the movie then has the background colour of the view.

A long movie can run out of memory

OrbViz, RassiViz and PathVibViz show an estimate of the memory the frames will need, from the number of frames and the width. Above about 250 MB on an iPhone or iPad, or 600 MB on other devices, they warn that the page may reload while recording. Use fewer frames or a smaller width. The tools only warn; they never stop you.

Leave the page alone while it records

The view does not update while the tool records. In OrbViz, RassiViz and PathVibViz, opening another file ends the recording. OrbViz and RassiViz wait until a running computation of orbitals or densities has finished, and say so.

The names say what is inside

In MolViz, OrbViz, RassiViz and GeoDiff the file is named from the file you opened, then the motion and the axis, for example <file>_spin_y.gif or, for a tilt, with the amplitude, <file>_tilt_y_20deg.gif. OrbViz adds the orbital, and GeoDiff names the pair <Mobile>_vs_<Reference>.

Crop to content

With this box ticked, every frame is cut to the smallest rectangle that holds the molecule in all frames, so the movie does not move around inside its frame.

items.title: In this tool
items.text:
MolViz

The toolbar button Anim GIF opens the window Export Animated GIF. It suggests that you use Auto-orient first. The button Record & Download closes the window and records. The measurements you have made, and the atom symbols if Include atom symbols is ticked in the Export menu, are drawn into the frames; atom labels are not. There is no memory estimate.

OrbViz

Anim GIF in the toolbar opens the window. Orbitals, densities and difference surfaces on show are in the movie. The window has the two notes on transparency and on memory, and Cancel. The window GIF ready, with Save GIF and Discard, appears on an iPhone or iPad. Opening another file drops a GIF that is waiting to be saved.

RassiViz

Anim GIF in the toolbar opens the window, with the same notes and buttons as OrbViz. The transition density or difference density on show is in the movie.

GeoDiff

The recording controls are at the bottom of the section Image export of the right panel, under the buttons for PNG and SVG: Motion, Axis, a tilt Amplitude, Frames, Frame delay (ms), Width (px), Supersample ×2, Transparent background and Crop to content. The box Include legend of the images applies to the movie too. ● Record GIF records; on an iPhone or iPad a button ⬇ Save GIF appears when the GIF is ready, with ✕ to throw it away. There is no memory estimate.

The recording controls are in the section Vibrations of the right panel, under Animated GIF of the chosen mode. There is no choice of motion: the movie is one full swing of the chosen mode, or of the g or h vector, from the equilibrium geometry, in the view you have now. Record & Download is off until a mode is chosen. The file is named from the file you opened and the mode, for example <file>_mode3.gif. See Vibrations.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
The tools with a 3D view save the picture you see in it as a file. There are up to three kinds, and the names on the buttons say which:

  • PNG: a picture made of pixels. Use it in slides and documents.
  • SVG (image): the same picture of pixels, wrapped in an SVG file. A drawing program can place and scale it, but it cannot edit the atoms or the bonds.
  • SVG (vector): a new drawing, rebuilt from the atoms and bonds as circles, lines and gradients. A vector editor such as Inkscape can edit every part, and it stays sharp at any size. It is an approximation of the screen, not a copy of it. The atom labels, where the tool draws them, are real text.

Not every tool offers all three; the notes below list them.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Turn and zoom the molecule to the view you want, and show what should be in the picture. The file holds the 3D view only, not the panels.
  2. Find the export control of your tool, described in the notes below. Set its options first (for example Transparent background, or the look of the vector drawing).
  3. Press the button of the kind of image you want.
  4. The file is saved with a name made from the file you opened. On an iPhone or iPad a share sheet opens instead; see Saving files on iPhone and iPad.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Choose the vector look first

The vector drawing comes in three looks: Gradient (shaded like the screen), Flat (plain colours) and Print (flat colours on white, for paper). The list for the look sits next to the vector button. It applies to the next file you save.

A transparent PNG looks dark on a dark page

A transparent background shows whatever lies behind the picture. Open the file on a white page, or tick off Transparent background where the tool offers it, to see the molecule as it will print.

SVG (image) is not vector graphics

The file ends in .svg, but it holds one picture of pixels. If you want to edit or rescale the drawing, use SVG (vector).

The plots are saved separately

The plots of GeoDiff and PathVibViz have their own export buttons, with true vector SVG, PNG and a ZIP for gnuplot. See Analysis plots and Export plots.

items.title: In this tool
items.text:
MolViz

Export ▾ in the toolbar opens a menu. Its options are Transparent background (ticked at the start), Include atom labels and Include atom symbols. Its buttons are PNG image, SVG (image) and SVG (vector). Below them are Vector style (Gradient, Flat or Print (white)) and Space-filling (van der Waals), which draws the atoms as van der Waals spheres and no bonds. The measurements you have made are drawn into the PNG and the SVG (image). The PNG is named <file>.png.

OrbViz

The toolbar has three buttons, PNG, SVG (image) and SVG (vector), and a list for the vector look beside the last one (Gradient, Flat or Print (white)). The PNG and the SVG (image) always have a transparent background. The vector drawing holds the molecule and, when one is shown, the outline of the lobes of the orbital, the density or the density difference. The files are named <file>_MO<n>.png, where n is the number of the orbital on show, or <file>.png when there is none. The vector drawing is named <file>_molecule.svg when only the molecule is drawn, and ends in _vector.svg when a surface is drawn too.

RassiViz

Export ▾ opens a menu with Transparent background (ticked at the start), PNG image, SVG (image), SVG (vector) and Vector style (Gradient, Flat or Print (white)). The vector drawing has the atoms, the bonds, the transition dipole arrows and the outline of each lobe of the density on show. The PNG and the SVG (image) are named <file>.png and <file>.svg. The vector drawing is named <file>_molecule.svg, or <file>_density_vector.svg when a density is drawn too.

GeoDiff

The section Image export of the right panel has Transparent background and Include legend, both ticked at the start, and the buttons ⬇ PNG, ⬇ SVG (image) and ⬇ SVG (vector). Two lists set the vector drawing: Vector look (Gradient, Flat or Print on white) and Vector structure (Reference, Mobile, or both as in the view). The image is cropped to the structures only when the background is transparent. The PNG and the SVG (image) are called <Mobile>_vs_<Reference>.png and .svg, without the extensions of the original files. The vector drawing has the same stem, then _reference, _mobile or _overlay. It carries the legend as text when Include legend is ticked; arrows and highlights are not drawn.

PathVibViz

The toolbar has Save PNG, a PNG with a transparent background cropped to the molecule, and SVG (vector) with a list for its look (Gradient, Flat or Print on white). SVG (path) draws several steps of the path in one picture, the first and last opaque and the others translucent; see The view. There is no SVG (image). The vector drawings leave out ghost centres and measurements. The buttons are off until a file is open. The names carry the step, for example <file>_view_step3.png.

IntCoords

The toolbar has only SVG (vector) and a list for its look (Gradient, Flat or Print (white)); there is no PNG and no SVG (image). The drawing has the atoms, the solid bonds, the declared and suggested bonds as dashed lines, and the labels as text. The halo around a selected atom is not drawn. The file is <file>_view.svg.

MolBuild

MolBuild saves the picture of its 2D drawing, not of the 3D pane; see Export 2D images.

items.title: What it does
items.text: You turn, move and zoom the molecule in the 3D view with the mouse or with your fingers. The gestures are the same in all seven tools that have a 3D view. Only the way back to the starting view differs from tool to tool.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Turn the molecule: press the left mouse button on the view and drag. The molecule follows the pointer as if you held it in a ball. On a touch screen, drag with one finger.
  2. Move the molecule across the view: drag with the right or the middle mouse button. On a touch screen, drag two fingers together.
  3. Zoom: turn the mouse wheel. Each step changes the distance by about 12 %. Scrolling down moves the molecule away. On a touch screen, pinch two fingers together or apart.
  4. Go back to the starting view with the control of your tool, listed in the notes below.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The right button does not open a menu

On the 3D view the right button is used to move the molecule, so the browser's own menu does not appear there.

A touch on the view never scrolls the page

The view takes every touch that starts on it. To scroll the page, or to use a panel, touch outside the view.

MolBuild has two views

In MolBuild these gestures work on the 3D pane. The 2D drawing has its own navigation; see Navigate the canvas.

items.title: In this tool
items.text:
MolViz

The button ⌂ Reset at the top right corner of the view brings back the starting orientation and fits the molecule into the view. See also Center and orient, which turns the molecule to its principal axes.

OrbViz

There is no reset button. Press the R key, when no window is open, to bring back the starting orientation, position and distance. Hold the pointer over an atom to see its label with its number and its coordinates in Å.

RassiViz

RassiViz has no button and no key that resets the view.

GeoDiff

The corner button ⟲ view brings both structures back to the starting orientation and fits them into the view. The view carries a legend at the bottom left; see The legend. When you pick the endpoints of a backbone path or the atom of a macrocycle, a click on an atom with the left button selects it, and a drag still rotates.

PathVibViz

The button ⌂ Reset at the top right corner of the view brings back the starting orientation. All steps of the path are drawn in one set of axes; see The view.

IntCoords

The toolbar button Reset view brings back the starting orientation, position and zoom. A click on an atom, without moving the pointer more than a few pixels, selects it or clears it; a drag rotates. Hold the pointer over an atom to see its label and its coordinates in Å. See The 3D view.

MolBuild

The 3D pane has the button ⟲ Reset that brings back the starting orientation and fits the molecule. See The 3D pane.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Each tool is one page that holds all its own code. Once a page is open, it needs no network to work: you can read your files, compute, draw and save with the connection off. This page says how to get the tools ready for a place with no network, such as a classroom or a train.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open the launcher on the published OPAL site, while you are online.
  2. Look for the line of text in the title area at the top of the launcher, below the words Orbitals, Plotting, Analysis and Layout. It says how many of the pages are available offline, for example 1 of 9 pages are available offline.
  3. Press Save for offline use in that line. The launcher saves the other pages in the browser, and the line changes to All 9 pages are available offline.
  4. From then on, open the launcher, or any tool, at the same address with the connection off. The saved copy is used.
  5. If you add the site to the home screen of an iPhone or iPad, or install it as an app, the launcher saves the missing pages by itself the first time it opens online.
Planned image: the top of the launcher with the line All 9 pages are available offline., and the card of Colab marked Needs a network connection.; file common-offline.png.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Only the nine pages are saved

The copy holds the launcher and the eight tools. The pages of this guide are not part of it: read them online, or print the ones you need.

The offline copy works only on the published site

Saving needs the site to be served over https. A page opened as a file from your own disk has no offline copy to save, and no status line, because it is already a local file. The saving feature is not available there.

What still needs a network

The card OpenMolcas on Colab runs a notebook on Google's servers, so it is marked Needs a network connection. when you are offline, and cannot be opened. The links to the literature in the citation windows also need a connection.

Updates are never forced

When newer files are published, the launcher shows Update available with the tool names and versions, and an Update now button. Until you press it, the saved copy stays as it is. The update replaces all the files or none, and the page reloads. If it fails, nothing was replaced, and you can try again with a steadier connection.

The browser decides how long the copy lasts

A browser may remove the saved files of a site when it needs space. If the line at the top of the launcher no longer says all the pages are available, press Save for offline use again while you are online.

items.title: What it does
items.text: All the tools that read a file offer two ways in: a button that opens your system's file picker, and drag and drop. This page describes what they have in common. Which file types each tool reads, and what it does with them, is on the tool's own page, linked below. The file is read inside the page, in your browser. It is not sent anywhere.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press the button that loads a file. Its name depends on the tool. It is Load File in MolViz and PathVibViz, Open File in OrbViz, Open .h5 in RassiViz, Open XYZ in IntCoords, ⬆ Load in MolBuild, and Reference and Mobile in GeoDiff. In CSFsCalc, click the box Drop .xyz file here or click to browse.
  2. Choose the file in the picker of your system.
  3. Or drag the file from your file manager onto the tool, and let go when the drop text appears.
  4. The name of the file appears in the tool, and the molecule in the view. Read the message of the tool: it says what it found, or why it refused.
Planned image: a tool with a file being dragged over the 3D view and the drop text visible; file common-opening-files.png.

items.title: In this tool
items.text: Tool Picker Where you can drop What a drop does CSFsCalc the box Drop .xyz file here or click to browse the same box reads the first file; .xyz only GeoDiff Reference and Mobile the 3D view the first file goes to the Reference if that is empty, otherwise to the Mobile, replacing it IntCoords Open XYZ the 3D view reads the first file MolBuild ⬆ Load nowhere MolBuild has no drag and drop MolViz Load File the 3D view reads the first file OrbViz Open File the 3D view reads the first file PathVibViz Load File the 3D view reads all the files you drop, so a file and its companion can go together RassiViz Open .h5 the 3D view reads the first file, if its name ends in .h5 or .hdf5; any other name gives the message Please drop an .h5 or .hdf5 file

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
MolBuild has no drag and drop, on purpose

MolBuild is for building molecules from scratch. It opens a file only to modify it, so the ⬆ Load button is the one way in. MolBuild does not read a file you drop on it.

On an iPhone or an iPad the picker shows every file

On a computer the picker offers only the types the tool can read. On an iPhone or iPad, the tools switch this filter off, because the system would otherwise grey out the files it cannot match to a type. You can pick any file; if the tool cannot read it, it says so in its message.

items.title: What it does
items.text: When a tool saves a file (an image, a table, an XYZ file, a GIF, a saved state), a computer puts it in the downloads folder of the browser. An iPhone or iPad does it differently: the tools open the share sheet of iOS, and you choose there where the file goes. This page tells you what to expect, so a save that needs one more tap does not look like a failure.
path: Save files on iPhone and iPad

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press the button of the tool that saves, for example an export button.
  2. The share sheet of iOS opens, with the file ready to send.
  3. Choose Save to Files, or another destination, such as AirDrop or an app. The sheet is also where you can rename the file: the tools do not ask for a name first.
  4. If you change your mind, close the sheet. The tool takes this as a cancel and shows no error.

For an animated GIF, which the tool needs time to build, the save has two steps:

  1. Start the GIF and wait until the tool says the GIF is ready.
  2. Press the save button of the tool again: in MolViz the window that opens says Save GIF and Discard. The share sheet opens on this second tap.
Planned image: the share sheet of an iPad over a tool, with Save to Files visible; file common-saving-on-ios.png.
path: Save files on iPhone and iPad

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A save can be refused: tap the button again

iOS lets a page open the share sheet only straight after a tap. If something else happens in between (you switch to another app, or you wait a long time), iOS refuses. The tool then says that it could not save and that nothing was saved. Press the save button again and do not leave the page before the sheet appears.

Why the GIF needs a second tap

Building a GIF can take longer than iOS allows between your tap and the share sheet. So the tool keeps the finished GIF and waits for a new tap. Until you tap, the GIF is held in memory; Discard frees it.

The file name comes from the tool

On iOS the tools propose a name themselves, usually from the molecule or the file you loaded. Change it in the share sheet if you want another. The question about the name that a computer may ask is not asked here.

Nothing is saved without a button

A tool writes a file only when you press a button that says so. CSFsCalc writes no file at all. See What is stored in your browser.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Most tools have a panel on the left and a panel on the right of the 3D view, with the controls. A small tab on the edge of each panel hides it, so the molecule gets the whole width of the screen, and shows it again. This helps most on a phone or a tablet, where the panels would cover much of the view.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Find the tab at the middle of the left or right edge of the view. It carries a small arrow: ‹ at the left edge when the left panel is open, › when it is hidden. The right edge shows the opposite arrows.
  2. Press or tap the tab. The panel slides away and the view widens to the freed space.
  3. Press the tab again to bring the panel back.
  4. On a phone, both panels start hidden. Opening one hides the other, so only one panel is on the screen at a time.
Planned image: a tool on a laptop with both panels open and the two tabs circled, and the same tool on a phone with the left panel open; file common-side-panels.png.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Hiding a panel changes nothing else

The values of the controls in a hidden panel stay as they are, and the tool keeps computing from them. Only what you see changes. A tap on a tab never rotates or picks anything in the view behind it.

The state is not kept

Whether a panel is open is not stored and is not part of a saved state or session. After a reload, a laptop shows both panels and a phone shows none. Turning a phone sideways, or changing the size of a browser window, never opens or closes a panel by itself.

CSFsCalc has no side panels

CSFsCalc is a single form with no 3D view, so it has no panels and no tabs. The launcher has none either. The other seven tools have them. This is by design.

In MolBuild the right tab is for the 3D pane

MolBuild draws on the left and shows the 3D result on the right. Its right tab controls the 3D pane, not a column of controls.

A tab with a name for screen readers

The tab is a button. A screen reader reads it as Hide left panel or Show left panel, and Hide right panel or Show right panel, according to its state.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Spin turns the molecule round and round, so that you see it from every side. Tilt swings it to and fro around its present orientation, which gives an impression of depth without a full turn. They are useful in a lecture, where a molecule that moves is easier to read than one that stands still. Three tools have them: MolViz, OrbViz and RassiViz.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Find the buttons Spin and Tilt in the toolbar. Each opens a small menu.
  2. Open Spin and choose an axis: Y — Vertical, X — Horizontal or Z — Depth. The molecule starts to turn about that axis: Y runs up the screen, X across it, and Z points at you. A full turn takes about 2.5 seconds.
  3. Or open Tilt and choose an axis. The molecule swings about 20° to each side of the orientation it had, and back. One full swing takes about 2 seconds.
  4. To stop, choose ■ Stop in either menu, or choose the same entry again.
  5. To change the axis, or to change from spin to tilt, choose another entry. Only one motion runs at a time, and the button of the one that runs is highlighted.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The speed and the swing are fixed

There is no control for the speed or for the size of the swing. The times above are for a screen that redraws 60 times a second. For a movie with another speed or amplitude, use the animated GIF, where you set both.

Turn the molecule while it moves

In OrbViz and RassiViz you can still drag the molecule with the mouse during a motion. A tilt then swings around the new orientation, and a spin carries on from it.

A new file stops the motion

In OrbViz and RassiViz, opening another file stops a running motion. Choose it again afterwards. A motion also needs a molecule: with no file open, the menus do nothing in these two tools.

Recording a GIF pauses the motion

While a GIF is recorded the motion is paused, and when the recording ends it goes on. The GIF has its own choice of motion and axis, independent of these menus.

items.title: In this tool
items.text:
MolViz, OrbViz, RassiViz

The two menus are the same, with the same five entries each, next to the button for the animated GIF.

GeoDiff, PathVibViz, IntCoords, MolBuild

These tools have no Spin or Tilt menu, and the view does not move by itself. GeoDiff can still record a spin or a tilt as an animated GIF; see Export an animated GIF. PathVibViz animates the molecule in a different way: it plays the steps of a path, or the swing of a vibration; see Vibrations.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The tools and the launcher open in a dark theme. A Theme button, near the right end of the toolbar, switches to a light theme, which reads better on a projector or in a bright room, and back again.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press Theme (the round yin-yang icon). The page turns light.
  2. Press it again to return to the dark theme.
  3. The button's hint, which you see when you hold the pointer over it, names the theme you would switch to.

When the page is light, the address in the browser's address bar ends with #theme=light. That ending is how the page remembers your choice. When you go back to the dark theme, the ending disappears.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The choice follows you from page to page

While the theme is light, the OPAL button of a tool and the Launch buttons of the launcher carry the ending with them. A tool you open from the launcher, and the launcher you reach from a tool, stay light. See Back to the launcher.

A reload keeps the theme, a new visit does not

Nothing is stored in the browser: no cookie, no saved setting. Reloading the page keeps the ending in the address and so keeps the theme. Typing the address of the tool without the ending, or opening a bookmark made while the page was dark, opens the dark theme. To start light, bookmark the page while it is light.

Plots and windows follow

The plots drawn by a tool, such as the spectrum window of RassiViz or the plots of PathVibViz, are redrawn in the colours of the new theme when you switch.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Next to the name of each tool in the toolbar, a small badge shows the version of that tool, for example v0.87. The launcher has one as well, for the launcher itself. Each tool has its own number: the tools are not released together, so two tools of the same suite can show different numbers.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Look at the toolbar, just after the tool's name and · OpenMolcas. The badge is the small framed text there.
  2. For a second place to read it, press ⓘ at the right end of the toolbar. The window How to cite shows the name of the tool and the same version under it.
  3. When you write to someone about a problem, or cite a tool, give this number. It tells which copy of the tool you used.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Pages say which version they were checked on

Each page of this guide carries the version of the tool it was checked on. If your badge shows a later number, a button or a label may have moved or changed; the page is still a good guide to what the tool does.

The badge is text only

Pressing it does nothing. The hint under the pointer reads the tool's name followed by version.

An installed offline copy can be older than the site

If you saved the tools for offline use, the badge shows the version of the saved copy. The launcher tells you when a newer set is published.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The OPAL tools keep very little in your browser. This page lists everything they keep, so you know what survives closing the tab and what does not. The files you load are never uploaded anywhere and never copied into the browser's storage: they are read in the page, and they are gone when you close it or load another.

items.title: How
items.text:
Read the list for the tool you use.

  1. MolViz keeps two things in the browser's storage: your presets and your sessions. They stay until you delete them or clear the data of the site. They belong to one browser on one computer, at one address: the same tool opened from another address or in another browser does not see them.
  2. The launcher keeps one note, and only after you have saved the tools for offline use: which versions of the files that copy was made from. It uses the note to tell you when newer files are published. The saved files themselves are kept in the browser's cache for the site.
  3. Every other tool keeps nothing: not the file you loaded, not the settings, not the view. Close the tab and you start from the beginning.
  4. The theme is not stored in any tool: it is carried by the address. See Light and dark theme.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
To keep your work, save a file

A tool writes a file only when you press a button that says so: an image, a table, a GIF, an XYZ or a saved state. Several tools can Save State into a small file and Load State from it later; that file is yours, and you can send it to a colleague. See the page of each tool.

Clearing the browser's data deletes presets and sessions

Clearing the site's data, or using a private window that is closed afterwards, removes the presets and sessions of MolViz. If they matter to you, use Export JSON in the Sessions window to keep a copy as a file.

Nothing is sent over the network

The tools do not send your files or your settings anywhere. The only request the page makes by itself is the launcher's check of the list of published versions, and only on the published site. The links to the literature and to Colab open other sites only when you click them.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Many buttons open a window on top of the page: the settings of the atoms, the presets and sessions of MolViz, the animated GIF, the spectrum, the analysis of GeoDiff, and the How to cite window of every tool. A window hides what is behind it until you close it. They close the same way, and the keyboard works in them in nearly the same way; the differences are below.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press the button that opens the window.
  2. To close it, press Esc. The How to cite window closes with a click on the dark area around it too.
  3. When the window closes, the keyboard focus goes back to the button you used to open it, so you can press Enter to open it again.
  4. If one window opens another, Esc closes the one on top, and a second press closes the one below.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Tab stays inside the window

In GeoDiff, MolBuild, MolViz, OrbViz, PathVibViz and RassiViz, Tab moves from control to control inside the open window only, and goes round from the last to the first. Shift+Tab goes the other way. You cannot reach the page behind a window by keyboard until you close it.

In MolViz the shortcuts are off while a window is open

Keys such as Delete act on the molecule only when no window is open. Typing a name in a window cannot delete a bond behind it.

CSFsCalc and IntCoords have only the citation window

These two tools have no other window. Their How to cite window closes with Esc, with Close, or with a click on the dark area around it, and returns the focus to the button you used. It does not hold Tab inside; if you press Tab in it, the focus can move to the page behind.

items.title: Tools
items.text: Every tool has a folder of short pages: an overview first, then one page for each feature. Things the tools share are not repeated in each folder; they are on the pages of Common to all tools.

items.title: The tools
items.text:
Build and look at a molecule:

  • MolBuild: draw a molecule, give it a 3D geometry, save it as an XYZ file.
  • MolViz: look at one geometry as balls and sticks, and measure on it.

Prepare a calculation:

  • CSFsCalc: count the configuration state functions of a RASSCF active space.
  • IntCoords: write the internal coordinates block that SLAPAF needs for a transition-state search.

Read the results:

  • OrbViz: orbitals, electron densities and density differences.
  • RassiViz: states, transition densities and the absorption spectrum from RASSI.
  • PathVibViz: optimisations, reaction paths, conical intersections and vibrations.
  • GeoDiff: compare two structures.

The entry page:

  • The launcher: one card for each tool.

items.title: Not a tool of OPAL
items.text: Running OpenMolcas in Colab is a notebook that runs OpenMolcas for you in the browser, so that you can produce files for the tools above without installing anything.

items.title: What it is for
items.text:
CSFsCalc tells you how big a RASSCF calculation will be before you submit it. You describe the active space (how many orbitals in RAS1, RAS2 and RAS3, how many electrons, how many holes and excitations you allow) and the tool counts the configuration state functions (CSFs) and the Slater determinants. If you also load a molecule and pick a basis set, it counts the basis functions and estimates the memory.

Open CSFsCalc. Nothing is calculated by OpenMolcas: the tool only counts. It updates at every keystroke, so there is no button to press. It writes no file and sends nothing anywhere.

On a fresh page the values are 4, 6 and 4 orbitals, 7 α and 7 β electrons, and limits of 2 holes and 2 excitations. Results then reads RAS(14, 2, 2; 4, 6, 4) with 96 495 CSFs.

The page has these parts, from the top:

  • the toolbar: the back link, the version badge, the Theme button;
  • a short paragraph that says the tool counts CSFs and Slater determinants with the Weyl–Paldus formula;
  • RAS Space Orbitals: the orbitals in RAS1, RAS2 and RAS3;
  • Electrons & Constraints: the α and β electrons, the holes in RAS1 and the excitations in RAS3;
  • Results: electrons, spin, the three counts and the RAS notation;
  • Molecule & Basis Set (optional): an XYZ file, the basis set, the number of roots, the memory estimate;
  • the Show CSF Distribution Details button;
  • a line with the author's name and the year;
  • at the foot, a box on the RAS notation and the list of references.

Three of these sections fold when you click their title: RAS Space Orbitals, Electrons & Constraints and Molecule & Basis Set. How a folding section works is explained once, in Parts of a tool page. Results does not fold.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
The CSF count is a sum over the ways of sharing the electrons among RAS1, RAS2 and RAS3. This view lists those ways with the number of CSFs each one contributes. You use it to see which excitation level makes most of your space.

The CSFs of each line are counted exactly, with the Weyl–Paldus formula, and so is their sum, the CSF count in Results. The determinant counts are not of the same kind: the combinatorial one is exact within the RAS limits, and the GUGA-adapted one is an approximation made from the CSF count (Determinant counts).

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Set the orbitals, the electrons and the limits.
  2. Click Show CSF Distribution Details, the button below the Molecule & Basis Set section. A box titled CSF Contributions by Electron Distribution opens, and the button now reads Hide CSF Distribution Details.
  3. Read a line such as (N1=6, N2=7, N3=1) → 15456 CSFs. N1, N2 and N3 are the numbers of electrons in RAS1, RAS2 and RAS3; the number after the arrow is the CSFs of your spin for that sharing.
  4. Work out the holes and excitations: holes in RAS1 are twice the RAS1 orbitals minus N1, and excitations are N3. With 4 RAS1 orbitals, N1=6 means 2 holes.
  5. Change any field. The lines follow, whether the box is open or not.
  6. Click Hide CSF Distribution Details to close the box.

With the starting values the box has nine lines. The largest is (N1=6, N2=6, N3=2) with 54 544 CSFs, a little over half of the 96 495 in total. The smallest is (N1=8, N2=6, N3=0) with 175 CSFs: RAS1 full, RAS3 empty, only RAS2 active.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The lines add up to the CSF count

The numbers of all the lines add up to Configuration State Functions in Results. A sharing that gives no CSF is not listed.

An empty box is not a fault

If your electrons cannot be placed within the limits, the box shows only its title: there are no lines because the count is 0.

The lines are written without separators

In the box the numbers are written as plain digits (15456), with no gap between groups of three digits, unlike the cards in Results.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
Under the CSF count, Results gives two numbers of Slater determinants: Slater Determinants (Combinatorial) and Slater Determinants (GUGA-adapted). They are different kinds of number. Read them when you need a determinant figure rather than a CSF figure.

How exact each number is differs. The CSF count is exact: the tool computes it with the Weyl–Paldus formula. The combinatorial determinant count is exact within the RAS limits you set. The GUGA-adapted determinant count is approximate.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Set the orbitals, the electrons and the limits (Limit holes and excitations).
  2. Read Slater Determinants (Combinatorial). It counts the ways to place the α electrons and the β electrons independently in the orbitals, keeping to your limits (at most the chosen holes in RAS1, at most the chosen electrons in RAS3). It does not select a spin: it counts determinants of every spin that has that α − β difference. With no limits it would be the number of ways to choose the α electrons among all the orbitals times the number of ways to choose the β electrons.
  3. Read Slater Determinants (GUGA-adapted). This is an estimate made from the CSF count, not a count of its own. For a singlet it is twice the number of CSFs plus the square root of that number; for any other spin it is the number of CSFs times the multiplicity.
  4. Read the box About the Two Determinant Counts under the cards. It says the same in words and cites the references.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The CSF count is the one to compare

The note in the tool says that programs like OpenMolcas work mainly with the compact CSF basis. The CSF count is therefore the number to set against the size of a CI space; use the determinant counts when you need a determinant figure.

The two counts are not expected to agree

With the starting values (a singlet) the combinatorial count is 369 712 and the GUGA-adapted estimate 193 301; for 8 α and 6 β (a triplet) they are 273 217 and 398 475. Neither is always the larger. The tool shows these counts with a small gap between groups of three digits and no comma.

items.text: You give the number of α and β electrons in the active space. Their sum is the number of active electrons, and their difference sets the spin: CSFsCalc counts the configurations of the lowest spin that those two numbers allow. Only the active electrons go here; the electrons of the inactive orbitals are not counted.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open CSFsCalc.
  2. Under Electrons & Constraints, type the number of Alpha Electrons and Beta Electrons. The tool starts with 7 and 7.
  3. Read the Total Electrons card: the sum, and under it the two numbers, for example (7 α, 7 β).
  4. Read the Spin State card. It shows S as half the difference between the two numbers, with one decimal, and under it the name of the multiplicity.
  5. To change the spin, change the difference. For 14 electrons as a triplet, type 8 and 6.
  6. Read Results. The counts are those of the spin shown on the card.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Compare two spin states

With the starting values, 7 α and 7 β give 96 495 CSFs (singlet). Change to 8 α and 6 β and the tool gives 132 825 CSFs (triplet), for the same orbitals and limits. On the screen the tool shows these counts with a small gap and no comma; see Read the results.

The spin is fixed by the difference

You cannot ask for a singlet with 8 α and 6 β electrons: the tool always counts the lowest spin allowed by the difference. Swapping the two numbers changes nothing (6 and 8 gives the same results as 8 and 6).

Empty fields count as 0

An empty field is read as 0. If there are more electrons than the orbitals can hold, every count is 0.

items.title: What it does
items.text: You give CSFsCalc a molecule and a basis set, and it counts the contracted basis functions (nbas). That number is what the memory estimate needs. Only the elements of the molecule are used; the coordinates are not.
path: Load a molecule and choose a basis set

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open CSFsCalc. Find the section Molecule & Basis Set.
  2. Drop an XYZ file on the box Drop .xyz file here or click to browse, or click the box and choose the file (Open a file). Water is enough: 
    3
water
O   0.000   0.000   0.117
H   0.000   0.757  -0.469
H   0.000  -0.757  -0.469
  3. Check the box. It shows ✅, the file name and the number of atoms loaded ("3 atoms loaded", or "1 atom loaded" for a single atom). Under it, a chip lists each element with its count (H ×2, O), in alphabetical order, and a last chip gives the total number of atoms. Loading another file replaces the molecule.
  4. Choose a Basis Set Family. The menu groups the ANO basis sets of OpenMolcas, the Pople, Dunning (cc and aug-cc) and def2 sets. The tool starts with ANO-RCC.
  5. For an ANO family, a second menu gives the contraction level; the other families have none. The menu lists only the levels the chosen family has: ANO-RCC and ANO-L offer VDZP, VTZP, VQZP, VDZ and MB; ANO-S offers VDZP, VTZP, VDZ and MB; ANO-XS offers VDZP, VDZ and MB; ANO-R offers R0 to R3; ANO-ORCA offers pVDZ to pV5Z. When you change the family, the tool keeps your level if the new family has it. If not, it sets a default: R2 for ANO-R, pVTZ for ANO-ORCA, VTZP for the others (VDZP for ANO-XS).
  6. Read Total contracted basis functions (nbas), with the basis set named under it. For water in ANO-RCC VTZP it is 58.
  7. Read the line under the menu: it describes the basis set. A list of references with links to the papers follows; it is there even before you load a molecule.
path: Load a molecule and choose a basis set

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A load that fails clears the molecule

If the file is not an XYZ file, a message "XYZ parse error" appears, and the box returns to empty, also when a molecule was loaded before. The first line must be the number of atoms, the second a comment. A file with fewer than three lines, a first line that is not a number, or no readable atom line each give their own message.

The first line decides how many atoms are read

If the first line says 3 and the file holds 5 atoms, only the first 3 are read. If it says more than the file holds, the atoms present are read. A line with fewer than four columns is skipped without a message. Check the atom total in the last chip.

A lower bound, or no value

If a basis set has no data for an element, a warning "No data for: …" says nbas is a lower bound. ANO-S at VTZP has no data for hydrogen, for instance, so water gives 23. If the family has no such level, the tool says "Basis set data not available for this combination." and shows no value. The level menu offers only the levels a family has, so you meet this message only if the data lack a level the menu offers.

iPhone and iPad

On an iPhone or iPad the file picker offers every file, not only those ending in .xyz.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Once a molecule and a basis set are in place, CSFsCalc gives an order-of-magnitude estimate of the memory a RASSCF calculation needs, term by term. It uses the active space you entered, the number of roots and the choice between Cholesky and conventional integrals.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Set the active space: the orbitals, the electrons and the limits (Set the RAS orbitals, Set the electrons and the spin). The estimate follows every change you make there.
  2. In Molecule & Basis Set, load a molecule and choose a basis set (Load a molecule and choose a basis set). The estimate appears only when nbas is above 0: with no molecule, or with a combination that has no data, there is none.
  3. Type the Number of Roots (States). The tool starts with 1.
  4. Set the Cholesky Decomposition switch. On, it reads Enabled (recommended); off, Disabled (conventional).
  5. Read the box. Its title gives the mode and the roots, for example Est. RAM — Cholesky/CD, 1 root (×1.5 safety), and the total in GB stands beside it. A line under the title says what the total contains: the terms listed below it, times 1.5.
  6. Read the line with the inactive orbitals, for example 1 inactive orb. (neutral, 8 active e⁻). It comes from the electrons of the molecule and the active electrons you entered.
  7. Read the terms. With Cholesky: 3-idx tensor (RAM peak) and K-matrix buffer. Conventional: AO 2e integrals and Half-transform buffer. Both: Active MO integrals, CI vectors (all roots), Density matrices and Orbital working arrays. With Cholesky, one more line, Chol. vectors (disk) — not in the total, shows the disk space, which is outside the figure.

For water (58 functions in ANO-RCC VTZP) with 0, 6 and 0 orbitals, 4 α and 4 β electrons and both limits at 0, the tool gives 0.004 GB, with one inactive orbital and 0.008 GB of Cholesky vectors on disk.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Read it as a size class

The tool itself says to take the figure with a grain of salt. It does not use symmetry, which can lower the integral count, and it assumes the number of Cholesky vectors is five times nbas. GB means 10⁹ bytes here. Terms below 0.001 GB are shown as < 0.001 GB.

The charge is a guess

The tool does not know the charge. It tries 0, −1, +1, −2 and +2, in this order, and takes the first for which the inactive electrons come in pairs. A neutral molecule with an even number of electrons and 9 active electrons is therefore shown as charge -1. If no charge from −2 to +2 works, for example with more active electrons than the molecule has, the tool warns "No charge from −2 to +2 gives a valid inactive-electron count" and uses an approximate count.

Unknown elements

An element the tool has no atomic number for gives the warning "No Z for: …", and the inactive count may be off.

Folding the section hides the estimate

The estimate lives inside Molecule & Basis Set. Fold the section and it disappears from view; open it again and it is there.
