items.title: What it does
items.text: In a RAS calculation the electrons of RAS1 and RAS3 are not free: you allow at most a few holes in RAS1 and at most a few electrons in RAS3. These two limits decide how large the configuration space is. CSFsCalc counts the effect as you type.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open CSFsCalc.
  2. Set the orbitals and the electrons as described in Set the RAS orbitals and Set the electrons and the spin.
  3. Go to Electrons & Constraints.
  4. Set Max Holes in RAS1: the most electrons that may be missing from RAS1. One hole is one missing electron, not one missing pair.
  5. Set Max Excitations in RAS3: the most electrons that may sit in RAS3. The two limits are independent: they need not be equal, and you can allow more holes than excitations or the other way round.
  6. Read Configuration State Functions and the two determinant counts under Results. They change at every keystroke; there is no button to press.
  7. Change one limit and watch the counts. The string at the foot of Results follows as well, in the form RAS(n, l, m; i, j, k).

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A quick check

With both limits at 0, RAS1 stays full and RAS3 stays empty, so only RAS2 takes part in the counting. The number you see is then the one for a complete active space over RAS2. With the starting orbitals and electrons, RAS1 holds 8 electrons and RAS2 the other 6, in 6 orbitals: 175 CSFs.

How fast the space grows

With the starting orbitals and electrons (singlet), the CSF count is 175 for limits of 0 and 0, 7 679 for 1 and 1, 96 495 for 2 and 2, and 1 346 370 for 4 and 4. Each step in this list makes the space more than ten times larger.

Different limits

With the same starting values, 2 holes and 1 excitation give 24 815 CSFs, between the 7 679 of 1 and 1 and the 96 495 of 2 and 2. The string at the foot of Results then reads RAS(14, 2, 1; 4, 6, 4).

Empty or non-numeric fields count as 0

A field you clear is read as 0, not left out. If the counts suddenly drop, check that no field is empty.

items.title: What it does
items.text: You tell CSFsCalc how many orbitals each of the three RAS subspaces holds. RAS1 is the subspace in which you allow a few holes, RAS3 the one in which you allow a few electrons, and RAS2 the one where the electrons are free. The three numbers fix the size of the active space.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open CSFsCalc.
  2. Find the section RAS Space Orbitals.
  3. Type the number of orbitals in RAS1 Orbitals, RAS2 Orbitals and RAS3 Orbitals. Use whole numbers from 0 up.
  4. Read Results. The counts change at every keystroke.
  5. Read the string at the foot of Results. Its last three numbers are the three orbital counts you typed, in the order RAS1, RAS2, RAS3.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A complete active space

Put 0 in RAS1 Orbitals and RAS3 Orbitals and all the orbitals in RAS2 Orbitals. Every electron is then free in RAS2, and the two limits no longer matter. With 6 orbitals and 3 α and 3 β electrons, the tool gives 175 CSFs.

A field you cannot read counts as 0

An empty field, or text that is not a number, is read as 0. A decimal is cut to its whole part (4.7 becomes 4). A negative orbital count gives zero for every count. If the counts suddenly drop to 0 or to a small number, check the three fields first.

More electrons than the orbitals can hold

If the electrons do not fit in the orbitals, every count is 0. The orbitals hold two electrons each.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The Results panel shows what your active space amounts to: the number of electrons, the spin, the number of CSFs, two determinant counts and the active space in the usual RAS notation. It follows every change of the fields above it.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Change any field in RAS Space Orbitals or Electrons & Constraints. There is nothing to press.
  2. Read Total Electrons and Spin State: the sum of the α and β electrons, and the spin and multiplicity name that follow from their difference (Set the electrons and the spin).
  3. Read Configuration State Functions. This is the number of CSFs of that spin, counted with the Weyl–Paldus formula for each way of sharing the electrons among RAS1, RAS2 and RAS3 that your limits allow, and added up. The ways it adds up are listed by Show the CSF distribution.
  4. Read the two Slater Determinants counts: Determinant counts.
  5. Read the string at the foot of the panel, for example RAS(14, 2, 2; 4, 6, 4). It reads RAS(n, l, m; i, j, k): n is the total number of electrons, l the most holes in RAS1, m the most electrons in RAS3, and i, j and k the orbitals in RAS1, RAS2 and RAS3. Select it with the mouse and copy it into a report or an input comment.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What the string does not carry

The string holds the orbitals, the electrons and the two limits. It does not hold the spin, so note the multiplicity next to it.

Large counts have a small gap, not a separator

The tool shows a large count in groups of three digits with a small gap between them, for example 96 495, the same in every browser language. The gap is not a character: when you select a count and copy it, you get the digits alone (96495).

The number of roots does not change the CSF count

The count is for the space, not for the states you ask for. The number of roots only enters the memory estimate.

Notation box and references

At the foot of the page the tool repeats the meaning of the RAS notation, with an example and its reference, and lists the references for the Weyl–Paldus formula and the graphical unitary group approach (GUGA). They are reading text; nothing in them is interactive apart from the links to the papers/Wikipedia entry.

items.title: What it is for
items.text:
GeoDiff compares two molecular structures. You load a Reference, which stays fixed, and a Mobile structure. GeoDiff fits the Mobile onto the Reference and tells you how far apart they are: the RMSD, the mass-weighted distance, and the change of every bond length, bond angle and dihedral. It also gives the rotation and translation you need to move the Mobile onto the Reference in a file of your own.

Open GeoDiff. It runs in your browser. According to its own About text it works offline and reads HDF5 files without a server.

items.title: Files it reads
items.text:
• .xyz files;
  • .molden files;
  • OpenMolcas .h5 or .hdf5 files. A file that uses symmetry shows all its atoms.

The two structures may come from different kinds of file. You can compare an optimised structure from a Molden file with a geometry from an HDF5 file, for example.

The page has these parts:

  • The toolbar, from the left: the back link, the version badge, the Reference and Mobile buttons that load a structure, Swap, the Overlay and Side-by-side switch, Analysis, About, Theme, and the ⓘ button, which opens a small window on how to cite OPAL and links to this tutorial.
  • The left panel, in three sections: Structures, Appearance and Alignment.
  • The view in the middle, with the legend at the bottom left and the ⟲ view button. Before any file is loaded it shows a welcome text with the two buttons Load Reference and Load Mobile.
  • The right panel, in two sections: Display and Image export.
  • The file bar along the bottom of the page: the name of each loaded file in the colour of its structure, and the kind of file.
  • Three windows that open over the view: Analysis, with the tables and plots, About, with notes on the method, and the citation window behind ⓘ.

Sections of the side panels fold. How that works is explained once, in Parts of a tool page. The tables in the Analysis window are not folding sections.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Two plots at the foot of the Analysis window show the two series that are most useful in a figure: the bond lengths along the backbone path (the BLA profile) and the displacement of every atom. You can save each as a vector SVG, as a PNG, or as the data plus a ready gnuplot script.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load two structures and press Analysis. Scroll to the plot below the tables.
  2. Under Plot, choose BLA profile — bond length along the path or Per-atom displacement |Δ|.
  3. The preview is the picture that will be saved. The BLA profile plots the bond length against the bond index for the Reference and the Mobile, along the path of the backbone section. The displacement plot plots the distance each atom moved after the fit against its atom number in the Reference.
  4. Press ⬇ SVG for a vector file that you can scale and edit, ⬇ PNG for a bitmap of the same picture, or ⬇ gnuplot + CSV (ZIP) for an archive with the data and a gnuplot script, to restyle the figure yourself.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The files and their names

The names follow the pattern <Mobile>_vs_<Reference>_bla_profile or ..._displacement (the file names without their extensions), with .svg or .png. The ZIP is called after the same pattern, ends with _gnuplot.zip, and contains a folder with a .csv file of the data and a .gp script.

The legend

Both plots have a legend to the right of the plot area, never over a curve. The BLA profile names its two curves Reference and Mobile; the displacement plot names its one curve. The legend is in the preview, the SVG and the PNG, and the gnuplot script puts its key outside, at the right.

Print colours

Whatever theme you use, the saved plots are drawn for white paper, with darker colours than on screen. Unlike the SVG of the 3D view, which wraps a picture, the SVG of a plot is true vector graphics.

No BLA plot where the analysis gives no BLA

Where the backbone section reports no BLA, or no automatic path for a macrocycle, the plot area gives the same reason instead of a curve. Pick two endpoints, or use the displacement plot.

Two molecules with a common core

The plot title then carries the mark "core-only" and the number of atoms.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The Analysis window gathers everything GeoDiff computes about the difference between the two structures: the RMSD, how many bonds, angles and dihedrals were compared, which bonds broke or formed, and the tables and plots. It opens over the view.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the Reference and the Mobile.
  2. Press Analysis in the toolbar. The window is titled Difference analysis.
  3. Read the window from the top. Notices come first, when there are any: the atom matching box and, for two different molecules, the partial comparison; a hint about very short bonds; and, if you ticked Allow reflection and the fit needs one, the mirror-image banner.
  4. Then come the summary lines:
    • RMSD (all / heavy) in Å, and the Mass-weighted distance;
    • compared: the numbers of bonds, angles and dihedrals in the tables. A bond counts if it exists in either structure, and the angles and dihedrals are built on those bonds;
    • connectivity Δ, shown only when it is not zero: bonds that exist only in the Reference ("broken") and bonds that exist only in the Mobile ("formed");
    • rotamer flags: how many dihedrals changed by more than 30°.
  5. Further down are the backbone path, the macrocycle, the difference tables, the plot and the buttons of the report.
  6. Close the window with ✕ Close, with Esc, or by clicking outside it.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The hint about short bonds

A line in amber, "Very short bond(s)", names up to three bonds that are unusually short in either structure. It means either a bad geometry or a real multiple bond; GeoDiff cannot tell which.

Empty or refused

With fewer than two structures the window asks you to load them. If the two have different numbers of atoms and no common core can be found, it says so and gives the reason; see Compare on a common core.

Windows

Esc, the Tab key and the return of focus behave in this window as in the windows of the other tools; see Windows.

items.title: What it does
items.text: To compare two structures GeoDiff must know which atom of the Mobile corresponds to which atom of the Reference. By default it decides this from the atoms themselves (element, neighbours and position) and not from the line they occupy in the file. Two files of the same molecule with the atoms in a different order then still compare correctly.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load two structures of the same molecule and press Analysis in the toolbar.
  2. At the top of the window, find Match atoms by identity, not by file order. It is ticked at the start. The ⓘ button next to it opens a short explanation.
  3. Read the box below it. If the atoms are in the same order in both files it says "file order confirmed". If they are not, it says "correspondence SOLVED", how many atoms sit on a different line, and that the match was checked to preserve elements and bonds. It also shows the list that mort.py -x needs; see The mort.py command.
  4. If the two files list interchangeable atoms in a crossed order (the two hydrogens of a =CH₂, the three of a methyl), the box says so and gives the RMSD before and after pairing each atom with its real partner. The larger value came from the numbering, not from the chemistry.
  5. Where the symmetry of the molecule leaves two or more pairings equally good, an amber box lists the atoms concerned. The results do not depend on the choice, but do not read the label of those atoms as identifying one specific atom.
  6. To compare strictly line by line, untick the box.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
With the box unticked, a crossed pair of atoms goes unnoticed

When matching is off, GeoDiff warns "Atom-order mismatch" only if the sequence of elements differs between the files. The warning has a button, ⇄ Match atom order (match atoms by identity), that switches matching on again. Two files in which only equivalent atoms are crossed have the same element sequence, so no warning appears and the RMSD is simply large. If a value looks too big, look at this tick box first.

After a reordering

When the Mobile had to be reordered, the section Alignment offers a choice of atom order for the transformed XYZ file. All tables use the numbering of the Reference file.

A different bond tolerance can change the match

The match is worked out again when you change Bond tolerance in Display settings.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Along a chain of heavy atoms, such as a conjugated backbone, GeoDiff measures the bond-length alternation (BLA): the mean of the bonds at odd positions minus the mean of the bonds at even positions. It does this for the Reference and the Mobile and gives the change. It also measures how much the chain bends out of its mean plane. Together they show how a structure changes along the chain.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load two structures of the same molecule and press Analysis.
  2. Find Backbone path — BLA & curvature. Auto (graph diameter) is the active choice at the start: GeoDiff takes the longest of the shortest paths between heavy atoms. The path is drawn in the 3D view in gold while show is ticked.
  3. To choose the chain yourself, press Pick two endpoints. Then do any of the following:
    • click a heavy atom in the 3D view; a third click replaces the second endpoint;
    • tap one of the suggested endpoints, the chain ends that GeoDiff lists as buttons;
    • type the labels, for example C31, C52, in the text field, and press set or Enter. A label is the element symbol and the atom's number in the Reference file.
    • press clear to start again. Pressing Auto (graph diameter) also discards your endpoints.
  4. Read the result under the path. It gives the number of atoms in the path, the path linearity, BLA (ref / mob) in Å, ΔBLA, and a table with the bond lengths along the path. Below it are the out-of-plane RMS and max of the chain in Å and its end-to-end bend in degrees, each for the Reference, the Mobile and the difference.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Heavy atoms only

A hydrogen cannot be an endpoint. GeoDiff says "Pick heavy atoms only". If you pick two atoms that are not joined through heavy atoms it says so, and no path is drawn.

When no BLA is reported

GeoDiff reports a BLA only where it means something: along an open chain, or around a ring with an even number of members. For a path through a ring of odd size, through fused rings, or through more than one separate ring system it says "BLA not reported — outside its valid domain" and gives the reason. The curvature is still reported for a path of three atoms or more. The per-bond differences are in the difference tables.

Low linearity

When the linearity is below 0.5 the path doubles back on itself, and the end-to-end bend is not a useful measure. Use the out-of-plane RMS and maximum instead.

No automatic path for some ring molecules

If the molecule has a ring around its centre, GeoDiff does not choose a path by itself: it says "the molecule has a ring around its centre" and points to the macrocycle analysis. Pick the endpoints yourself to define a chain anyway. Your endpoints are kept when you load another Mobile, and are forgotten when the Reference changes.

The profile as a plot

The bond lengths along the path are also available as a plot you can save; see Analysis plots.

items.title: What it does
items.text: You can give each structure its own colour and its own opacity, and choose which one is drawn in front. When the two overlap, a transparent structure lets the other one show through, so you can see where they differ.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the Reference and the Mobile.
  2. In the left panel, find the section Structures. Click the colour swatch of a place and pick a colour. At the start the Reference is red-pink and the Mobile is blue. The colour is also used for the file name in the file bar and for the legend.
  3. In the section Appearance, move Reference opacity and Mobile opacity. The values run from 0.10 to 1.00. At the start the Reference is 1.00 (solid) and the Mobile is 0.65.
  4. Under Render in front, choose Mobile in front or Reference in front. The structure in front hides what lies behind it where it is solid, and shows it through where it is transparent.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Which one to make transparent

Make the structure in front the more transparent one. If both are solid (1.00), the one in front hides the other wherever they coincide, and you see only the places where they differ.

The colours are used elsewhere

The same colours appear in the file bar, the legend, and the exported images of the 3D view. The plots in the Analysis window do not follow them: their curves keep the starting red-pink and blue (and green for the displacement), and the exported plots use darker versions of these that print well on white paper.

items.title: What it does
items.text: When the two molecules are not identical but share a scaffold and differ by one to three substituents (an –NH₂ against an –OH, for example), GeoDiff compares only the atoms they have in common. Everything it reports is then restricted to that common core, and says so.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the two molecules.
  2. A window titled "These are not the same molecule" opens. It states the number of atoms in the core and what percentage of each molecule that is, and names what differs: for example "–NH₂ (3 atoms) on Reference ↔ –OH (2 atoms) on Mobile, attached at core atom C11". Press Understood.
  3. Press Analysis. The box near the top, "Partial comparison on a common core", repeats the description and states that the match was checked.
  4. Read the numbers. Wherever one appears, it carries a mark such as "core-only · 23/26 vs 23/25", which means 23 atoms of the 26 of the Reference and 23 of the 25 of the Mobile. The RMSD is labelled "core". The RMSD, the tables, the path and ring analyses, the displacement and the plots all use the core only.
  5. The 3D view still shows every atom of both molecules. Tick Superimpose Mobile → Reference as usual; the fit is made on the core.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The mort.py −x list is not given

A reordering list needs every atom to have a partner, which is not the case here. The copied mort.py command contains only the rotation and the translation, with a comment saying that the list was declined; see The mort.py command. The transformed XYZ file contains all the atoms of the Mobile, in the order of the Mobile file, and its name ends with _aligned_core.

When GeoDiff declines

If the molecules differ by more than three separate groups, a window says that the difference is out of scope. If the shared part is too small, another says that the structures are too dissimilar to compare. In both cases the section Alignment reports that the number of atoms differs, and the Analysis window adds the reason. If the connectivity was misread, change Bond tolerance in Display settings and try again.

An ambiguous core

If the core could be chosen in more than one way, an amber note says so. Do not read the atom labels of the affected part as one specific atom.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Four tables in the Analysis window list what changed, one coordinate at a time: the displacement of each atom, the bond lengths, the bond angles and the dihedrals. Each table is ranked, so the largest change comes first.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load two structures of the same molecule and press Analysis.
  2. Find Per-atom displacement (Å). Each row is an atom, named by its element and its number in the Reference file (C6 is the sixth atom), and the distance it moved after the fit.
  3. Find Bond lengths — Δr (Å). The columns are the bond, its length in the Reference (r_ref), its length in the Mobile (r_mob) and the difference Δr. A bond that exists in only one structure is marked "(broken)" or "(formed)".
  4. Find Bond angles — Δθ (°), with θ_ref, θ_mob and Δθ.
  5. Find Dihedrals — Δφ (°), with φ_ref, φ_mob and Δφ. A dihedral that changed by more than 30° carries the mark ⚑, and, where the two values fall in different classes, the change of class (for example gauche→anti).
  6. Each table shows its 15 largest rows. Click ▸ show all N below the title to see all N rows, and ▾ show top 15 to go back.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Sign of the dihedral

Dihedrals carry the sign that SLAPAF prints, and run from −180° up to but not including +180°. The value in GeoDiff, in MolBuild, in MolViz and in PathVibViz is therefore the same number for the same four atoms.

The tables follow the connectivity

A bond is a pair of atoms closer than the bond tolerance allows; see Display settings. A bond that exists in either structure is listed, and the angles and dihedrals are built from those bonds. For two different molecules, only the common core is listed, and each title carries the core mark.

The same numbers in a file

The report holds the same tables, the text version with the 20 largest rows of each, the JSON version with all rows.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Four settings change how the atoms and bonds are drawn, for both structures at once. One of them, the bond tolerance, also decides which atoms count as bonded in the analysis.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the right panel, find the section Display.
  2. Move Ball scale (0.05 to 0.60, 0.30 at the start) to change the size of the atoms.
  3. Move Bond radius (0.03 to 0.30, 0.10 at the start) to change the thickness of the bonds.
  4. Move Bond tolerance (1.00 to 1.60, 1.25 at the start). Two atoms are drawn as bonded when their distance is at most this number times the sum of their covalent radii. A larger value draws more bonds, a smaller value fewer.
  5. Tick or untick Atom outlines to draw an outline around each atom. It is ticked at the start.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The bond tolerance changes the numbers, not only the picture

The bonds that GeoDiff compares in the difference tables, the path and ring searches, and the atom matching all use the same connectivity as the drawing. When you move Bond tolerance, the Analysis window is recomputed a moment after you stop moving the slider. If a bond is missing from the tables, or an unwanted one appears, adjust the tolerance first.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The legend tells you which colour is which structure. It lists the Reference and the Mobile with their colours and the names of their files.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load at least one structure. The legend appears at the bottom left of the view, with one line for each loaded structure: a colour swatch, REF or MOB, and the full file name.
  2. Change a colour in the section Structures; the swatch in the legend follows.
  3. To see the whole molecule again after turning, zooming or moving, press ⟲ view in the corner of the view. It returns to the starting orientation and fits both structures.
  4. To keep the legend in an exported image, tick Include legend in the section Image export; see Export images. It is ticked at the start. It is also drawn into an animated GIF if the box is ticked when you record; see Export an animated GIF.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The legend is not the file bar

The file bar along the bottom of the page shortens long names and shows the kind of file. The legend always shows the whole name. Both use the colours of the structures.

items.title: What it does
items.text: GeoDiff holds two structures: the Reference, which stays fixed, and the Mobile, which is fitted onto it. This page shows how to fill, clear and exchange the two places. It accepts .xyz, .molden and OpenMolcas .h5 or .hdf5 files.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open GeoDiff.
  2. Press Reference in the toolbar, or Load Reference in the welcome text, and choose a file. A message at the bottom of the view gives the file name and its number of atoms.
  3. Press Mobile (or Load Mobile) and choose the second file.
  4. Instead of the buttons you can drop a file on the view. The first file you drop becomes the Reference. Every file you drop after that replaces the Mobile. Drop one file at a time: when you drop several together, only the first is read.
  5. In the left panel, find the section Structures. Each place shows the colour swatch, the role, a ✕ button, and below them the file name, the formula, the number of atoms and the kind of file. Ghost atoms, if there are any, are counted there too.
  6. To empty a place, press its ✕. When both places are empty, the welcome text comes back.
  7. To exchange the roles, press Swap in the toolbar. The Mobile becomes the Reference and the other way round.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
OpenMolcas files without atomic numbers, and files with symmetry

A SLAPAF file stores nuclear charges and no atomic numbers. GeoDiff takes the elements from the charges and says so under the file name. If the file uses symmetry, GeoDiff builds the missing atoms from the symmetry operations stored in the file, so you always see the whole molecule. A line under the file name states how many atoms the file stores and how many it generates.

A file that cannot be read

GeoDiff shows a message that starts with Error:, for example "no atoms parsed" for a text file with no atoms, or "This is not an HDF5 file." for an .h5 file that is not one. The place keeps whatever it held before.

Replacing a structure resets what you picked

The endpoints you picked for the backbone path and the atom you picked for the macrocycle belong to the Reference. They are forgotten when you load another Reference, swap the roles, or clear a place. A new Mobile keeps the path endpoints.

Names in the file bar

The file bar at the bottom shows the name of each file in the colour of its structure. A long name is shortened in the middle, and the whole name appears when you hover over it or tap it. The title of the browser tab lists the names of the two files.

The ways of opening a file that all tools share are on Opening files.

items.title: What it does
items.text: For a large ring, such as a porphyrin or a chlorin, GeoDiff finds the ring and measures how it leaves its own mean plane: the saddle, the wave and the other deformations, with their amplitudes in Å. It does so for the Reference and the Mobile and gives the change.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load two structures of the same macrocycle and press Analysis.
  2. Find Macrocycle — out-of-plane modes. Auto (largest ring) is active at the start: GeoDiff takes the largest round ring that runs around the centre of the molecule. A metal at the centre is not part of the ring. While show is ticked, the ring is drawn in the 3D view in teal.
  3. To choose the ring, press Pick an atom on the ring and click one heavy atom of the ring in the 3D view. GeoDiff uses the largest ring through that atom.
  4. Read the result. It gives the number of atoms of the ring and their elements, the enclosed area in Å², the circularity for the Reference and the Mobile, and the out-of-plane RMS and maximum.
  5. Read the table of modes, with the amplitude in Å for the Reference, the Mobile and the difference: saddling / ruffling (m=2), waving (m=1), doming (m=0) and higher (m=3).

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Read the caveats under the table

The amplitudes come from a Fourier fit of the out-of-plane displacements around the ring. The mode m=2 combines saddling and ruffling; GeoDiff does not separate them, and it is the amplitude to trust. Doming (m=0) is close to zero by construction, and waving (m=1) is partly absorbed by the plane fit, so these two are only indicative.

When no ring is found

GeoDiff says "No ring enclosing the centre was found" for a molecule without a ring around its centre, or when the ring would pass only through metal atoms. If the ring it finds looks elongated rather than round (circularity below 0.35) it suggests picking an atom yourself. If the search stopped at its limit, a note says the ring may not be the largest. If you click an atom that lies on no such ring, GeoDiff says so and keeps the previous ring.

The path analysis steps aside

For such a molecule the automatic backbone path is not chosen.

items.title: What it does
items.text: mort.py is the OpenMolcas helper that applies a rotation and a translation to the molecule stored in an HDF5 file, and can reorder its atoms. GeoDiff gives you the rotation and the translation that move the Mobile onto the Reference, in the form mort.py takes, so you can apply the same fit to an HDF5 file of your own.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the Reference and the Mobile. The values appear in the section Alignment of the left panel as soon as both are loaded; you do not need to tick Superimpose.
  2. Under mort.py −r (column-major), read the nine numbers of the rotation, listed column by column. Press copy to put them on the clipboard.
  3. Under mort.py −t (Å / bohr), read the translation in Å and in bohr. copy gives the three values in bohr, which is the unit mort.py expects.
  4. To copy a whole command, press Copy mort.py command. It has the form python mort.py input.h5 output.h5 -r … -t …. Replace the two file names with your own.
  5. When the Analysis window shows that the atoms were reordered (see Atom matching), the copied command also carries -x, followed by a list of atom numbers. With -x, the atoms of the output file are written in the order of the Reference.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The numbers on the screen are rounded

The boxes show six decimals. The copied values have ten.

A common-core comparison gives no −x

For two different molecules, a list that reorders atoms would be wrong, so GeoDiff leaves it out. The copied text then contains only -r and -t, with comment lines that say the list was declined and why. See Compare on a common core.

The −x list

The list gives, for each place of the output, the number (starting at 1) of the Mobile atom that goes there. It is not the place where each Mobile atom goes. mort.py rotates and translates first and reorders afterwards, as GeoDiff does.

items.title: What it does
items.text: GeoDiff can draw the two structures on top of each other (Overlay) or next to each other (Side-by-side). Overlay shows how they differ in the same space. Side-by-side lets you inspect each one without the other in the way.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the Reference and the Mobile.
  2. In the toolbar, press Overlay or Side-by-side. The one that is active is highlighted. At the start it is Overlay.
  3. In Overlay, both structures are drawn with the coordinates of their files. If the two files use different positions and orientations, the structures will not coincide. Tick Superimpose Mobile → Reference in the Alignment section to move the Mobile onto the Reference; see Superimpose the structures.
  4. In Side-by-side, the Reference goes to the left and the Mobile to the right, along the horizontal axis of the view, with a gap that grows with the size of the molecules. If Superimpose is ticked, the Mobile keeps the orientation it has after the fit.
  5. Rotate, move and zoom the view as in Navigate the 3D view. Pressing ⟲ view fits both structures into the view again.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The arrows of the displacement are drawn in Overlay only

The arrows of Show the displacement need the two structures in the same space. In Side-by-side they are not drawn. The heat-map works in both.

The view is refitted when you change the mode

Switching between the two modes fits the camera to the new arrangement, so both structures stay in view. Colours and opacity are kept; see Colours and opacity.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The report saves the result of the comparison in a file, as plain text for reading or as JSON for a script. It holds the same numbers as the Analysis window.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load two structures and open the Analysis window.
  2. At the foot of the tables, press Download report (.txt) for a text file, or .json for a JSON file.
  3. The file is called geodiff_<Mobile>_vs_<Reference>, with the extension .txt or .json.
  4. The text report starts with a line naming the version of GeoDiff. The two file names follow, after the notice about the domain when only a common core was compared. Then come, in this order: the RMSD, the mass-weighted distance, the determinant of the fit, the numbers of compared bonds, angles and dihedrals, any atom-order warning, the backbone path with its BLA and curvature, the macrocycle, and then the 20 largest rows of the tables of displacement, bonds, angles and dihedrals. The JSON file holds the complete tables.
Planned image: the text report opened in an editor next to the buttons of the Analysis window. File geodiff-report.png.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The domain comes first

When only the common core of two different molecules was compared, the text report says so in its first lines, with the number of atoms of the core and what differs. If a comparison was declined, the reason is written there too.

Nothing to save

The buttons give "No analysis to export" if the two structures cannot be compared.

For saving files on an iPhone or iPad, see Saving files on iOS.

items.title: What it does
items.text: After the fit, each atom of the Mobile sits a certain distance from its partner in the Reference. GeoDiff can draw that displacement in the view, either as arrows or by colouring the atoms, so you see at once where the structures differ.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the Reference and the Mobile and tick Superimpose Mobile → Reference in the section Alignment. The displacement is only available while the Mobile is superimposed.
  2. In the right panel, find the section Display and tick Show displacement (aligned).
  3. Under Mode, choose:
    • Arrows (Mob→Ref): one arrow from each Mobile atom to its Reference partner, coloured by the size of the displacement. Atoms that move less than 0.02 Å get no arrow.
    • Heat-map: the atoms of the Mobile are recoloured from blue (the smallest displacement) to red (the largest displacement of this pair).
  4. For the numbers behind the picture, open the ranked list Per-atom displacement in the Analysis window.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Arrows need the Overlay view

Arrows connect atoms that sit in the same space, so they are drawn only in Overlay; see Overlay or side by side. The heat-map also works in Side-by-side.

Atoms without a partner

Ghost atoms, and atoms outside the common core of two different molecules, have no displacement: they get no arrow and no value.

items.title: What it does
items.text: GeoDiff finds the rotation and translation that bring the Mobile as close as possible to the Reference (a best fit by the Kabsch method) and tells you how close that is. The numbers are there as soon as both structures are loaded. The tick box only decides whether the Mobile is also moved in the view.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the Reference and the Mobile.
  2. In the left panel, find the section Alignment. Under the tick boxes it shows the results: RMSD (all), RMSD (heavy) (heavy atoms, that is all but hydrogen), Mass-weighted distance in Å and in bohr, and det(R), the determinant of the rotation.
  3. Tick Superimpose Mobile → Reference to draw the Mobile in its fitted position. It is unticked at the start, and it stays disabled until both structures are loaded and have the same atoms to compare.
  4. To find out whether the Mobile is the mirror image of the Reference, tick Allow reflection (detect mirror). When the best fit then needs a reflection, a warning appears in the section Alignment and a red banner "Enantiomer / mirror image" at the top of the Analysis window. det(R) is then −1.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The mass-weighted distance

It is the straight-line distance between the two structures when every atom is counted by its mass: the square root of the sum of mass times squared displacement, divided by the total mass. It is the quantity SLAPAF prints for a step of an IRC or MEP path, in bohr, so you can compare two points of a path with the step of the run. SLAPAF reports the arc length, which is slightly longer when the path is bent. A line under the value says where the masses come from: the Reference file when it holds them, otherwise the masses of the most abundant isotope.

With Allow reflection ticked, the fit itself can change

By default the fit is a proper rotation, so a mirror image gives a large RMSD and det(R) stays at +1. With Allow reflection ticked, GeoDiff may fit a reflection, and the RMSD then refers to the reflected Mobile. Leave it unticked for ordinary comparisons and tick it only to ask whether two structures are enantiomers.

What is left out

Ghost atoms are not part of the fit and are not counted in the RMSD. When the two molecules differ by a substituent, only the common core is fitted; see Compare on a common core. The pairing of the atoms is explained in Atom matching.

items.title: What it does
items.text: GeoDiff writes the Mobile structure, after the best-fit rotation and translation, as an XYZ file. In this file the Mobile lies on the Reference, ready to be opened in another program or used as a starting geometry.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the Reference and the Mobile. You do not need to tick Superimpose.
  2. In the left panel, find the section Alignment.
  3. If the atoms of the Mobile had to be reordered (see Atom matching), a choice Transformed XYZ — atom order appears. Choose Reference's order (reordered) or Mobile's own file order. The geometry is the same; only the order of the lines differs.
  4. Press ⬇ Transformed XYZ. The file is called <Mobile>_aligned.xyz, without the extension of the original file.
  5. The file has the coordinates in Å with six decimals. Its comment line holds the version of GeoDiff, the two file names, the RMSD, the mass-weighted distance and, if the atoms were reordered, which order was used.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Two different molecules

When only the common core was compared, the file holds all atoms of the Mobile, in the order of the Mobile file, moved by the fit of the core. It is called <Mobile>_aligned_core.xyz, and its comment line states that the fit is core-only. See Compare on a common core.

Nothing to export

If the two structures cannot be fitted, the button only gives "No alignment to export".

items.title: What it is for
items.text:
IntCoords writes the Internal coordinates block of an OpenMolcas &SLAPAF transition-state search. You give it a structure that is a guess for the transition state, say which bonds form and break, and choose the reaction coordinate, the combination of internal coordinates that SLAPAF follows uphill. IntCoords builds a full set of internal coordinates around it, puts the reaction coordinate first in the list of coordinates to vary, and checks that the set is complete and independent before it lets you copy it.

Open IntCoords. It runs in your browser, holds one structure at a time, and sends nothing anywhere.

items.title: Files it reads
items.text:
• .xyz files, or XYZ text pasted into the tool. The tool carries a small example of its own, so you can try it without a file.

The page has these parts:

  • The toolbar, from the left: the back link OPAL, the version badge, Open XYZ, Example, Labels, H labels, Reset view, SVG (vector) with the menu of looks beside it, Theme and the ⓘ button, which opens a small window on how to cite OPAL and links to this tutorial.
  • The left panel, in five sections: 1 · Structure, 2 · Bonds, 3 · Reaction coordinate, Generated primitives and Advanced.
  • The view in the middle. Before a structure is loaded it shows a welcome text with the box to open a file.
  • The right panel, in two sections: Check and SLAPAF input.
  • The file bar along the bottom of the page: the name of the loaded file and its kind.

Sections of the side panels fold. How that works is explained once, in Parts of a tool page.

The usual order of work follows the numbers in the left panel: load the structure, declare the forming and breaking bonds, choose the reaction coordinate, read the result in Check, and copy the block from SLAPAF input.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The last section of the left panel, Advanced, holds three things that you seldom need: the atom from which the set of primitives is built (the root atom), the rule that swaps a nearly flat dihedral for an out-of-plane angle, and a command line that gives the same result with the Python script this tool began as.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the left panel, find the section Advanced. It starts folded.
  2. Z-matrix root atom: the menu starts at Automatic (most bonded atom). To choose another, pick an atom by name. The list of primitives and the block change.
  3. Replace near-planar dihedrals by OutOfP: ticked at the start. When a dihedral of the generated set lies within a number of degrees of 0° or of ±180°, an out-of-plane angle takes its place, and a warning names the one replaced. The number is the box below it, … when within (degrees) of 0 or ±180, 20 at the start; it takes values from 0 to 90.
  4. Equivalent command line (make_internal_coords.py) shows the command of the Python script that gives the same block, with your terms, your declared bonds, the root, the tolerance and the other settings.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Why the out-of-plane replacement

A planar centre, such as the flat CH₃ group at an SN2 transition state, puts a dihedral exactly on its ±180° wrap-around, where SLAPAF's back-transformation fails. An out-of-plane angle has no wrap-around. Untick the box only if you know you need the dihedrals.

The command line

The command line is for cross-checking against the script. If your reaction coordinate uses a primitive the script cannot add, the box says so instead of showing a command. The script's own default tolerance is not the one of this tool; the command always states the tolerance in use.

When to change the root

Most users never do. The root is the atom from which the Z-matrix is grown, so a different root gives a different set of primitives; the tool checks each set with the same rank test.

items.title: What it does
items.text: IntCoords decides which atoms are bonded from the distances alone. The block it writes is built on this bond graph, so it matters that the graph is right. The section 2 · Bonds lists the bonds it found and lets you change how generous the rule is.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load a structure and open the left panel, section 2 · Bonds.
  2. Find Detected bonds. The number of bonds is in brackets and the bonds follow as pairs of atom names, for example C1–H2. Each one is also a grey stick in the 3D view and appears in the last column of the atom table in 1 · Structure.
  3. Two atoms count as bonded when their distance is more than 0.4 Å and less than the sum of their covalent radii multiplied by a factor. The factor is the box Detection tolerance (× sum of covalent radii), 1.2 at the start. Type another value between 0.5 and 3 and leave the box: the list, the table and the view are updated at once.
  4. If the box is left empty or holds something that is not a positive number, the starting value 1.2 comes back.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Why a transition state has missing bonds

A bond that is forming or breaking is longer than a normal one, so the rule does not find it. Raising the tolerance to catch it also adds bonds elsewhere that you do not want. It is usually better to keep the factor and to declare the partial bonds.

The radii

The covalent radii are the single-bond radii of Alvarez (2008), the same table the other OPAL tools use. An element the table does not have is given a radius of 0.90 Å, and a warning in the section Check says so.

Check the list before you go on

A bond the rule invents, or one it misses inside a molecule, changes the block. Read the list once, and the atom table beside it, before you build the reaction coordinate.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Every time you change something, IntCoords rebuilds the block and checks it. The section Check at the top of the right panel tells you whether the set can be used. The check counts the coordinates and tests that they are independent (the rank of the Wilson B matrix), so that SLAPAF does not stop with a linear-dependency error. Until the check passes, the block cannot be copied or saved.
path: Check the result and read the warnings

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open the right panel and find the section Check.
  2. Read the status line:
    • ✓ Rank check OK — n of n (green): the set has the right number of independent coordinates. The line under it says that the name of your coordinate is coordinate 1 of the Vary list, and how many warnings follow.
    • ✗ Rank MISMATCH — n of m: the set is not complete. Do not use it. Change the reaction coordinate or the bonds.
    • ✗ No usable block yet: there is an error to fix first.
    • Load a structure to begin. before any structure is loaded.
  3. Under it come the messages. Each begins with error: or warning:. Errors stop the block. Warnings leave it usable but tell you to look.
  4. Below the messages, lines that begin with # report the numbers: the root atom, the number of primitives, the rank of the final set and the number of coordinates in the Vary list, each against the number expected.
path: Check the result and read the warnings

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Nearly linear angles

An angle close to 0° or 180° does not give a well-defined bending coordinate, and it leaves the torsion or the plane built on it nearly undefined. Angles between 8° and 172° raise no concern. An angle term you add yourself outside that range only gets a warning. A dihedral or an out-of-plane term that is not among the generated primitives (it becomes a new primitive, u1, u2, …) is stopped when an angle that defines it lies from 172° to 175° (or from 5° to 8°), and the message offers a box Use it anyway; ticking it accepts the term and leaves a warning. Beyond 175° (or below 5°) the stop cannot be lifted. If that angle is what changes along the reaction, use it as the term itself. A term that is already among the generated primitives only gets a warning.

The messages worth reading

Fragments that were joined for you; a primitive added as u1, u2 with the ones it made redundant; a dihedral replaced by an out-of-plane angle; a dihedral within the planar window of its wrap-around; an element with no covalent radius; a label longer than 8 characters. Each message states what it is about.

No copy while a check fails

Copy and Download .txt stay disabled and a line under the block says why. See Copy or save the block.

items.title: What it does
items.text: At a transition state the bonds that form and break are longer than ordinary bonds, so IntCoords does not find them. You tell it about them by declaring a partial bond between two atoms. A declared bond counts as a bond in everything that follows. A structure that falls into separate pieces cannot give a block until its pieces are joined, by declared bonds or by letting IntCoords join them.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the left panel, find the section 2 · Bonds.
  2. Click the two atoms of the bond, in the 3D view or in the atom table. The button below the steps then reads Declare bond followed by the two names and their distance, for example "Declare bond C1–F6 (2.00 Å)".
  3. Press it. A message says "Declared bond C1–F6 (2.00 Å)". The bond appears under Declared (partial) bonds with its distance in Å, and in the view as an orange dashed line.
  4. To take a declared bond away, press ✕ at the end of its line.

When the structure is in pieces, the section also shows a box, The structure falls apart into N fragments:

  1. Each button in it, such as "Declare C1–F6 (2.00 Å)", declares the closest pair of atoms between two of the fragments. The buttons are sorted from the shortest distance.
  2. Press the ones that are real forming or breaking bonds. The box disappears when the pieces are joined.
  3. Or tick Generate anyway, joining the fragments through their closest atoms. IntCoords joins the pieces itself, draws those bonds as blue dashed lines, and keeps a warning on the result.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The presets declare for you

The two presets of Reaction-coordinate presets declare their two bonds if they are missing, so for an SN2 guess you rarely need this page's buttons.

Generate anyway is a guess

The closest atoms between two pieces are not always the atoms that react. When you use Generate anyway, the status line keeps a yellow reminder and the warning names the bonds it added. Read it, and declare the right bonds if they differ.

Pairs that are already bonded

For two atoms that are already bonded, the button is disabled and reads "… is already a bond". A bond you declared that the distance rule also finds is marked "also detected" in the list.

items.title: What it does
items.text: IntCoords carries one small structure inside it: a guess for the transition state of an SN2 reaction, fluoride attacking chloromethane (F⁻ + CH₃Cl → CH₃F + Cl⁻), with six atoms and a flat CH₃ group. You can load it without any file, to try the tool or to follow the other pages of this tutorial.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press Example in the toolbar. Before a structure is loaded you can also press load the example in the text under the drop box in the middle of the view.
  2. The structure appears. Its name is ABC-sn2asym-FCl-guess-v7.xyz, and the atoms are C1, H2, H3, H4, Cl5 and F6. The carbon atom has the three hydrogen atoms around it in one plane; chlorine and fluorine sit on opposite sides of that plane, on a line through the carbon atom, at 2.35 Å and 2.00 Å from it.
  3. Look at the section 2 · Bonds: the structure falls apart into three pieces, because the C–Cl and C–F distances are too long to count as bonds. This is the usual state of a transition-state guess, and the pages Declare partial bonds and Reaction-coordinate presets show what to do next.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The example replaces what you have

Loading the example, like loading any structure, removes the declared bonds, the selection and the terms you had. Save the block first if you want to keep it: see Copy or save the block.

items.title: What it does
items.text: IntCoords starts from one structure in XYZ format, usually a guess for a transition state. You can open an .xyz file, drop it on the 3D view, or paste its text. Loading a structure replaces the one you had, together with everything you built on it: declared bonds, selected atoms and the terms of the reaction coordinate.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press Open XYZ in the toolbar, or click the box Click here or drag & drop an .xyz file in the middle of the view. You can also drag a file onto the 3D view; while it is over the view, the text Drop file to load appears.
  2. Choose the file. If you drop several files, only the first is read.
  3. To paste instead, open the left panel and find the section 1 · Structure. Open Paste XYZ text instead of opening a file, paste the text into the box and press Load pasted text. An empty box gives the message "Paste the XYZ text first".
  4. The structure appears in the view. In 1 · Structure the name of the file is shown with the number of atoms, then the comment line of the file, and a table lists the atoms with their coordinates. The file bar along the bottom shows the name and the kind, XYZ geometry. For pasted text the name is pasted.xyz.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What the file must look like

The first line is the number of atoms. The second line is a comment and may be empty. Then come exactly that many lines, each with an element symbol and three coordinates in Å. Atoms after that count are ignored.

The names of the atoms

Each atom is named by its element symbol and its position in the file: C1, H2, Cl5, F6. These are the names OpenMolcas gives to atoms read from an XYZ file, and they are the names in the block IntCoords writes. Do not reorder the atoms in the input file you later use it with.

A file that cannot be read

When the first line is not a number, a line is not "symbol x y z", a coordinate is not a number, or the file has fewer atoms than the header says, a message names the problem and, where it applies, the line. The previous structure is gone and nothing is loaded.

Other files

IntCoords reads XYZ text only, not Molden or HDF5 files. How files are opened in all the tools is described in Opening files.

items.title: What it does
items.text: When the check has passed, the section SLAPAF input of the right panel shows the finished block, from Internal coordinates to End of Internal. It lists the primitives, then under Vary your reaction coordinate first, followed by the remaining coordinates. You copy it into the &SLAPAF section of your OpenMolcas input, or save it as a text file.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the right panel, find the section SLAPAF input.
  2. Choose what goes with the block:
    • RowH, ticked at the start, adds a RowH line after the Vary list. It makes SLAPAF compute the Hessian rows of the reaction coordinate and of its complement numerically, so the search starts from the true curvature along the path. At most 10 labels are listed; if there are more, a note says only the first 10 are.
    • Tick Show the surrounding &SLAPAF lines of a transition-state search to add &SLAPAF, TS, PRFC and MODE = 1 around the block, with a line of comment. An explanation of the three keywords appears under the tick.
  3. Press Copy to put the text on the clipboard. The message says "Copied — paste it into the &SLAPAF section of your input". If the browser refuses, the message tells you to select the text in the box and copy it by hand.
  4. Or press Download .txt. The file is named after your structure file with _internal.txt in place of its extension, for example ABC-sn2asym-FCl-guess-v7_internal.txt. Its first line is a comment line with the version of IntCoords, the name of the structure file and the rank check, such as * IntCoords v0.61 | ABC-sn2asym-FCl-guess-v7.xyz | rank 12/12 OK.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The buttons are disabled until the check passes

While the section Check shows an error or a rank mismatch, Copy and Download .txt are disabled, and a line under the block says "Copy and download are disabled until the errors are fixed" or "… the rank check failed". Fix the cause first: see Check the result.

MODE = 1 and the order of the list

MODE = 1 follows the first internal mode, which is your reaction coordinate because it is coordinate 1 of the Vary list. If you reorder that list by hand in your input, change this number too.

What is copied is what you see

Both buttons use the text in the box, with the options you chose. The saved file adds the comment line first. On an iPhone or iPad the file goes through the share sheet; see Saving files on iPhone and iPad.

items.title: What it does
items.text: SLAPAF works with internal coordinates: bond lengths, angles and dihedrals. From your bond graph IntCoords builds a complete set of them, one for each internal degree of freedom, in the way of a Z-matrix: every atom after the first is placed by one bond, one angle and one dihedral (or out-of-plane angle) relative to atoms already placed. This set is the primitives. The section Generated primitives lists them with their current values, and the terms of your reaction coordinate are made from them.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load a structure and give it its bonds. In the left panel, find the section Generated primitives.
  2. Each line has a label, the kind with its atoms, and the present value: in Å with three decimals for a bond, in degrees with one decimal for the others. For example rCl5 is the bond of Cl5 to its neighbour in the graph. The labels start with r for a bond, a for an angle, d for a dihedral and o for an out-of-plane angle, followed by the name of the atom being placed.
  3. The list holds N−1 bonds, N−2 angles and N−3 dihedrals or out-of-plane angles for N atoms, so 3N−6 in all (3N−5 for a linear molecule).
  4. Press + at the end of a line to add that primitive to the reaction coordinate with the coefficient 1. The button is disabled for a primitive that is already a term, and the line is then highlighted.
  5. A line marked with a star ★ was added by you: a term that the generated set did not contain. Hold the pointer over it for the text "Added for the reaction coordinate".

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The signs of dihedrals and out-of-plane angles

A dihedral runs from −180° up to, but not including, 180°. The dihedral and the out-of-plane angle are shown with the sign that SLAPAF prints.

What the list depends on

The generated primitives depend on the bonds and the root atom, not on the reaction coordinate. Declaring a bond, changing the tolerance or choosing another root atom changes the list. While the structure is still in separate pieces the list shows only a dash.

A flat group

Where a dihedral would sit on its ±180° wrap-around, the tool uses an out-of-plane angle instead. See Advanced options.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The reaction coordinate is the combination of internal coordinates that SLAPAF follows uphill to the transition state. For two common cases IntCoords builds it with one click: a combination of two bond lengths with the coefficients +1 and −1 (Antisymmetric: one bond forms while the other breaks, as in an SN2 reaction), or +1 and +1 (Symmetric: both bonds stretch together). A bond that is not yet a bond is declared for you.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the left panel, find the section 3 · Reaction coordinate and select the atoms, in this order:
    • three atoms, X, centre, Y: the preset uses the bonds centre–X and centre–Y. For the example of Load the built-in example click Cl5, then C1, then F6;
    • or four atoms, A, B, C, D: the preset uses the bonds A–B and C–D.
  2. Press Antisymmetric (+1, −1) or Symmetric (+1, +1).
  3. A message names the coordinate set. If a bond was missing it also says which bond it declared, for example "Antisymmetric reaction coordinate set — declared C1–Cl5, C1–F6".
  4. Under Terms (coefficient × primitive) the two bonds are listed with their coefficients, and the selection is cleared. The result is checked at once: see Check the result.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The right number of atoms

With any other number of selected atoms you get "Select three atoms (X, centre, Y) or four atoms (A, B, C, D) first". If the two bonds are the same bond, you get "The two bonds must be different".

A preset replaces the terms

Pressing a preset throws away the terms you had and puts its two. To change them afterwards, edit the coefficients or add terms as in Reaction-coordinate terms.

The order of the atoms sets the sign

The first bond gets the coefficient +1 and the second +1 or −1. Selecting the atoms the other way round gives the same coordinate with the opposite sign.

items.title: What it does
items.text: When a preset is not what your reaction needs, you build the reaction coordinate term by term. Each term is a coefficient times one internal coordinate: a bond length, an angle, a dihedral or an out-of-plane angle. The terms are added together, and the sum is placed first in the list of coordinates SLAPAF varies. You also give the coordinate a name.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the left panel, find the section 3 · Reaction coordinate and select two, three or four atoms, in order.
  2. Press the button under Add a single term from the selection. It reads Add bond term for two atoms, Add angle term for three and Add dihedral term for four. With four atoms, Add as OutOfP adds an out-of-plane term instead: the bond from the first atom to the fourth, against the plane of the second, third and fourth.
  3. The term appears under Terms (coefficient × primitive) with its kind, its atoms and a coefficient of 1. Repeat for the other terms. You can also add a line of the list Generated primitives with its + button; see Primitive internal coordinates.
  4. Change a coefficient by typing in its box. A comma is accepted as the decimal sign. The box turns red if the text is not a number, and the result follows a moment after you stop typing.
  5. Remove a term with ✕.
  6. While the result is valid, a note next to each term says which primitive it is, for example "= rCl5" or "= u1 (added)".
  7. Type the name of the coordinate in Name of the reaction coordinate. It starts as TS1.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A bond term needs a bond

For two atoms that are not bonded you get "… are not bonded — declare the bond first (section 2) if it is a partial bond". Angles and dihedrals must also follow bonds; if they do not, the section Check says that the term "cannot be used" and why, and no block is shown as ready.

A term the tool did not generate

A term that is not among the generated primitives becomes a new primitive, u1, u2 and so on, and the generated primitives it makes redundant are removed. A warning lists what was added and what was removed. This is the way to make an angle or a dihedral the reaction coordinate.

The name

The name has at most 12 characters, and an empty box gives TS1 again. It should start with a letter and hold only letters, digits and underscores. SLAPAF limits primitive labels to 8 characters, so a short name is safer. With two or more terms the block also holds labels made of the name followed by _c and a number, and a warning appears if the longest of them has more than 8 characters.

A term cannot appear twice

The same bond, angle or dihedral twice in the coordinate is refused. So are terms of which one is almost a combination of the others, and more terms than the molecule has internal degrees of freedom.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Almost everything in IntCoords starts from atoms you pick: the two atoms of a bond you declare, the three or four atoms of a preset, the atoms of a term of the reaction coordinate. You pick them in the atom table or by clicking them in the 3D view. The order of your clicks matters, and at most four atoms can be selected.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load a structure. In the left panel, find the section 1 · Structure: its table lists every atom with its name, its coordinates in Å and, in the last column, the atoms it is bonded to.
  2. Click a row of the table, or click an atom in the 3D view. A number appears at the start of the row (1 for the first atom you picked, then 2, 3, 4), and the atom in the view gets a translucent red halo.
  3. Find the section 3 · Reaction coordinate. Under Selected atoms (in click order) your atoms are listed in the order you clicked them, joined by arrows.
  4. Click a selected atom, or its row, again to take it out of the selection. The others keep their order.
  5. Press Clear selection to remove all of them.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Four atoms at most

A fifth click is refused with the message "At most 4 atoms can be selected — clear the selection first". A bond needs two atoms, an angle three and a dihedral or an out-of-plane angle four.

Hydrogen atoms are small

A hydrogen atom is a small target in the view. Click its row in the table instead, which works with every atom. With the mouse, hovering over an atom shows its name and coordinates; see The 3D view in IntCoords.

The selection is used and then cleared

A preset, Add term, Add as OutOfP and Declare bond use the selection and then empty it. Loading another structure empties it too.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The view in the middle of the page shows the structure as balls and sticks. It is where you check the geometry and where you can pick atoms by clicking them. It also shows which bonds IntCoords has found and which you declared.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Move the molecule as in the other tools: drag to rotate, right-drag to pan, wheel or pinch to zoom. The details are in Navigate the 3D view.
  2. Press Reset view in the toolbar to bring back the starting orientation, position and zoom.
  3. Labels switches the atom names on and off, and H labels the names of the hydrogen atoms. Both are on when the tool starts, and a lit button means on. A selected hydrogen atom keeps its label even when H labels is off. A selected atom's label carries its number in the selection, for example "Cl5 (1)".
  4. With a mouse, hold the pointer over an atom: a small box shows its name and its x, y and z in Å.
  5. Click an atom to select it. See Select atoms.

The lines between atoms have three looks:

  • a grey solid stick: a bond found from the distances;
  • an orange dashed line: a bond you declared;
  • a blue dashed line: a bond that IntCoords added by itself when you asked it to join fragments.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
When the 3D view cannot start

If the browser cannot start WebGL, the view shows the message "The 3D view is not available in this browser (WebGL could not start). Everything can still be done from the atom table on the left." Select atoms in the table, and use all the sections as usual. Only the drawing is missing.

Saving the view

SVG (vector) in the toolbar saves the view as a drawing you can edit in a vector program, in the look chosen in the menu beside it. See Export images.

items.title: What it is for
items.text:
The launcher is the front page of OPAL. It shows one card for each tool, and a button on the card opens the tool. It does no chemistry and reads no file. Every tool has a button, OPAL, at the left end of its toolbar that brings you back to it (Back to the launcher).

Open the launcher. The cards sit in the order in which the tools are usually used: MolBuild, MolViz, OrbViz, PathVibViz, RassiViz, GeoDiff, IntCoords and CSFsCalc, then OpenMolcas on Colab and Tutorials.

items.title: Files it reads
items.text:
None. The launcher opens no file. You choose your files inside each tool.

The page has these parts:

  • The toolbar: the name OPAL · OpenMolcas, a small badge with the launcher's version, the words Orbitals, Plotting, Analysis and Layout (hidden on a narrow screen), the Theme button and the ⓘ button.
  • The title area, with a short description of the suite and the words Orbitals, Plotting, Analysis and Layout again. On the published site it also shows a line about the offline copy (Offline use).
  • Available Tools: the grid of cards.
  • How to cite: the references to quote when you use OPAL in published work. While a reference is not yet published, the section says so.
  • The footer: the copyright line, the licence, a link to OpenMolcas and a light-hearted line about cookies (the launcher uses none).

items.title: The cards
items.text:
Each card has the name of the tool, a line saying what kind of tool it is, a short description, a badge and a button.

  • Launch opens a tool in the same browser tab. The tools are plain files that sit beside the launcher, so this works on the published site and in a downloaded copy of the suite where the files are kept in one folder.
  • Open (with a small arrow) is on the two cards that leave the suite: OpenMolcas on Colab, which opens the notebook described in Running OpenMolcas in Colab, and Tutorials, which opens these pages. They open in a new tab and need a network connection. Without one, the two cards are dimmed and say so.
  • The badge says how settled a tool is: Stable, Dev (in development) or Being written. At the time of writing PathVibViz carries Dev and the Tutorials card carries Being written.
  • A last, dashed card says that more tools are coming.

items.title: The light theme
items.text: The Theme button switches between the dark and the light look. The choice is kept in the address of the page, not stored anywhere, and the Launch buttons pass it on to the tool they open, so the tool opens in the same look. See Light and dark theme.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Open the launcher first to work offline

The launcher is where you save the whole suite for use without a network. Read Offline use before a lesson in a room with no connection.

Keep the files together

If you save the tools to your own disk, keep the launcher and the tools in one folder. The buttons and the OPAL link in each tool refer to the others by file name.

items.title: Feature pages
items.text:
The launcher has no feature pages of its own. These pages from the common part describe what it takes part in:

  • Back to the launcher
  • Light and dark theme
  • Offline use
  • What is stored in your browser
  • The tools

items.title: What it is for
items.text:
MolBuild builds a molecule for an OpenMolcas calculation. You draw it in two dimensions, as on paper, or type a SMILES text, or load an existing structure. MolBuild tidies the drawing, builds a three-dimensional structure from it, relaxes that structure with a quick force field, and saves it as an .xyz file. Distance, angle and dihedral constraints, and a move of one fragment, let you shape the geometry before you export it. The result is a starting geometry, not a quantum-chemical one.

Open MolBuild. It runs in your browser and holds one molecule at a time.

When the page opens, a small molecule (ethanol, C₂H₆O) is already drawn on the canvas, with its 3D preview in the pane on the right, as a sample to play with. The file bar still reads New drawing. Click ✕ Clear to start from an empty canvas; the pane keeps showing the sample until you draw something.

items.title: Files it reads
items.text:
• .xyz files and .molden files, with the button ⬆ Load: see Load a structure;
  • SMILES text, typed or pasted into the section SMILES: see SMILES.

It saves .xyz files, and 2D pictures as PNG or SVG.

The page has these parts:

  • The toolbar, from the left: the back link OPAL, the version badge, ↩ Undo, ↪ Redo, ⊡ Fit, ✕ Clear, H, ▦ Grid, ✦ Clean, ⚡ Optimise, ⬆ Load, ⬇ XYZ, ⧉ View XYZ, ⎘ SMILES, ⬇ Export ▾, Theme, and the ⓘ button, which opens a small window on how to cite OPAL and links to this tutorial. A button Snap appears beside ▦ Grid when the honeycomb background is chosen.
  • The left panel, with the sections Tools, Element, Bond order, Formal charge, Templates, SMILES, Constraints and Move; a box Selected atom (or Selection) appears when you select atoms.
  • The 2D canvas in the middle, where you draw. Under it are the status bar, with the formula, the count of valence errors and the i button for the list of gestures, and, while an optimisation runs, its progress panel.
  • The 3D pane on the right, which shows the three-dimensional structure and holds the Move panel.
  • The file bar along the bottom of the page: the name of the loaded file and its kind, or New drawing.
  • Windows that open over the page: the periodic table, the template library, XYZ Coordinates, the list of gestures and shortcuts, and the short notes behind the ⓘ of Constraints and Move.

The two panels have a handle at the edge that hides them. Sections of the left panel fold. How that works is explained once, in Parts of a tool page.

A usual order of work: draw (or load, or type a SMILES), set hydrogens and charges, ✦ Clean, ⚡ Optimise, check the 3D pane, then export the .xyz and, if you want a picture, the 2D drawing.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Bond order of the left panel chooses the type of the bonds you draw next: Single, Double, Triple or Arom. (aromatic). The same choice is stamped on a bond you click. Wedge and dash bonds, in the same section, are described in Stereochemistry.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Find the section Bond order and click Single, Double, Triple or Arom.. Single is chosen when the tool opens. The keys 1, 2 and 3 choose single, double and triple when the pointer is not over an atom or a bond; there is no key for aromatic.
  2. Draw with the Bond tool. New bonds, whether you drag to a new atom or to an existing one, have the chosen order.
  3. To change a bond already drawn, click it with the Bond tool. It takes the chosen order.
  4. To step through the orders, click the same bond again within half a second. Each fast click moves it on one step: single, double, triple, aromatic, single again.
  5. The Select tool does the same on a click on a bond, without drawing.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A slow click stamps, a fast click cycles

Two clicks on one bond more than half a second apart each stamp the chosen order, so the second does nothing new. The cycle starts only when the second click comes quickly.

Hydrogens change with the order

Changing a bond order changes the valence left over, and MolBuild adds or removes hydrogens on its two atoms to match. See Hydrogens.

Over an atom or a bond the number keys do something else

With the pointer over an atom, 1, 2, 3, 6 and 7 add a bond, a carbonyl and rings. Over a bond they set its order, and 4 to 8 fuse a ring. See Shortcuts and gestures.

items.title: What it does
items.text: MolBuild draws new atoms with the element chosen in the section Element of the left panel. You can choose from a grid of common elements or from the whole periodic table, and you can change the element of an atom that is already drawn.

items.title: How
items.text:
For the atoms you are about to draw

  1. Find the section Element. Click one of the fourteen buttons: H, C, N, O, F, Si, P, S, Cl, Br, I, Fe, Cu or Zn. Carbon is chosen when the tool opens.
  2. For any other element click More…. The button also shows the element chosen now. A window with the periodic table opens; click an element, and the window closes.
  3. Or type a symbol in the box Symbol… at the foot of that window and click Set. The first letter is read as a capital and the second as lower case, so cl gives Cl. Only the first two characters count, and MolBuild does not check that the symbol is an element, so look at what the button More… shows afterwards.

For an atom already drawn

  1. Double-click the atom. A small palette of the same fourteen elements opens next to it; click one and that atom, and no other, changes. More… in the palette opens the periodic table for that atom.
  2. Or choose the element in Element, then click the atom with the Bond tool, without dragging.
  3. Or, with the pointer over an atom, press a letter key: C, N, O, S, F, L (for Cl), B (for Br), I, P or H. See Shortcuts and gestures.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Choosing an element does not change what is drawn

Clicking a button in Element only decides what the next new atom is. No atom already on the canvas changes until you retype it as in steps 4 to 6.

Hydrogens follow the element

After a retype MolBuild rebalances the hydrogens of the atom and of its neighbours. Retyping an atom to hydrogen removes the hydrogens it carried, because a hydrogen carries one bond at most.

Closing the palette without a change

A click anywhere outside the small palette closes it and changes nothing.

items.title: What it does
items.text: ✦ Clean tidies the drawing before you optimise it in 3D. It does two things: it recognises aromatic rings and marks their bonds as aromatic, and it lays the structure out again, with regular rings, even bond lengths and tidy angles, and the hydrogens placed around their atoms. The order of the atoms and bonds does not change, only where they are on the canvas and, for aromatic rings, the bond order.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Draw or import your molecule.
  2. Click ✦ Clean in the toolbar. The message 2D cleaned · ready to Optimise appears.
  3. Look at the drawing. If a ring was drawn with alternating single and double bonds and is aromatic, its bonds now show as aromatic.
  4. Click ⚡ Optimise when you are happy with it (see Optimise in 3D).

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The button tells you when it is due

After any change to the drawing, ✦ Clean is outlined in the accent colour. It goes back to normal after a Clean.

Optimise cleans for you

If the drawing has changed since the last Clean, ⚡ Optimise runs Clean first, and says Auto-cleaned · starting 3D optimisation…. Clicking ✦ Clean yourself is still useful: you see the result, and you can undo it, before the optimisation starts.

Which rings become aromatic

Only five- and six-membered rings are tested, with the rule of 4n + 2 π electrons: two for each double bond in the ring and two for each lone pair of a nitrogen, oxygen or sulfur atom that is bonded twice in the ring. Large conjugated rings (porphyrins are the case MolBuild handles specially) are treated as a whole. A saturated ring such as piperidine or tetrahydrofuran is left alone.

One step to undo

✦ Clean is a single step in the history: ↩ Undo returns to the drawing as it was, including the old positions and bond orders.

It changes the drawing, not the 3D coordinates

After a Clean the 3D pane shows ⚠ stale for a moment, and then ✓ current again. A structure you optimised or loaded keeps its coordinates and its label (OPTIMIZED or IMPORTED); only the 2D drawing is tidied. The preview of a drawing that was never optimised (EMBED) is built again from the cleaned drawing.

An empty canvas

With nothing drawn, the message is Nothing to clean.

Templates and the SMILES import run the same tidy-up when they place a molecule, so a molecule built from them is already clean.
