items.title: What it does
items.text:
A constraint tells Optimise to hold something fixed: an atom in place, or a distance, an angle or a dihedral at a value you choose. Use it to build a structure with a given twist, to keep a bond at a length you want, or to leave a part of a loaded structure where it is.

The section Constraints in the left panel has four buttons:

Button What it holds Atoms to click 🔒 Atom one atom, where it is 1 ↔ Dist the distance between two atoms, in Å 2 ∠ Angle the angle at the middle atom, in degrees 3, the middle one second ↻ Dihed the dihedral angle across a chain of four atoms, in degrees 4, in chain order

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Find the section Constraints in the left panel and click the button for the kind you want. It lights up and a line under the buttons reads, for example, Adding distance: click atom 1 of 2 · Esc = cancel.
  2. Click the atoms in the 2D canvas, one after another. Atoms you have clicked get a gold ring. After the last one the constraint is added.
  3. The constraint appears in the list below the buttons, named by its atoms (such as C3–N4: the element and the atom's position in the list of atoms), and is drawn on the canvas.
  4. For a distance, angle or dihedral, change the number in the list to the value you want and press Enter. The unit (Å or °) is shown next to it.
  5. Click ⚡ Optimise. The constraint is applied during the run.
  6. To remove a constraint, click ✕ at the end of its row.

To give up while picking, click the same button again, or press Esc.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Start values are only starting values

A distance or an angle starts at the value measured on your 2D drawing. A dihedral always starts at 60°, because a flat drawing has no real dihedral. Always set the value you want before you optimise.

A value of exactly 0 is not taken

If you type 0 in the box of a constraint, the box keeps showing 0 but MolBuild keeps the previous value, which the number on the canvas shows. For a dihedral or an angle close to zero, type a small number such as 0.1 instead.

How a constraint looks on the canvas

A fixed atom has a gold ring with a cross, a distance is a dashed line with its value, and an angle or a dihedral is a dashed chain with a ring on each atom and the value above the second atom.

Hydrogens need a real 3D position

You can pick a hydrogen only when it is shown (the H button) and the 3D structure is a trustworthy one: after you loaded a structure from a file or optimised it. Otherwise the tool says Import or Optimise a 3D geometry before constraining or moving a hydrogen — a sketched H has only a provisional position.

A constraint is a penalty, not a wall

The optimiser adds an energy term that grows as the value moves away from your target, so the result is close to the target, not exactly on it. A fixed atom is the exception: it does not move at all.

Constraints go with the drawing

↩ Undo and ↪ Redo bring back the constraints that went with each step. ✕ Clear, a SMILES import and loading a file remove them, because the atoms they referred to are gone.

Pick with the constraint buttons, not with a tool

While a constraint is being picked, a click on an atom only adds it to the constraint. It does not select, draw or erase. Starting a fragment move cancels the pick, and the other way round.

Click the ⓘ beside the section title for the same advice in a short window.

items.title: What it does
items.text: With the Bond tool on, you build a structure by placing atoms and joining them with bonds. The element of a new atom is the one chosen in the section Element; the type of a new bond is the one chosen in the section Bond order. Hydrogens are managed for you: an atom gets the hydrogens its valence asks for.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the section Tools click Bond (or press B).
  2. In Element click the element you want to draw. Carbon is chosen when the tool opens. For an element that is not in the grid, see Choose the element.
  3. Click on empty canvas. A new atom of that element appears where you clicked.
  4. Press on an atom and drag. A line follows the pointer; release on empty canvas to create a new atom joined to the first, or release on another atom to bond the two.
  5. To retype an atom, click it without dragging after choosing another element in Element. It becomes that element. If it already is that element and has only one bond, the click extends the chain by one atom.
  6. To change a bond you have drawn, click it. It takes the order chosen in Bond order; see Set the bond order.
  7. The status bar below the canvas shows the formula, and counts any valence errors in yellow.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Where the new atom lands

A new atom at the end of a drag is placed at the bond length from the atom you started on, in the direction of the pointer rounded to a multiple of 30°; it is not placed under the pointer.

A click on an atom is not a click on empty canvas

A click on an atom retypes it or extends the chain; it never places a second atom on top. To add an atom beside it, drag from the atom.

Wedges and dashes

With Wedge or Dash chosen in Bond order, a dragged bond is a stereo bond; see Stereochemistry.

items.title: What it does
items.text: MolBuild has four drawing tools, chosen in the section Tools of the left panel: Select, Bond, Erase and Charge. The tool decides what a click or a drag on the canvas does. Bond is on when the tool opens.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Find the section Tools and click one of the four buttons. The button that is on is the active tool. You can also press S (Select), B (Bond) or E (Erase) on the keyboard. Charge has no key.
  2. Use the tool on the canvas:
    • Bond places a new atom where you click on empty canvas, and draws a bond when you drag from an atom. See Draw atoms and bonds.
    • Select selects an atom when you click it, and moves it when you drag it. A drag that starts on empty canvas draws a selection rectangle. See Select and move.
    • Erase deletes the atom or the bond you click.
    • Charge adds +1 to the charge of the atom you click, and −1 if you hold Shift. See Formal charge.
  3. Switch tool whenever you like. Changing tool abandons a bond you were dragging, but keeps your selection.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The right mouse button always deletes

Whatever tool is on, a right-click (or Ctrl/⌘ and a click) on an atom or a bond deletes it. A right-drag does something else (zoom and rotate, see Navigate the canvas), so deleting needs a click that does not move.

A deletion can be undone

Undo (Ctrl/⌘ + Z) brings back what Erase removed; see Undo and redo.

items.title: What it does
items.text: You can delete one atom or one bond, or empty the whole canvas. MolBuild keeps the hydrogens consistent: when you delete an atom or a bond, the atoms next to it get back the hydrogens their valence needs.

items.title: How
items.text:
Delete one atom or one bond

  1. In the section Tools click Erase (or press E), then click an atom or a bond. The pointer shows a "not allowed" sign over something you can delete.
  2. With any tool, a right click (or Ctrl/⌘ and a click, without moving) on an atom or a bond deletes it.
  3. Or select an atom and press Delete or Backspace.

Empty the canvas

  1. Click ✕ Clear in the toolbar. The drawing and any constraints are removed at once, with no question asked.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Deleting a heavy atom takes its hydrogens

The hydrogens that hang on only that atom (like those of a methyl carbon) go with it. A hydrogen that is the other half of an H₂, or that bridges two atoms, stays.

Delete removes one atom

The Delete key removes one atom, the one MolBuild treats as the selected atom, and not a whole group. To delete several atoms, erase them one by one. If you deleted too much, use Undo and redo.

Clear can be undone

✕ Clear records an undo step first, so ↩ Undo brings the drawing back. It asks nothing, so look before you press it.

items.title: What it does
items.text: ⬇ Export ▾ in the toolbar saves the 2D structure as a picture, in one of two forms: a PNG image, which is a snapshot of the canvas, or an SVG vector file, which is drawn again from the structure and can be edited in a vector program. Neither contains the 3D pane; for the coordinates use Export XYZ.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Draw or load the molecule, and set the view you want: the H button, the stereo marks, the size of the window.
  2. Click ⬇ Export ▾ and choose 🖼 PNG image or ✎ SVG vector.
  3. On a computer, type a file name in the box Save PNG as: or Save SVG as: (it starts with molecule) and confirm; the extension is added if you left it out. Cancel stops the export. On an iPhone or iPad no question is asked: the file is named molecule.png or molecule.svg and the share sheet opens.
  4. A message confirms the export: for the PNG the size in pixels, for the SVG the number of atoms.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The PNG is what you see

The image has the size of the canvas and shows the drawing as it is on screen: your zoom and pan, and also a selection, a highlighted atom or a bond being drawn. Deselect first (Esc), and make the window the size you want the picture to be. The grid background of the canvas is never in the picture, and the image has a transparent background.

The SVG does not depend on the view

The SVG is drawn from the structure, with the same coordinates whatever the zoom, and the page is cut tightly round the molecule with a margin of about four-fifths of a bond length. Selections, highlights, the template ghost and other signs of the mouse are never in it. What it keeps is the red ring and ! of an atom with too many bonds, which reflects the chemistry. It follows the H button: hydrogens hidden on screen are hidden in the file.

Both are drawn for a dark background

The bonds are light grey and the symbols of the atoms sit on small dark discs, because the tool is dark. On white paper or a white slide the bonds are faint and the discs show as dark spots. Put the picture on a dark background, or recolour the lines and the discs in a vector program (easy with the SVG).

What the drawing shows

Single, double, triple and aromatic bonds (a solid line and a dashed one), wedges as filled triangles and dashes as a hatch. A carbon with bonds is a small dot, and an atom of another element, a charged atom or an isolated carbon is its symbol, with its hydrogens and its charge. The symbols are real text in the SVG.

Empty canvas

With nothing drawn the message is Nothing to export. If the encoder cannot make the picture, the message begins Could not save or reads PNG export failed.

For the 3D structure, see Export XYZ. For the images of the other tools, see the pages of those tools.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
⬇ XYZ saves the three-dimensional structure of the drawing as an .xyz file, the usual starting point for an OpenMolcas input. ⧉ View XYZ shows the same text in a window, from which you can copy it or save it.

The coordinates are the ones the 3D pane holds: those of a loaded file, or the optimised geometry, or, when the drawing has never been optimised, a quick embedding of the drawing. The comment line of the file says which.

items.title: How
items.text:
To save a file:

  1. Draw the molecule, optimise it (Optimise in 3D) and wait for Optimised ✓.
  2. Click ⬇ XYZ in the toolbar.
  3. In the box that asks Save XYZ as:, type a name (the box starts with molecule) and confirm. .xyz is added if you left it out. Cancel stops the export. On an iPhone or iPad no question is asked: the file is named molecule.xyz and the share sheet opens, where you can rename it and choose where to save it.
  4. A message confirms the export and gives the number of atoms. Read the comment line of the file, not the message, to know what kind of geometry it holds (see below).

To look at the text first:

  1. Click ⧉ View XYZ. The window XYZ Coordinates opens with the whole file.
  2. Click ⎘ Copy to clipboard (the message Copied! appears beside the buttons) to paste it into an input file, or ⬇ Download .xyz to save it as above.
  3. Close the window with ✕ Close, a click outside it, or Esc.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What the file contains

The first line is the number of atoms, the second is a comment, then one line per atom: the element symbol and x, y, z with six decimals, in ångström. The atoms come in the order of the drawing; for a loaded file that is the order of the file. A drawing made here has its hydrogens added after the drawn atoms.

Read the comment line

It starts with MolBuild and the version of the tool, then says what the coordinates are: UFF-optimised; Phase-2 embedded, a quick geometric embedding of the drawing that has not been relaxed; imported geometry; or optimised from an imported geometry, followed by the largest and the rms shift from the file. If you changed the atoms of a loaded or optimised structure after that, it adds edited with the number of atoms added and removed. If the drawing has wedges or dashes, they are listed after stereo: as pairs of atom numbers. A file marked Phase-2 embedded is only a starting guess: run ⚡ Optimise first.

The window is a snapshot

⧉ View XYZ builds the text when you open it. If you change the drawing afterwards, close the window and open it again. A short message, Showing Phase-2 geometry — run Optimise for 3D-optimised coordinates, warns you when you open it on a drawing that has neither been optimised nor loaded.

When nothing is exported

An empty canvas gives Nothing to export (or Nothing to show). If the geometry cannot be computed, for example because of a valence error marked with a red !, the message says so and suggests ✦ Clean or Optimise. No file is written in that case.

If you edit after Optimise

The atoms that were already there keep their optimised coordinates, and the atoms you added are placed roughly next to their neighbours (see Optimise in 3D). The comment line then ends with edited. Optimise again after your last edit, and export after that.

iPhone and iPad

If the share sheet is refused, the message points to ⧉ View XYZ, then ⎘ Copy to clipboard, and pasting the text into a new file.

items.title: What it does
items.text: You can give an atom a formal charge, for an ammonium, a carboxylate or any other ion. The charge is written next to the atom, and MolBuild adjusts the hydrogens of the atom to its new valence: an N of charge +1 takes four bonds.

items.title: How
items.text:
With the Charge tool

  1. In the section Tools click Charge.
  2. Click an atom. Its charge goes up by one. Hold Shift and click to take it down by one.

With the widget

  1. Select one atom: click it with the Select tool. The section Selected atom appears at the foot of the left panel.
  2. In the section Formal charge click + or −. The number between the two buttons is the charge of the selected atom; it is blue below zero and in the accent colour above.
  3. Without a selected atom the buttons answer "Select an atom first".

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The widget acts on one atom

The widget is meant for one selected atom; with two or more selected, the section Selected atom shows only their number. Select one atom, or use the Charge tool, which acts on the atom you click.

The hydrogens follow the charge

Raising the charge of a three-bonded nitrogen adds a hydrogen; lowering it removes one. If you build a structure where you want to place every hydrogen yourself, see Auto H in Hydrogens.

items.title: What it does
items.text: In MolBuild the hydrogens are real atoms, and MolBuild looks after them: when you draw, retype, change a bond order or set a charge, the atoms involved get the hydrogens their valence needs. Two controls change how this looks or works: the H button in the toolbar, which shows or hides hydrogens in the drawing, and Auto H, which stops MolBuild managing the hydrogens of one atom.

items.title: How
items.text:
Show the hydrogens of carbon

  1. Click H in the toolbar above the canvas. It is on when it is highlighted, and the hydrogens bonded to carbon appear. Click again to hide them.
  2. Hydrogens on other elements (O–H, N–H and so on), H₂ and a lone H are always shown. Only those on carbon are hidden until you switch H on.
  3. The button changes only what you see. It adds no atom, removes none, and does not touch a 3D geometry.

Take over the hydrogens of one atom

  1. Select the atom (click it with the Select tool).
  2. In the section Formal charge click the button Auto H. It changes to Manual H, in yellow, and a line under it counts the atoms on manual H. MolBuild now neither adds, removes nor valence-checks the hydrogens of this atom.
  3. Click the button again to return the atom to automatic hydrogens. They are rebalanced at once.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
For exceptional structures only

Manual H is meant for bridging hydrides, radicals and fragments you are still editing. For an ordinary molecule leave it off.

Hydrogen atoms cannot be locked

With a hydrogen selected, or nothing selected, the button is disabled: a hydrogen is never managed automatically, so there is nothing to lock.

Hydrogens and the 3D geometry

A hydrogen you can see in the drawing may be only a 2D guess. It becomes available for a constraint or a move once the structure has been loaded from a file or optimised; see Constraints.

items.title: What it does
items.text: ⬆ Load reads a three-dimensional structure from an .xyz or a .molden file and turns it into a drawing. MolBuild finds the bonds from the distances between the atoms, works out the bond orders and any formal charges, and lays out a 2D picture from the connectivity. The 3D coordinates of the file are kept: they are what the 3D pane shows, and what Export XYZ writes, until you optimise or edit.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Click ⬆ Load in the toolbar. The file picker of your system opens. MolBuild has no drag and drop: the button is the only way in.
  2. Choose an .xyz or a .molden file.
  3. The drawing is replaced by the molecule of the file, with every hydrogen drawn as an atom, in the order of the file. The message reads Loaded n atoms · m bonds from "name" · 2D laid out from connectivity. The 3D pane shows the structure with the label IMPORTED.
  4. Look at the file bar along the bottom of the page: it shows the name of the file and its kind, XYZ geometry or Molden file.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What the file must look like

An XYZ file has the number of atoms on the first line, a comment on the second, then one atom per line: the element symbol and three coordinates in ångström. Lines with fewer than four fields or with coordinates that are not numbers are skipped without a message. A Molden file is read for its [Atoms] section only; coordinates are taken as ångström when the header says Angs and as bohr otherwise (and converted). The orbitals, basis sets and frequencies in a Molden file are not read.

The extension decides, then the content

A file whose name ends in .xyz is read as XYZ and one ending in .molden as Molden. For another extension, MolBuild looks at the content: a first line that is a whole number means XYZ, and a file that contains [Atoms] means Molden. Anything else, and every .input file, gives Unrecognised format — use .xyz or .molden.

Messages when it does not work

Unrecognised format — use .xyz or .molden, No atoms found in file, Parse error: … with the reason, or Could not read name — the file could not be opened. The drawing you had is not touched by the first two, which are the usual ones.

Bonds and orders are a perception, not data from the file

Two atoms are bonded when they are closer than 1.2 times the sum of their covalent radii. The bond orders and the formal charges are then chosen so that every valence is satisfied. For an open-shell molecule, such as a radical, MolBuild leaves the unpaired electrons as they are and does not invent bonds. It prepares the warning ⚠ Open-shell/odd-electron species: n unpaired — left as radical (no fabricated bonds), but the message Loaded … replaces it at once, so you will not see it. Check the drawing against what you know of the molecule.

The 2D picture is new

The 2D drawing is made from the connectivity alone; it is not a projection of the 3D coordinates. Wedges and dashes are put on the stereocentres, and the cis/trans arrangement of the double bonds is taken from the 3D structure. The 3D coordinates stay as they were in the file.

It replaces what you had

Loading discards the drawing and drops any constraints. It is recorded as three steps in the history of Undo and redo: the first two ↩ Undo clicks leave the molecule you loaded on the canvas, and the third brings back the drawing you had before. A run of Optimise that is still going is stopped. If you pick a second file while the first is still being read, the later pick wins.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
Move changes one bond length, one bond angle or one dihedral of the structure you see in the 3D pane, and carries along everything that is attached on one side. The rest of the molecule stays where it is. Use it to stretch a bond, open an angle or twist a group without redrawing, for example to set up a starting geometry for a scan.

The section Move in the left panel has three buttons:

Button What moves Atoms to click ↔ Bond the bond length 2 ∠ Angle the angle at the middle atom 3, the middle one second ↻ Dihed the dihedral angle about the central bond 4, in chain order

The buttons are greyed until the 3D pane holds a structure and the drawing has enough atoms.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Make sure the 3D pane shows the structure you want to change (draw a molecule and wait for the preview, optimise it, or load a file).
  2. Find the section Move and click a button. A line under the buttons reads, for example, Move dihedral: click atom 1 of 4 · Esc = cancel.
  3. Click the atoms in the 2D canvas, in chain order. The last atom you click decides which side moves: the part of the molecule that hangs on it moves, and the other part stays.
  4. A small panel opens over the 3D pane with the title (such as Move Dihedral: C1–C2–C3–C4), a slider and the current value. Drag the slider: the fragment moves in the 3D pane as you drag. The ranges are 0.1 to 5.0 Å for a bond, 0 to 359° for an angle and −180 to 179° for a dihedral.
  5. Click Apply to keep the new geometry, or Cancel (or press Esc) to put everything back.

After Apply the label in the 3D pane reads MOVED, and the 2D drawing is redrawn from the new 3D structure.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The two sides must really be separate

The pivot bond has to be the only link between the two parts. If the atoms are not joined by bonds in a chain, MolBuild says Those atoms aren’t connected by existing bonds — pick along a bonded chain. If the bond is part of a ring, it says These atoms are connected another way (e.g. part of a ring) — they can’t be moved independently. Pick a bond outside the ring.

While the panel is open, the 2D canvas is locked

Clicks in the 2D canvas do nothing until you press Apply or Cancel. Hiding the 3D pane cancels the move, because the panel lives in it.

Hydrogens

A hydrogen can be one of the atoms, or part of the moving fragment, only when it is shown (the H button) and the 3D structure is a trustworthy one (loaded from a file, optimised or already moved). Otherwise the tool tells you to import or optimise first.

The start value is the one in 3D

The slider starts at the value measured in the 3D structure, not in the drawing. If the value is outside the slider's range, the slider starts at its end.

A move is not an optimisation

Apply moves the atoms exactly, with no relaxation. If the new geometry has atoms too close together, run ⚡ Optimise, with a constraint on the value you set if you want to keep it.

Click the ⓘ beside the section title for a short version of this advice.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The 2D canvas can be panned and zoomed, so that a large molecule fits and a small detail can be reached. Fit brings the whole drawing back into view. Two gestures also turn atoms: they change the drawing, not only the view.

items.title: How
items.text:
Pan

  1. Scroll with the wheel, or swipe with two fingers on a trackpad.
  2. Or hold the Space bar and drag, or drag with the middle mouse button.

Zoom

  1. Hold Ctrl (⌘ on a Mac) and scroll, or pinch on a trackpad. The zoom is limited to between about 0.08 and 10 times.
  2. Or press the right mouse button (or hold Ctrl/⌘ and press the left button) and drag up to zoom in and down to zoom out. The zoom is centred on the point where you pressed.

Fit the drawing

  1. Click ⊡ Fit in the toolbar. The whole drawing is centred and scaled to fill the canvas, up to a zoom of 4 times. With an empty canvas it returns to the starting view.

Turn atoms

  1. Press the right button (or Ctrl/⌘ and the left button) and drag sideways to turn atoms. If two or more atoms are selected, only they turn; otherwise the whole molecule turns.
  2. Or hold Shift and drag from empty canvas to spin the whole molecule about its centre. This needs two atoms or more, and with the Select tool Shift-drag makes a selection rectangle instead.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Turning changes the coordinates

Panning and zooming change only what you see. The sideways drag with the right button and the Shift-drag move the atoms themselves, and each can be undone (see Undo and redo).

A right click without a drag deletes

A right click (or Ctrl/⌘ and a click) that does not move deletes the atom or bond under the pointer, with any tool. Once the pointer moves it is a zoom and turn instead, so press and move in one gesture.

No right button on a touch screen

On a touch screen use two fingers: drag to pan, pinch to zoom. The right-button gestures and the Shift-drag have no touch equivalent.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
⚡ Optimise turns your drawing into a three-dimensional structure and relaxes it with a force field (UFF). The result appears in the 3D pane and in the file you export with ⬇ XYZ. It is a quick, approximate geometry that is good as a starting point for an OpenMolcas input; it is not a quantum-chemical result.

It works in three stages, each freeing more atoms than the one before: first the heavy atoms, then the hydrogens on heteroatoms as well, then every atom. Any constraints you set are respected throughout.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Draw the molecule, or import it with SMILES. Make the hydrogens and charges right first.
  2. Click ⚡ Optimise in the toolbar. If the drawing changed since the last Clean, MolBuild cleans it first and says Auto-cleaned · starting 3D optimisation….
  3. A progress panel opens at the bottom of the 2D canvas. It shows the stage (⅓ — heavy atoms, ⅔ — + heteroatom H, 3/3 — all atoms), a bar, and the gradient (∇RMS, in kcal/mol/Å) with the iteration count. The ⚡ Optimise button is greyed while it runs.
  4. Wait for the message Optimised ✓ followed by the final ∇RMS. The panel closes and the 3D pane shows the result. A molecule you drew keeps your drawing; a molecule you loaded from a file gets a 2D drawing made from its 3D structure.
  5. To end early, click ■ Stop in the progress panel. You keep what was reached, and the message reads Stopped by user.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Run Clean first if you want to see what it did

Optimise cleans a drawing that needs it, but without stopping. Click ✦ Clean yourself first when the drawing is untidy, so that you can look at it and undo it.

Large molecules get more iterations

Above 20 heavy atoms the iteration limits grow with the size of the molecule (up to twelve times the base values), and so does the time limit. If the run still ends with Stopped (time limit), the geometry is only partly relaxed: start ⚡ Optimise again, or add constraints that hold the parts you care about.

A loaded or optimised structure starts from its own coordinates

If you loaded a 3D file (Load a structure), or you run Optimise again on a structure you have already optimised, Optimise starts from the coordinates that structure holds, not from a new embedding of the drawing. When it finishes, the message adds the largest and the rms shift of the atoms in ångström.

An edit after the run keeps the optimised atoms

After you change the drawing, the 3D pane shows ⚠ stale for a moment. Then it is ✓ current again, still labelled OPTIMIZED: the atoms that were already there keep their optimised coordinates, and any atom you added is placed next to its neighbours. The new part is only roughly placed, so optimise again after your last edit, and export after that. The comment line of an .xyz saved in between says edited, with the number of atoms added and removed. The exception is a change of a cis/trans arrangement of a double bond: then the 3D structure is built again from the drawing, and a message tells you so.

Constraints are soft

A distance, angle or dihedral constraint is a penalty added to the energy, so the result is close to the value you asked for, not exactly equal to it.

↓ Log

↓ Log in the progress panel downloads a text record of the run, which is useful when you report a problem.

↩ Undo, ↪ Redo, ✕ Clear or loading another file while the run is going stops it, with the message Optimisation cancelled — the molecule changed.

items.title: What it does
items.text: With the Select tool you pick atoms in the drawing, move them, and turn a group of them around its centre. A selected atom is shown in the box Selected atom in the left panel, with its element, charge, implicit hydrogens and degree (the number of bonds it has).

items.title: How
items.text:
Select atoms

  1. In the section Tools click Select (or press S).
  2. Click an atom to select it. The box Selected atom appears with Element, Charge, Implicit H and Degree.
  3. To select several atoms, drag a rectangle on empty canvas. Every atom whose centre ends inside the rectangle is selected. Hold Shift when you start the drag to add the atoms to the selection you already have. The box is then called Selection with the number of atoms in brackets, and shows "multiple" and dashes.
  4. Select All (also Ctrl/⌘ + A) selects every atom. Deselect, or a click on empty canvas, or Esc, clears the selection.

Move atoms

  1. Drag one atom with the Select tool to move it. Its bonds follow.
  2. With two or more atoms selected, drag any one of them to move the whole group. This works with any tool, not only Select.

Turn a group

  1. With two or more atoms selected, a round ⟳ handle appears above the selection. Drag it around the group's centre to rotate the group. Hold Shift to turn in steps of 15°.
  2. The keys ← and → turn the selected group by 30° (Shift: 15°).

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A click on a bond is not a selection

With Select (and with Bond), a click on a bond does not select it: it applies the bond order or the stereo mark chosen in the section Bond order. See Bond order. To avoid changing a bond by accident, click the atoms and not the bond between them.

Shift and a single click

Shift adds atoms to the selection only with the rectangle. A Shift-click on an atom selects that atom alone.

Turning needs a group

The ⟳ handle and the keys ← and → act only when two or more atoms are selected. To turn the whole molecule see Navigate the canvas.

items.title: What it does
items.text: This page lists the mouse, trackpad, touch and keyboard actions of the 2D canvas in one place. The same list is in the tool: click the round i button at the right end of the status bar under the canvas, and the window Gestures & Shortcuts opens. Close it with ✕ Close, a click outside it, or Esc. While it is open, the keys do nothing to the drawing.

items.title: How
items.text:
Find the action in the tables below. Each row points to the page that explains it. No key acts on the drawing while a text box has the cursor or a window is open. The letters and digits that act on an atom or a bond also wait while you are picking atoms for a constraint or a move, or placing a template.

Mouse

You do MolBuild does Click empty canvas (Bond) places an atom; see Draw atoms and bonds Drag from an atom (Bond) draws a bond to a new atom, or to the atom where you stop Click an atom without dragging (Bond) changes it to the chosen element; if it is already that element and terminal, extends the chain Click an atom or a bond (Select) selects the atom; a click on a bond changes its order to the chosen one; see Select and move Drag on empty canvas (Select; Shift adds) selects the atoms in a rectangle Drag an atom (Select) moves that atom Drag one atom of a selection of two or more moves the whole group, with any tool Click an atom or a bond (Erase) deletes it; see Erase and clear Click an atom (Charge); Shift + click +1 charge; −1 charge Double-click an atom opens the quick palette of elements; see Choose the element Scroll wheel pans the canvas Ctrl or ⌘ + scroll wheel zooms Right-click, or Ctrl or ⌘ + click deletes the atom or bond under the pointer Right-drag, or Ctrl or ⌘ + drag up and down zoom; left and right turn the selection, or the whole molecule if nothing is selected Shift + drag from empty canvas spins the whole molecule (not in Select, where Shift adds to the rectangle) Drag the ⟳ handle (two or more atoms selected) rotates the selection; Shift gives steps of 15° Middle-drag, or hold Space and drag pans

Trackpad

You do MolBuild does Two-finger swipe pans Pinch, or Ctrl + two-finger swipe zooms Tap, click, click-drag as the matching mouse action Ctrl + click, held, then drag as a right-drag: zoom and turn

Touch screen

You do MolBuild does One finger: tap, drag draws, selects or places, according to the tool Tap a terminal atom (Bond) extends the chain by one atom, when the chosen element is the atom's own Tap the atom that is selected opens a ring of actions around it (below); tap again to close it Two fingers: drag, pinch pans, zooms Two fingers: twist (two or more atoms selected) rotates the selection One finger on the ⟳ handle rotates the selection

There is no touch equivalent of the right-drag and of Shift + drag.

The ring of actions has two circles. The inner one grows the structure from the atom: a bond with the chosen element, a carbonyl oxygen, a benzene ring, a cyclohexane, a cyclopentane. The outer one changes the element: C, N, O, S, F, Cl, Br, I, P, H. The ring closes when you press anywhere else on the canvas, or on Esc. Each action is one undo step.

Keyboard

Key Action S, B, E tool Select, Bond, Erase 1, 2, 3 bond order single, double, triple over an atom (or one atom selected): C N O S F L B I P H change its element (L is chlorine, B is bromine); S and B stay tool keys when the atom is only selected over an atom (or selected): 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 add a bond of the chosen element; a carbonyl; a benzene ring; a cyclohexane; a cyclopentane over a bond (or one bond selected): 1, 2, 3 set its order over a bond (or selected): 4 to 8 fuse a new ring of that size on the side away from the molecule ← and → rotate a selection of two or more atoms by 30° (Shift 15°); while a template is placed, turn the template Delete, Backspace remove the selected atom Ctrl or ⌘ + A select all Ctrl or ⌘ + Z; Ctrl or ⌘ + Y, or + Shift + Z undo; redo Esc cancel the action in progress, close the ring or palette, clear the selection hold Space and drag pan

With the Bond tool and the pointer over an atom, a dashed preview shows where the next bond would go.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The digits and letters mean two things

With nothing under the pointer and no atom selected, 1, 2, 3 set the bond order for the next bond, and S, B, E choose a tool. With the pointer over an atom or a bond, or one atom selected, the same keys act on that atom or bond instead. Move the pointer away if you want the tool keys.

A selected bond

A bond you clicked is shown in red, and the bond keys act on it without hovering.

Rotating

The ⟳ handle and the arrow keys need two or more selected atoms. The right-drag turns the selection when there is one, and the whole molecule when there is not. Shift + drag from empty canvas always turns the whole molecule.

Delete removes one atom

Delete and Backspace remove the one selected atom (with several selected, the last one picked), not the whole selection.

What the status bar button is for

The i button is the only way to this window; there is no key for it.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section SMILES of the left panel builds a drawing from a SMILES text, and shows the SMILES of the drawing you have. The button ⎘ SMILES in the toolbar copies that text to the clipboard.

items.title: How
items.text:
To build a molecule from a SMILES text:

  1. Find the section SMILES and click the box that reads Paste SMILES and press →.
  2. Type or paste the text, for example c1ccccc1 for benzene.
  3. Press Enter, or click →. The molecule replaces the drawing, with its hydrogens, laid out and fitted to the canvas. The message SMILES imported appears.

To read the SMILES of what you have drawn:

  1. Look under the box of the section SMILES. The text appears there about a quarter of a second after each change. It reads (empty) when the canvas is empty.
  2. To copy it, click ⎘ SMILES in the toolbar. The message SMILES copied confirms it; with an empty canvas the message is Nothing to copy.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The import replaces the drawing

The molecule you had is discarded. The import is one step: ↩ Undo brings the previous drawing back.

MolBuild is lenient: check the formula

MolBuild does not reject most wrong texts. It reads what it can and says SMILES imported. A text with a stray bracket such as C(( gives methane, an unclosed ring such as C1CC gives propane, and a symbol it does not know, such as Q, is drawn as an atom of that name, and a word such as hello becomes a few atoms. After every import, look at the formula in the status bar and at the drawing, and compare them with the molecule you meant. The message begins Parse error only for a few malformed texts, for example an unclosed square bracket ([ or C[), and then it gives a technical reason. A text that gives no atom at all gives No atoms found. In both cases the drawing you had is not touched, and neither is a running optimisation. An empty box does nothing.

The text MolBuild writes is not a standard form

The SMILES shown under the box follows the order in which the atoms were drawn, so the same molecule drawn differently can give different texts. Hydrogens are written as atoms and aromatic bonds as :: propane appears as C(H)(H)(H)C(H)(H)C(H)(H)H, and a charged nitrogen as [N+](H)(H)(H)H. The text carries the bond orders, the charges and the ring closures, but no stereochemistry: wedges, dashes and cis/trans are not written. A drawing in several pieces is written with a dot between them. Another program may need the text cleaned before it reads it.

While you type

The Enter key in the box imports the text; other keys, including the shortcut keys of the tools, do not act on the drawing while the cursor is in the box.

Several templates of the template library (the porphyrins and chlorins) work by importing a SMILES text in the same way.

items.title: What it does
items.text: A wedge and a hashed wedge (a dash) mark a bond that points toward you or away from you, the usual way to show a stereocentre on a flat drawing. In MolBuild they are two more choices in the section Bond order, next to single, double, triple and aromatic. A wedge or a dash is always a single bond.

items.title: How
items.text:
Draw a wedge or a dash

  1. In the section Bond order click Wedge ▲ (solid) or Dash ▽ (hashed).
  2. With the Bond tool, drag from the atom that carries the stereocentre to a new place, or to another atom. The bond is drawn with its narrow end at the atom you started from and its wide end at the other atom.

Turn an existing bond into a wedge or a dash

  1. With Wedge ▲ or Dash ▽ chosen, click a plain bond with the Bond or the Select tool. It becomes a single wedge or dash bond.

Flip the direction

  1. With the same button still chosen, click the wedge (or the dash) again. Its two ends swap: the narrow end moves to the other atom.

Take the stereo mark off

  1. Choose Single, Double, Triple or Arom. and click the bond. It becomes an ordinary bond of that order.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Which end is narrow

The narrow end of a wedge, and the end of a dash where the hashes are shortest, is at the atom the bond was started from. If you drew the bond from the wrong atom, click it again to flip it.

Flip needs the matching button

A click flips a bond only when the chosen button is the same kind as the bond. A click with Wedge ▲ on a dash turns it into a wedge, and does not flip it.

items.title: What it does
items.text: More Templates…, under the nine quick templates, opens the window Template Library. It lists many more building blocks in ten categories: aromatic carbocycles, six-membered N-heterocycles, five-membered heterocycles, fused bicyclics, saturated rings, nucleobases, functional groups and fragments, amino acids, metal coordination centres, and porphyrins and chlorins. Most of them are placed like the quick templates. The porphyrins and chlorins are different: they replace the whole drawing.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the section Templates of the left panel, click More Templates….
  2. Find the category you need and click the name of a template. Hold the pointer over a name to see its description, when it has one.
  3. For every category except the porphyrins and chlorins, the window closes and the template is ready to place, exactly as for a quick template: move it over the canvas, turn it with the wheel or ← and →, and click to place it. Cancel ✕ or Esc stops.
  4. For a porphyrin or a chlorin, the window closes and the molecule appears on the canvas at once, in place of what was there. The SMILES box shows the text that was imported.
  5. To close the window without choosing, click ✕ Close, click outside the window, or press Esc.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Porphyrins replace the drawing

Choosing one of the porphyrins or chlorins discards the molecule on the canvas. ↩ Undo brings it back as one step. Save your work first if you are unsure.

The coordination centres are a starting point

The templates of metal coordination centres place a metal and its neighbours in the shape named on the button (linear, trigonal planar, octahedral, and so on). Look at the elements they place before you use them; to change one, retype it with Choose the element.

Same behaviour as the quick templates

Placing, fusing, rotating and undoing work as described on Templates.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Templates of the left panel holds nine ready-made rings and ring systems: Benzene, Cyclohex, Cyclopent, Naph., Pyridine, Furan, Thioph., Imidaz. and 3-ring. You pick one, move a translucent copy over the canvas, turn it if you like, and click to place it. A template that lands on atoms you have already drawn is fused to them, so you can build a ring onto a chain or onto another ring.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Find the section Templates and click one of the nine buttons. The button is highlighted, a Cancel ✕ button appears under the grid, and a short hint shows how to place the template.
  2. Move the pointer over the canvas. A translucent copy of the template follows it. Atoms other than carbon are shown as coloured discs with their symbol.
  3. To turn the template, scroll the wheel, or press ← or →. Each step is 30°; hold Shift for 15°. On a touch screen, twist two fingers. Once the angle is not zero, the angle is written next to the pointer.
  4. To fuse the template to an atom you have drawn, bring one of its atoms close to that atom. The atoms that will merge turn green in the preview.
  5. Click to place the template. On a touch screen, lift your finger to place it.
  6. To change your mind, click Cancel ✕ or press Esc.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
One step, already tidied

Placing a template also runs the same tidy-up as ✦ Clean on the whole drawing (see Clean the 2D drawing). One ↩ Undo removes the template and the tidy-up together.

Fusing only to heavy atoms

A template atom merges only with a heavy atom that is within about half a bond length of it, and never with a hydrogen, even one that is hidden. If a ring atom lands on a carbon that carries hydrogens, the carbon becomes that ring atom, and the hydrogens it no longer needs are removed for you. A template atom never merges with another atom of the same template.

Placing a template ends the mode

After one click the template mode is over. Choose the button again to place the same ring twice.

Honeycomb background

With the honeycomb grid background and its Snap button on, a template snaps to the grid, and its angle goes to a multiple of 30°. Holding Alt suspends the snap. A template that would fuse to an atom you have drawn is left where the pointer is.

Rings and fragments not in the nine buttons are in the template library.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
The pane on the right, titled 3D PREVIEW, shows the three-dimensional structure that goes with your drawing: balls and sticks. It is a viewer only. You cannot draw, select or pick atoms in it; you draw in the 2D canvas on the left, and the pane follows.

A small label next to the title says where the structure comes from and whether it is up to date:

Label Meaning OPTIMIZED the result of Optimise IMPORTED read from a file (Load a structure) EMBED a quick preview built from the drawing, not optimised MOVED the result of a fragment move

Beside it, ✓ current means the structure belongs to the drawing as it is now, and ⚠ stale means the drawing has been edited since.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Draw a molecule. About half a second after your last edit, a preview appears in the pane (EMBED). The pane already holds the preview of the ethanol that MolBuild shows when it opens. If you click ✕ Clear, the pane keeps the last structure, marked ⚠ stale, until you draw something again. The text No 3D geometry yet and Run ⚡ Optimise or ⬆ Load a 3D file belongs to a pane that has never held a structure, which you will normally not see.
  2. Turn the structure: drag with the left mouse button (or one finger). Drag with the right or middle button to pan. Scroll the wheel to zoom. On a touch screen, one finger turns the structure, and two fingers pan and pinch to zoom.
  3. Click ⟲ Reset at the right end of the pane's header to bring back the first orientation, with the whole molecule in view.
  4. Click ⚡ Optimise to replace the preview by an optimised structure, or ⬆ Load to show a structure from a file.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The preview is not the optimised structure

EMBED is a fast guess at the geometry. Use it to see that the drawing makes sense, and run ⚡ Optimise before you export.

What an edit does to the pane

After you edit the drawing, the pane briefly shows ⚠ stale, and then it is ✓ current again. What it shows depends on where the structure came from. An EMBED preview is built again from the new drawing. A structure you loaded or optimised keeps its coordinates for the atoms that were already there, and its label (IMPORTED or OPTIMIZED); only the atoms you added are placed, next to their neighbours.

↻ Rebuild 3D from the drawing

When the pane holds coordinates read from a file, or the result of ⚡ Optimise (on a drawn molecule too), a button ↻ Rebuild 3D from the drawing appears in the header. It throws those coordinates away and builds a new structure from the drawing. The first click asks you to confirm; click again within four seconds, or nothing changes.

Hiding the pane

The handle at the right edge of the canvas hides and shows the pane, which the 2D canvas then fills. The pane keeps drawing while it is hidden. See Side panels.

Hydrogens in the 2D drawing

The H button in the toolbar affects the 2D drawing only; the 3D pane does not follow it.

items.title: What it does
items.text: ↩ Undo takes back the last change to the drawing and ↪ Redo brings it back. MolBuild remembers the last 30 changes. Each step holds the molecule together with its constraints, so undoing an edit also restores the constraints that went with it.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Click ↩ Undo in the toolbar, or press Ctrl/⌘ + Z.
  2. Click ↪ Redo, or press Ctrl/⌘ + Y (or Ctrl/⌘ + Shift + Z), to bring back what you undid.
  3. Keep clicking to go back or forward step by step. Nothing happens when there is nothing left to undo or redo.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A new edit ends the redo

As soon as you make a change after an undo, the steps you had undone are lost: Redo has nothing to bring back.

What counts as a step

Placing, deleting, retyping, a bond order, a charge, a move, a turn, a template, ✦ Clean and ✕ Clear are each one step. A click on an atom with the Select tool is also recorded, so the first Undo after it can look as if nothing happened.

Undo and the 3D pane

An undo or a redo stops an optimisation in progress, with the message Optimisation cancelled — the molecule changed, and clears the selection. The 3D pane catches up about half a second later; read its label. ✓ current means the structure belongs to the drawing you see. A ⚠ stale that stays on means it does not, which is what you see when you click ↩ Undo straight after ⚡ Optimise: optimise again before you export.

Only the drawing is undone

Zoom and pan, the H button and the grid background are not part of the history.

Keys and typing

The keys do nothing while the cursor is in a text box (the SMILES box, for example) or while a window is open.

items.title: What it is for
items.text:
MolViz shows one molecular geometry as balls and sticks. You open a file, turn the molecule, change how it looks, pick atoms and bonds, measure distances, angles, dihedrals and out-of-plane angles, draw arrows such as transition dipole moments, and save the result as an image, an animated GIF or a session you can come back to.

Open MolViz. It runs in your browser. It holds one molecule at a time: opening another file replaces the first.

items.title: Files it reads
items.text:
• .xyz files;
  • .molden files;
  • OpenMolcas .h5 or .hdf5 files. MolViz reads the geometry only, not orbitals or densities.

The page has these parts:

  • The toolbar, from the left: the back link OPAL, the version badge, Load File, Export, Atom Settings, Presets, Sessions, Center COM, Auto-orient, Spin, Tilt, Anim GIF, the name of the loaded file, Theme, and the ⓘ button, which opens a small window on how to cite OPAL and links to this tutorial.
  • The left panel, in five sections: Display, Atom Outline, Surface Finish, Background and Selection.
  • The view in the middle. Before any file is loaded it shows a welcome text. Afterwards it shows the molecule, a line with the number of atoms, bonds and vectors, and the corner button ⌂ Reset.
  • The right panel, in four sections: Vectors, Atom Labels, Measurements and Center of Mass.
  • The file bar along the bottom of the page: the name of the loaded file and the kind of file.
  • Windows that open over the view: Atom Settings, Presets, Sessions and the GIF window.

Sections of the side panels fold. How that works is explained once, in Parts of a tool page.

A usual order of work: open a file, look at it from several sides, set the look, then add labels, measurements or vectors, and finally export an image.

items.title: What it does
items.text: When one atom is selected, the section Selection lets you change the colour and the radius that MolViz uses for its element, and put a small marker beside the atom: a charge, a radical mark, a partial charge or a lone pair.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Click an atom. See Select atoms.
  2. In the section Selection, change Color with the colour box, or type a new Radius (from 0.1 to 3) and press Enter or leave the field.
  3. To put a marker beside the atom, press one of the buttons under Atom symbol: ⊕ (positive charge), ⊖ (negative charge), ✱ (radical or marker), δ+ (partial positive), δ− (partial negative) or ⊙ (lone pair dot).
  4. To remove the marker, press ✕, or press the same button again.
  5. To undo a colour and radius change for the element, press Reset element.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Colour and radius belong to the element, not to the atom

A change of colour or radius applies to every atom of the same element. The selected atom changes colour at once and the others follow at the next rebuild of the picture, for example when you change the radius or press Apply & Rebuild in Element colours and radii. The marker, in contrast, belongs to the one atom.

Markers are lost with the file

Loading another file clears all the markers. A session keeps them.

Markers and exported images

A marker is drawn over the view, and an exported image shows it only when you tick Include atom symbols in the Export menu. See Export images.

The size of the markers

The slider Symbol size in the section Atom Labels sets it. See Atom labels.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Background sets the colour behind the molecule and can fade the atoms that are far from you into that colour (fog).

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the left panel, find the section Background.
  2. Choose a colour with the colour box next to Color. The view changes at once. It starts as a dark blue.
  3. Tick Fog to fade distant atoms into the background colour.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Choose the colour before you tick Fog

The fog takes the background colour at the moment you tick it. If you change the colour afterwards, the fog keeps the old one. Untick Fog and tick it again.

Backgrounds in exported images

The background you choose here is what you see on screen. Images and GIFs can be exported with a transparent background instead; see Export images.

Background and presets

The background and the fog are not part of a preset. They are part of a session.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Two toolbar buttons put the molecule in a standard place. Center COM moves it so that its centre of mass is at the origin. Auto-orient does that and also turns the molecule so that its principal axes lie along the axes of the screen. The section Center of Mass in the right panel shows where the centre of mass is.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load a molecule. See Open a file.
  2. Press Center COM. The molecule is moved, the camera is fitted to it again, and a message says "Centered at center of mass".
  3. Press Auto-orient to turn the molecule too. The direction in which the molecule is widest lies along the horizontal axis of the screen, the middle direction is vertical, and the shortest direction points into the screen. The camera returns to the view along that last direction.
  4. In the right panel, find the section Center of Mass. It shows the x, y and z coordinates of the centre of mass, with three decimals. After either button the three values are close to zero.
  5. To return to the starting view without changing the coordinates, press ⌂ Reset in the corner of the view.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A file is centred when it is loaded

MolViz moves every molecule to its centre of mass when it opens the file, so Center COM changes nothing you can see until the coordinates have moved again. It also brings back the camera position if you moved the molecule sideways.

Auto-orient changes the coordinates, and there is no undo

Auto-orient rotates the atoms themselves, not only the view. The coordinates that the tool shows for an atom change, a session you save afterwards holds the rotated molecule, and ⌂ Reset does not turn it back. Load the file again to get the original orientation.

Masses and ghost centres

The centre of mass uses atomic masses. A ghost centre has no mass and is left out.

Before you record a GIF

The GIF window advises pressing Auto-orient first, so that the molecule turns about a sensible axis.

To turn the molecule with the mouse or your fingers, see Navigate the 3D view.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Display sets the size of the balls and sticks and controls how MolViz finds the bonds from the geometry. It can also draw hydrogen bonds as dashed lines.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the left panel, find the section Display. Its title shows the number of atoms and bonds, for example "12a 12b".
  2. Move Ball scale to make the atoms larger or smaller. It runs from 0.10 to 2.00 and starts at 0.50.
  3. Move Bond radius to make the sticks thicker or thinner. It runs from 0.03 to 0.40 and starts at 0.12. Both sliders act at once.
  4. To change which atoms are bonded, move Bond detect tol. (from 1.00 to 1.50, starting at 1.20). A pair of atoms is bonded when its distance is shorter than the sum of the two covalent radii times this value. A higher value gives more bonds.
  5. The tickbox Auto multi-bond lets MolViz give a shorter bond the order 2 or 3. When it is ticked, a second tickbox, Detect aromatic bonds, appears.
  6. Press Re-detect bonds. MolViz finds the bonds again with the current values, and a message says "Bonds re-detected".
  7. Tick Find H-bonds to draw a dashed line for every hydrogen bond found in the geometry. It acts at once.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The tolerance and Auto multi-bond need Re-detect bonds

Moving Bond detect tol. or ticking Auto multi-bond changes nothing in the picture by itself. Press Re-detect bonds afterwards. The tickbox Detect aromatic bonds is different: it finds the bonds again as soon as you tick or untick it.

Re-detecting throws away your bond edits

Every re-detection builds the whole list of bonds again. A bond you added, removed or changed by hand with Edit bonds is lost.

How Find H-bonds decides

A donor is a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O, F or S, and an acceptor is an N, O, F or S atom. A contact is drawn when the H···acceptor distance is at most 2.5 Å (2.9 Å for S), the donor···acceptor distance is at most 3.5 Å (3.9 Å when S is the donor or the acceptor), the angle donor–H···acceptor is at least 120°, and the acceptor is at least four bonds away from the hydrogen. The contacts are a separate layer: you cannot select them, a pair that already has a bond is drawn once as that bond, and they are not saved in the list of bonds. The option is off when MolViz starts, and a session remembers it.

The H-bond drawing is the same as a bond of order 0

A hydrogen bond you add yourself with H··· in Edit bonds looks the same, but it belongs to the list of bonds, so you can select and remove it.

items.title: What it does
items.text: MolViz finds bonds from the distances between atoms, and the result is not always what you want to show. You can add a bond between two atoms, change the type of a bond, and remove a bond. The types are a hydrogen bond (a dashed line), single, partial double, double, partial triple and triple.

items.title: How
items.text:
To add a bond:

  1. Click an atom, then hold Shift and click a second atom. See Select atoms. The section Selection shows the controls for adding a bond, under "Bond type:".
  2. Choose the type: H···, ─ ×1, ─·×1½, = ×2, =·×2½ or ≡ ×3. The single bond is chosen when you start.
  3. Press Add bond. A message says which kind of bond was added.

To change or remove a bond:

  1. Click the bond. The section Selection shows the bond, its length and its type.
  2. Press another type button to change the order. The picture changes at once.
  3. Press Remove bond, or press the Delete key.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A new bond replaces an old one

If the two atoms already have a bond, Add bond replaces it with the type you chose.

Re-detecting bonds throws your edits away

Re-detect bonds in Display settings builds the whole list again, and so does ticking or unticking Detect aromatic bonds. Edit the bonds last. A new file also clears them.

Hydrogen bonds

The type H··· is a dashed line between two atoms, whatever they are. It does not count as a bond when MolViz looks for hydrogen bonds on its own. For the automatic search, see Find H-bonds in Display settings.

The Delete key

The key works when a bond is selected and the cursor is not in a text or number field. It is not available on a touch screen without a keyboard; use Remove bond.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The window Atom Settings lists every element with its colour and its radius, so you can change them for the whole molecule at once. The starting values are the usual CPK colours and covalent radii.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press Atom Settings in the toolbar. The window Atom Visual Settings opens.
  2. Find your element. The elements in the molecule come first, with a coloured frame; the others follow.
  3. Choose a colour with the colour box, or type a radius in Å in the field Radius (Å).
  4. Press ↺ at the end of a row to put that element back to its default.
  5. Press Reset to CPK defaults to put every element back to its default.
  6. Press Apply & Rebuild. The window closes and the molecule is drawn again. A message says "Settings applied".

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Nothing changes until Apply & Rebuild

The colour boxes, the radii and the buttons ↺ and Reset to CPK defaults only edit the table. The molecule follows when you press Apply & Rebuild. To close the window without applying, press ✕ or Esc.

The radius is the size you see, not the bonding rule

The ball you see has the radius in this table times Ball scale (see Display settings). The rule that decides which atoms are bonded uses its own radii and does not change here.

One element at a time, from the molecule

You can also change the colour and the radius of one element from the section Selection, by clicking an atom of it. See Atom style and element symbols.

Where the changes are kept

Colours and radii stay when you load another file, are stored in a preset and in a session. They are lost when you reload the page.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Atom Labels writes the element symbol and the number of every atom beside it, for example C3 or N7. The numbers are the ones you need to read a measurement, to pick atoms for an input file, or to compare with a calculation.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the right panel, find the section Atom Labels.
  2. Tick Permanent labels. Every atom except hydrogen gets a label.
  3. Tick Show hydrogens to label the hydrogen atoms too.
  4. Move Font size (from 8 to 24, starting at 13) to make the labels larger or smaller.
  5. Symbol size (from 8 to 22, starting at 14) sets the size of the charge and radical markers you put beside atoms. See Atom style and element symbols.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What the number means

The number is the position of the atom in the file you opened, counted from 1, with all elements counted together: N7 is the seventh atom of the file, and it happens to be a nitrogen. The same number appears in the hover label of Select atoms and in the list of Measurements.

Labels in exported images

The labels on the screen are not part of an exported image by themselves. Tick Include atom labels in the Export menu to have them in the image. See Export images.

Labels and sessions

Whether the labels are on, with the two sizes, is saved in a session. It is not part of a preset.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Measurements measures four things between atoms you click: a Distance (two atoms, in Å), an Angle (three atoms), a Dihedral (four atoms in a chain) and an Out-of-plane angle (four atoms). Each measurement is drawn on the molecule with its value and is kept in a list.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the right panel, find the section Measurements. Its title shows how many measurements you have.
  2. Press the tool you want: Distance, Angle, Dihedral or Out-of-plane. The button lights up, and a line under the buttons says what to click.
  3. Click the atoms in the order given:
    • Distance: two atoms.
    • Angle: three atoms, the vertex (the atom at the corner of the angle) second.
    • Dihedral: four atoms in the order of the chain, 1–2–3–4.
    • Out-of-plane: four atoms. The bond runs from the first atom to the fourth, and the plane is the one of the second, third and fourth.
  4. Each atom you click is ringed and numbered. When the last atom is picked, a message says "Measurement added", and a row appears in the list with the value, the kind and the atoms, for example "C3 – N7".
  5. The tool stays on, so you can pick the next set at once. To stop, press the tool button again, or press Esc.
  6. In the list, tick or untick Value label and Atom labels for that measurement, change its colour with the colour box, or press ✕ to delete it. The slider Label size sets the size of the values on the picture.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What the values are

The distance is shown in Å with three decimals. The angle goes from 0° to 180°. The dihedral goes from −180° up to, but not including, 180°, with the sign that SLAPAF prints, and the out-of-plane angle goes from −90° to 90° with the sign SLAPAF prints too. Angles are shown with two decimals.

The numbers of the atoms

The atoms are named as in Atom labels: the element and the position in the file, such as C3. The same atom cannot be picked twice for one measurement.

A dihedral or an out-of-plane angle can have no value

When two neighbouring atoms of a dihedral are at the same place, or three atoms lie on a line, the angle is not defined. The row shows a dash, and a sentence under it says which atoms are the cause. The same holds for the out-of-plane angle when the first and the fourth atom coincide, or the second, third and fourth lie on a line.

Measurements and files

Loading another file clears the measurements. A session keeps them. They are drawn into exported images; see Export images.

items.title: What it does
items.text: MolViz opens one geometry at a time from an .xyz file, a .molden file or an OpenMolcas .h5 or .hdf5 file. It draws the atoms, finds the bonds from the distances, and moves the molecule so that its centre of mass sits in the middle of the view.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open MolViz.
  2. Press Load File in the toolbar, or click the box in the welcome text, and choose a file. You can also drop the file on the view. If you drop several files, only the first is read.
  3. A short message at the bottom of the view says how many atoms and bonds were found. The name of the file appears in the toolbar, and the file bar at the bottom shows the name and the kind of file: XYZ geometry, Molden file or OpenMolcas HDF5 geometry.
  4. In the left panel, the title of the section Display shows the same counts.
  5. To open another file, repeat step 2. The new molecule replaces the old one.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What each kind of file must contain

An .xyz file starts with the number of atoms, then one comment line, then one atom per line: the element symbol and three coordinates in Å. A Molden file is read from its [Atoms] section, in Å or in atomic units as the header of that section says. In a Molden file an element name with a serial number after it, as OpenMolcas writes it (C18), is accepted and read as the element. An .xyz file needs the plain element symbol. A text file that contains an [Atoms] section is read as Molden whatever its name.

OpenMolcas HDF5 files

MolViz reads the Cartesian coordinates of the first geometry in the file, and nothing else. For a file that uses symmetry it reads the full list of atoms when the file stores it; if it cannot, the message says "symmetric file: geometry not verified". A ghost centre (a centre without a nucleus) is drawn translucent, takes no bonds and does not count in the centre of mass.

A file that cannot be read empties the view

MolViz clears the old molecule before it reads the new file. If the new file fails, with a message such as "Could not parse file" or "This is not an HDF5 file.", the view is empty and you have to open a file again.

What a new file keeps and what it clears

Loading a file clears the selection, the measurements, the atom symbols and every bond you edited by hand. The vectors you drew, the element colours and radii, and the settings of the panels stay.

The coordinates are shifted

The molecule is moved so that its centre of mass is at the origin. The coordinates that MolViz shows for an atom are therefore not the ones in your file.

The ways of opening a file that all tools share are on Opening files.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Atom Outline draws a dark edge around each atom, which separates atoms that overlap in the picture. Surface Finish sets how the atoms and bonds catch the light, from matte to shiny.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the left panel, find the section Atom Outline.
  2. Move Thickness to set the width of the edge, from 0 (no outline) to 0.25. It starts at 0.055.
  3. Choose Outline color with the colour box. It starts as a near-black.
  4. Tick Auto-contrast to let MolViz choose a black or a light grey for each atom from the colour of that atom, instead of your colour.
  5. Find the section Surface Finish. Matte ←→ Shiny goes from 0 to 120 (it starts at 20), Specular level from 0 to 100 (it starts at 18) and Ambient light from 0 to 1.5 (it starts at 0.70). All three act at once.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A higher ambient light flattens the picture

Ambient light lights every surface equally. Raise it for a flat, even look; lower it, and raise Specular level, for a more three-dimensional one.

These settings go into presets

The outline settings and the three sliders of Surface Finish are stored when you save a preset, and in a session.

items.title: What it does
items.text: A preset keeps the look of the molecule under a name, so you can bring it back for another molecule. It holds the colours and radii of the elements and the sliders of the left panel that describe the look, and nothing about the molecule itself.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Set the look you want. See Element colours and radii, Display settings and Outline and surface finish.
  2. Press Presets in the toolbar. The window Visualization Presets opens.
  3. Type a name in the field and press Save. A message says the preset was saved, and it appears in the list under Saved presets.
  4. To use a preset later, open the window again and press Load beside its name. The window closes and the look changes.
  5. To delete a preset, press ✕ beside its name.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What a preset holds

The element colours and radii, Ball scale, Bond radius, Bond detect tol., the three sliders of Surface Finish, and the thickness, colour and Auto-contrast of Atom Outline. It does not hold the background, the fog, the labels, Find H-bonds, the ticks for multiple and aromatic bonds, the bonds or the camera. A session holds more.

A name used twice is overwritten

Saving under a name that already exists replaces the old preset without asking. A name with nothing in it is refused.

Presets stay in this browser

They are kept in the storage of the browser, for this address on this computer. They do not travel with a file, and clearing the data of the site in the browser deletes them. To carry a look to another computer, use the Export JSON button of Sessions.

Loading does not detect bonds again

A preset brings back Bond detect tol. but does not rebuild the bonds. Press Re-detect bonds if you want the new tolerance to apply.

More on what stays in the browser: What is stored in your browser.

items.title: What it does
items.text: You select an atom or a bond by clicking it. The section Selection in the left panel then shows what you picked and the controls that apply: the colour and radius of an atom, the type of a bond, the symbol of an atom. Selecting two atoms lets you add a bond between them.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the left panel, find the section Selection. Before you pick anything it says "Click atom or bond to select".
  2. Click an atom. It glows, and the section shows its element and its x, y and z coordinates in Å, with four decimals.
  3. To pick a second atom, hold Shift and click it. The section then shows the two elements, for example "C–N", and the controls for adding a bond.
  4. Click a bond to select it. The section shows the two elements, the bond length in Å and the bond type.
  5. To clear the selection, click empty space or press a Clear button in the section.
  6. Move the mouse over an atom without clicking: a small label shows its element and number and its coordinates.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Two atoms at most

Shift-click on a third atom drops the older of the two and keeps the newer. Shift-click on a selected atom deselects it.

A click is not a drag

If the pointer moves more than a few pixels between pressing and releasing the button, MolViz takes it as a drag that turns the molecule, and selects nothing.

The number of an atom

The number after the element, in the hover label, in atom labels and in the measurements, is the position of the atom in the file, counted from 1. The coordinates are those of the molecule after it was moved to its centre of mass, not those of your file. The hover label needs a mouse; a touch screen has no hover.

While you measure, a click measures

When a tool of Measurements is active, a click on an atom is a pick for the measurement and does not change the selection.

  • Measure distances and angles

items.title: What it does
items.text: A session keeps the whole scene under a name: the atoms, the bonds, the vectors, the measurements, the element colours and radii, the settings of the panels, and the zoom. You can store it in the browser, or save it as a file that you can open on another computer.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press Sessions in the toolbar. The window Sessions opens.
  2. To keep the scene in the browser, type a name under Save current state and press Save. The session appears under Saved sessions, the newest first, with its date and its number of atoms.
  3. To bring one back, press Load beside its name. The window closes, and the scene replaces the current one.
  4. To delete one, press ✕ beside its name.
  5. To save a file, press Export JSON. The file is named after the loaded file, with .molviz.json at the end.
  6. To open such a file, press Import JSON and choose it. A message says "Session loaded", or "Invalid session file" if the file is not one.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The turn of the molecule is not saved

A session keeps the atoms as they are in the scene, the zoom and the sideways shift, but not the angle to which you turned the molecule with the mouse. A restored scene opens in the starting orientation. Rotation made with Auto-orient is kept, because it changed the atoms. See Centre and orient.

Sessions in the browser stay in this browser

They live in the storage of the browser, for this address on this computer, and are deleted when you clear the data of the site. Use Export JSON for anything you want to keep or to move.

What a restored session replaces

Loading a session replaces the molecule, the bonds, the vectors and the measurements. The file bar then shows the name and the words Saved session. The selection is not kept.

Presets are smaller

A preset holds only the look. A session holds the molecule too.

More on storage: What is stored in your browser. On a tablet or phone the exported file goes through the share sheet; see Saving files on iOS.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Vectors draws arrows on the molecule from numbers you type: a transition dipole moment, a dipole moment, or any direction you want to show. MolViz does not compute them; it draws what you give it.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the right panel, open the section Vectors. It is folded when MolViz starts.
  2. Type the components in X, Y and Z.
  3. Type a Label if you want one, choose a colour, and decide with Double-headed whether the arrow has a head at both ends.
  4. Press Add Vector. The arrow appears, and a message names it.
  5. In the list below, each vector has its colour, its label (you can edit both), the buttons ⇔ or ⇒ (switch between double and single head), the eye (show or hide) and ✕ (delete), with its components and its length |v|.
  6. Scale factor (from 0.10 to 5, starting at 1) makes all arrows longer or shorter. Arrow radius (from 0.02 to 0.30, starting at 0.08) makes them thicker.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Where the arrow is drawn

The arrow is centred on the centre of mass of the molecule and points along (X, Y, Z). Its length is the length of the vector times Scale factor, in Å. A vector with all three components zero is refused.

Vectors do not turn with Auto-orient

Auto-orient rotates the atoms but not the vectors. Components typed for the axes of your file no longer fit the molecule afterwards. Orient first, then add the vectors in the new axes, or leave the molecule as it was loaded. See Centre and orient.

Writing labels

The section gives three examples. S_0 -> S_1 writes subscripts, S^{T_1} writes a superscript, and \mu_{x} gives a Greek letter.

Vectors stay when you open another file

They are not cleared by a new file, so you can draw the same arrow on several molecules. A session keeps them, and so does an exported image.
