items.title: What it is for
items.text:
OrbViz draws the orbitals and the electron density of a calculation done with OpenMolcas. You open the file the program wrote, pick an orbital from a list, and see its lobes around the molecule. You can also draw the density of a state, the difference between the densities of two states, and prepare the block of orbital exchanges that the RASSCF module reads when you want a different active space.

Open OrbViz. It runs in your browser. It holds one file at a time: opening another file replaces the first.

items.title: Files it reads
items.text:
• OpenMolcas .h5 or .hdf5 files written by the SCF or RASSCF module. These hold the orbitals, so you can see orbitals; a RASSCF file also holds the densities of its states.
  • .molden files. They give the orbitals and one density from the orbital occupations, but no density of separate states.
  • A RASSI or a SLAPAF .h5 file is opened for its geometry only, with a message that says why there is nothing to draw. A RASSI file is read in RassiViz.

The page has these parts:

  • The toolbar, from the left: the back link OPAL, the version badge, Open File, Save State, Load State, PNG, SVG (image), SVG (vector) with its choice of look (Gradient, Flat, Print (white)), Std. Sets, Spin, Tilt, Anim GIF, a line of status text, Theme and the ⓘ button, which opens a small window on how to cite OPAL and links to this tutorial.
  • The left panel, in three sections: Molecule, Atoms and Bonds.
  • The view in the middle. Before a file is loaded it shows a welcome text. Afterwards it shows the molecule and whatever surface you switched on.
  • The right panel, in six sections: Surface Finish, Advanced, Molecular Orbitals, Active Space · ALTEr, Orbital Order · ALTEr and Electron Density.
  • The file bar along the bottom of the page: the name of the loaded file and the kind of file.
  • Windows that open over the view: the one of Std. Sets and the two of the GIF export.

Short messages appear over the view when something succeeds or fails, and go away by themselves after a few seconds. The status text in the toolbar tells you what OrbViz is doing, for example which orbital it is computing.

Sections of the side panels fold. How that works is explained once, in Parts of a tool page. When a file is loaded only Molecule, Atoms, Bonds and Molecular Orbitals are open; fold out the others when you need them.

A usual order of work: open a file, look at it from several sides, choose an orbital in the list, set the surface (contour value, opacity, colours), and finally export an image. The density, the density difference and the two ALTEr sections are used when you need them.

items.title: What it does
items.text: RASSCF takes its active orbitals from the orbitals of the starting file, in the order they have there. When the orbitals you want are not in the right positions, you tell RASSCF to exchange pairs of orbitals with an ALTEr block in its input. This section of OrbViz works out that block for you. You give the sizes of the spaces, look at the orbitals, say for each one which space it should be in, and OrbViz writes the block to paste into the input.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open the file of the orbitals to start from, for example the SCF file. In the right panel, fold out the section Active Space · ALTEr.
  2. Tick Select the active space. If the box is grey, the message under it says why; see the notes below.
  3. Fill in the five numbers: RAS1 orbitals, RAS2 orbitals, RAS3 orbitals, Active electrons and Molecular charge. RAS2 orbitals and Active electrons start empty, the others at 0.
  4. A line shows the number of electrons, the number of inactive orbitals and the number of secondary orbitals that follow from your numbers. The table below it has one row for each space (inactive, RAS1, RAS2, RAS3, secondary), with the Positions it has in the file, the number Chosen and a sign.
  5. In the orbital list of the section Molecular Orbitals, the column Type is replaced by Now, the space of the position the orbital sits in, and Move to, a menu where you choose the space you want for it. Choose a space for each orbital that must move.
  6. Watch the table: a ✓ in the last column means that the space has as many orbitals as positions, +2 or -1 says how many more or fewer orbitals you chose for it than it has positions. Move orbitals until every row shows ✓.
  7. When all rows show ✓, the box below the buttons holds the block. Press Copy to put it on the clipboard, or Download to save it as a text file named after your file with _ALTEr.txt added.
  8. Paste the block into the RASSCF input. Reset choices puts every orbital back in the space it sits in.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Only molecules without symmetry

The section works for files without symmetry (point group C1). For a file with several symmetry species the box stays grey and a message gives their number. It is also grey when the section Orbital Order · ALTEr is on: switch that one off first.

The block

The block starts with ALTEr and the number of pairs. For each pair there is a comment line that starts with a star and names the two orbitals, their new spaces, their energies (in hartree) and their occupations, and a line such as 1 12 15 that exchanges the orbitals in positions 12 and 15. The numbers are the positions in the file, as listed in the orbital list. If every orbital already sits in the space you chose, no block is needed, and a message says so.

At most 16 pairs

RASSCF accepts at most 16 pairs. If a choice would need more, OrbViz does not accept it: the menu returns to its old value and a message says RASSCF accepts at most 16 pairs; run RASSCF with these swaps first, then check the new orbitals again for any further swaps.

Choices that cannot be written

OrbViz writes exchanges of pairs. If a choice would send orbitals round three or more spaces, it says so and names the orbitals; change the choices so that two spaces exchange orbitals. If the numbers are impossible, for example more active electrons than electrons, or an odd number of electrons outside the active space, the message says that too.

Changing a number

Changing a number that alters the size of a space clears your choices. They are not saved with the state: they are lost when you open another file.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The sections Atoms and Bonds of the left panel set how the atoms and the bonds are drawn, find the bonds again with other settings, and let you add, change or remove a bond by hand. The bonds are only a picture: they are found from the distances, and they do not change the orbitals.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the section Atoms, move Ball radius scale (0.1 to 1.2, starting at 0.25) to make all the balls larger or smaller.
  2. Under it, the table has one row for each element in the molecule. Click the colour swatch to choose a colour for that element, and move the slider in the column R (0.3 to 2.0, starting at 1.0) to change the radius of that element only.
  3. In the section Bonds, move Bond radius (0.02 to 0.3, starting at 0.09) for the thickness of the sticks. Both radius sliders act at once.
  4. Move Bond tolerance (0.8 to 1.4, starting at 1.20) and press ↺ Re-detect bonds. Two atoms are bonded when their distance is smaller than the sum of their covalent radii times the tolerance. The message says how many bonds were found. The tolerance acts only when you press the button.
  5. Tick Auto multi-bond to let OrbViz find double, triple and partial bonds from the distances; it takes effect the next time bonds are found, so press ↺ Re-detect bonds after ticking it. Tick Detect aromatic bonds (it appears only when Auto multi-bond is on) to find aromatic bonds as well; this one finds the bonds again at once.
  6. Tick Find H-bonds to draw a dashed line for each hydrogen bond found from the geometry. They form a separate layer; they are not added to the list of bonds.
  7. To edit a bond, click an atom: its name, its number and its coordinates in Å appear in the section Bonds. Hold Shift and click a second atom. Choose a bond type among the six buttons (H···, single, partial double, double, partial triple, triple) and press Add bond. A bond that already joined the two atoms is replaced.
  8. To change or remove a bond, click the bond itself. Its length in Å and its type are shown. Press another type to change it, or Remove bond (or the Delete key) to remove it. Clear drops the selection.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Re-detect bonds replaces the whole list

↺ Re-detect bonds, and ticking Detect aromatic bonds, find all the bonds again. The bonds you added, changed or removed by hand are lost.

The tolerance does nothing until you press the button

The slider Bond tolerance changes its number at once, but the bonds change only when you press ↺ Re-detect bonds.

Bonds in a saved state

The bonds, with the changes you made, are kept in the file written by Save State. See Save and load a state.

items.title: What it does
items.text: OrbViz subtracts the density of one state from the density of another and draws where the density has grown and where it has shrunk, as two surfaces. This shows, for an excitation, where the electrons come from and where they go.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open a RASSCF file with at least two states. In the right panel, fold out the section Electron Density.
  2. Find the second part of the section, below the line. Tick Density difference.
  3. Choose the two states with the menus State A and − B. They start with the first state as A and the second as B, so the caption starts as Δρ = ρ(S₀) − ρ(S₁) for a singlet file. The caption always shows the formula with the names of the chosen states.
  4. Read the colours in the caption: a blue surface is where Δρ is positive, the density that state A has more than state B (the caption calls it donor), and a red surface is where Δρ is negative (acceptor).
  5. Move Contour (|Δρ|) to change the value of the surfaces, or type an exact value in the box. The same value is used for the blue and the red surface.
  6. Move Opacity (0.05 to 1, starting at 0.60) and choose Quality, Fast (flat) or Smooth.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Choose two different states

If both menus show the same state, OrbViz draws nothing and a message asks you to select two different states. A file with only one state, such as a Molden file, always gets this message.

Needs density matrices

The difference is computed from the density matrices of the two states. A file with several states but no density matrices gets the message Density matrices not available — cannot compute difference. A RASSCF file with symmetry and several states gets the message about symmetry described on Electron density.

The same rules as the density

The range of the slider, the starting value, the grid shared with the orbitals and the Fast (auto), High quality and Diffuse / Rydberg choices work as for the density. The starting value encloses 85 percent of the absolute value of Δρ. Drawing the difference removes the orbital or the density that was on show.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Orbitals made of very diffuse basis functions, for example Rydberg orbitals or orbitals on a ghost centre, reach far from the molecule. The ordinary grid ends 5 bohr beyond the outermost atoms and cuts such a lobe. The option Diffuse / Rydberg makes the grid larger so that the lobe is drawn whole.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the section Molecular Orbitals, tick Diffuse / Rydberg. The small i beside it repeats, as a tooltip, that the grid is enlarged and that computing and drawing become noticeably slower.
  2. A message says Diffuse/Rydberg mode enabled — grid recompute will take longer. OrbViz starts the grids again.
  3. If an orbital was on show, it is drawn again on the new grid. Otherwise click a row of the orbital list.
  4. Untick the option to go back to the ordinary grid; a message says the mode is disabled.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
How large the grid becomes

OrbViz sizes the margin from the most diffuse function of the basis set. It is never smaller than the ordinary 5 bohr and never larger than 60 bohr. The grid also gets more points: up to 64 along each side in Fast (auto) and 80 in High quality, instead of 42 and 60. If the basis set asks for more than the largest margin, a message says the margin was clamped and the outermost part of a lobe may still be cut.

Use it only when you need it

The mode is slower, and it is switched off every time you open a file. It is kept by Save State; see Save and load a state.

items.title: What it does
items.text: OrbViz draws the electron density of one state as a single surface: the surface where the density has the value you choose. For a RASSCF file the density of each state comes from its density matrix over the active orbitals, with the inactive orbitals doubly occupied.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open a RASSCF file. In the right panel, fold out the section Electron Density.
  2. Tick Show density.
  3. Under State for density, press the button of the state you want. Each button names the state and gives its energy in hartree, for example S₁ (-123.4567 Ha). For a triplet the states are named T1, T2 and so on, for a quintet Qu1, Qu2 and so on.
  4. Move Contour (ρ) to change the value of the surface, or type an exact value in the box and press Enter or leave the box.
  5. Move Opacity (0.05 to 1, starting at 0.50) to make the surface more or less transparent.
  6. Choose Quality: Fast (flat) or Smooth.
  7. Press another state button to see the density of another state with the same settings.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The surface follows the grid

As for orbitals, the slider is logarithmic and its range follows the largest density on the grid. The first time the density is drawn, OrbViz sets the value so that the surface encloses 85 percent of the density; a value you set is kept. See Show an orbital isosurface.

The first time takes longer

The density needs the orbital grids of the inactive and active orbitals. OrbViz computes the ones it does not have, and a message says how many. The orbital grid is shared with Molecular Orbitals, so the choices Fast (auto) and High quality and the mode Diffuse / Rydberg there also apply here. The choice Quality of this section only decides how smooth the surface is made.

A Molden file, or a file without density matrices

A Molden file has one state and no density matrices, so there is a single state button. For it, and for any file that has orbitals but no density matrices, the density is made from the occupations of the orbitals.

Files with symmetry

OrbViz has not checked how a RASSCF file with symmetry stores its density matrices. For such a file it draws neither the density nor the density difference, and a message says so; the orbitals are drawn.

One surface at a time

Drawing the density removes the orbital or the density difference on show.

items.title: What it does
items.text: OrbViz opens one file at a time: an OpenMolcas .h5 or .hdf5 file, or a .molden file. It draws the atoms, finds the bonds from the distances, fills the orbital list, and keeps the orbitals ready to be drawn.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open OrbViz.
  2. Press Open File in the toolbar, or click the box in the welcome text, and choose a file. You can also drop the file on the view. If you drop several files, only the first is read.
  3. A spinner with the words Loading … file is shown while the file is read. OrbViz decides from the first bytes whether the file is HDF5 or Molden text, whatever its name.
  4. When it is done, a message says Loaded and the name of the file, and the toolbar shows the name, the number of atoms, of orbitals and of states. The file bar at the bottom shows the name and the kind of file, for example OpenMolcas HDF5 (RASSCF), OpenMolcas HDF5 (SCF) or Molden file.
  5. In the left panel, the section Molecule shows the formula, the number of atoms, of basis functions, of states and of primitives, and a line with the number of electrons, the nuclear charge and the net charge.
  6. In the right panel, the section Molecular Orbitals lists the orbitals; see The orbital list.
  7. To open another file, repeat step 2. The new molecule replaces the old one.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A file that cannot be read

OrbViz clears the old molecule before it reads the new file. If the new file is refused, the view is empty and you have to open a file again. The message says why. A file that does not start as an HDF5 file is read as Molden text, so a file of another kind gets a message from the Molden reader, for example Error: Molden: no atoms found in [Atoms] section. For an HDF5 file it can be that the file uses a newer file layout or a feature OPAL cannot read yet (the file itself is not damaged), or that it holds no orbitals.

Files that hold a geometry but no orbitals

A RASSI file or a geometry-optimisation (SLAPAF) file is opened for its geometry, and a message for a few seconds says why there is nothing to plot: This is a RASSI file: it contains no orbitals. Open the RASSCF or SCF file from the same job in OrbViz, or open this file in RassiViz. The file bar then says OpenMolcas HDF5 (RASSI) or OpenMolcas HDF5 (SLAPAF).

Molecules with symmetry

A file from a calculation with symmetry is read through the matrix that turns the orbitals of each symmetry species into orbitals on all the atoms, so its orbitals are drawn on the whole molecule. A RASSCF file with symmetry holds density matrices that OrbViz has not checked: its density and density difference are not drawn, and a message says so. The two ALTEr sections need a molecule without symmetry.

The electron count

The line Electrons in the section Molecule adds up the occupations of the orbitals and compares the result with the nuclear charge. If the net charge is larger than 2 in size, a warning under it tells you to check INACtive and NACTel in the RASSCF input. A file that stores no occupations says Electrons: not stored in this file.

What a new file clears and what stays

Loading a file clears the selection, the bonds you edited, the choices in the two ALTEr sections, the diffuse mode, the orbital grids, and the contour values, which go back to their starting values. The colours and radii of the elements, the sliders of the finish and the choice of colour scheme stay.

The ways of opening a file that all tools share are on Opening files.

items.title: What it does
items.text: OrbViz draws an orbital as two surfaces: one where the orbital is positive and one where it is negative, each at the value of the orbital that you choose. This value is the contour value. You also choose the colours, the transparency and the quality of the surface.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Click a row in the orbital list; see The orbital list. The surface appears.
  2. Under Show orbital, find the row Contour (|ψ|). Move the slider to change the contour value, or type an exact value in the box at its right and press Enter or leave the box. The surface is redrawn each time.
  3. Move Opacity (0 to 1, starting at 0.70; 1 is opaque) to make the surface more or less transparent.
  4. Under Colour scheme, click one of the six pairs. The first colour is for the positive lobes, the second for the negative ones: Blue / Red (the starting choice), Yellow / Cyan, Gold / Green, Purple / Orange, White / Coral and Black / White.
  5. Choose Quality: Fast (auto) or High quality. The line under it names the grid in use, in the form Grid: Fast (N³ auto) or Grid: High quality (N³ + blur + smooth), where N is the number of points along each side; N depends on the size of the basis set for Fast (auto).
  6. Click another row to show another orbital with the same settings.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The slider follows the orbital's grid

The slider is logarithmic: it reaches four decades below the largest value found on the grid of the orbital. When an orbital is first drawn, OrbViz sets the contour value so that the surface encloses 85 percent of the squared orbital. When you move the slider or type a value, OrbViz keeps your value, and it keeps it for the next orbitals too. A value typed in the box is kept exactly, and the slider widens to hold it. A value of zero or a text that is not a positive number is not accepted, and the box goes back to the old value.

Only one kind of surface at a time

Drawing an orbital removes the density or the density difference that was on show, and the other way round.

Black / White

The positive lobes are drawn in a dark grey, because pure black is not visible on the dark background of the view. The scheme keeps its name.

The first time takes longer

The first time an orbital is drawn, OrbViz computes its values on a grid. It keeps the grid, so going back to the same orbital, or changing the contour value, is quick. Changing Quality or Diffuse / Rydberg makes OrbViz start the grid again.

Transparency in the exported images

A translucent surface on a transparent background in an exported image has its own warnings; see Export an animated GIF.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Molecular Orbitals lists every orbital of the file, with its energy, its occupation and its type. You click a row to draw that orbital.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the right panel, find the section Molecular Orbitals. It is open when a file is loaded.
  2. Read the table. Each row is one orbital, numbered from 1 in the order of the file:
    • #: the number of the orbital;
    • E (eV): its energy in electronvolt;
    • Occ: its occupation, as a short bar and a number with three decimals (2 for a doubly occupied orbital);
    • Type: the space it belongs to, one of occ, ras1, ras2, ras3, act, virt or del.
  3. Scroll the table. When the file is opened, it scrolls to the first active orbital by itself.
  4. Click a row. It is highlighted, the box Show orbital is ticked, and the orbital is drawn; the first time for an orbital the status text in the toolbar says Computing MO and its number. See Show an orbital isosurface.
  5. Untick Show orbital to hide the surface, and tick it again to bring the current orbital back.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Where the type comes from

A RASSCF file records the space of each orbital, and OrbViz shows it: occ is an inactive orbital, ras1, ras2 and ras3 are the three active spaces, virt is a secondary orbital and del a deleted one. The label act is used for an orbital that the file marks as active without naming a space. A file without this information, such as an SCF file or a Molden file, gets the type from the occupation: occ above 1.95, act above 0.05, otherwise virt.

The numbers are the file's numbers

OrbViz does not sort the orbitals. The numbers in the first column are the positions in the file, and they are the numbers you give to RASSCF in an ALTEr block. See Choose the active space (ALTEr).

Another view of the list

When you switch on Select the active space the column Type gives way to two columns, Now and Move to.

items.title: What it does
items.text: When the orbitals of a file are not in order of occupation, you may want the next RASSCF run to start with them in that order. Reorder by occupation sorts all the orbitals of the file together by their occupation, the most occupied first, whatever their space, and writes the ALTEr block that makes RASSCF do it. It does not move any orbital in OrbViz itself, and it does not change the file.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open the RASSCF file. In the right panel, fold out the section Orbital Order · ALTEr.
  2. Tick Reorder by occupation. If the box is grey, the message under it says why; see the notes below.
  3. A line gives the number of orbitals and the number of swaps needed to sort them. The box holds the block.
  4. Press Copy to put the block on the clipboard, or Download to save it as a text file named after your file with _reorder_ALTEr.txt added.
  5. Paste the block into the RASSCF input, and keep the order of its lines.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The lines depend on each other

RASSCF applies the lines one after another, each to the order that the previous ones left. An orbital may appear in several lines, and the order of the lines matters. Orbitals with the same occupation keep their order. The numbers are the positions in the file, as listed in the orbital list, and the occupations used are the averaged ones.

At most 16 swaps

RASSCF accepts at most 16 pairs. If more swaps are needed, OrbViz writes the first 16, adds a comment line that says how many are needed, and a message says to run RASSCF with them, open the new orbitals and reorder again.

Nothing to do

If the orbitals are already in order of decreasing occupation, there is no block and a message says so.

Only molecules without symmetry

As in Choose the active space (ALTEr), the box is grey for a file with several symmetry species, and while Select the active space is on. The two sections exclude each other: each says to switch the other one off.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Save State writes the way the picture looks into a small text file: the colours, the sliders, the contour values, the orbital and the state on show, the bonds, and the position of the camera. Load State reads such a file back, so that you can return to the same picture, or give the same picture to another molecule.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Set up the picture you want to keep.
  2. Press Save State in the toolbar. The browser saves a file named orbviz_state_ followed by a long number (the time of saving, in milliseconds since 1 January 1970) and .json. A message says State saved.
  3. Later, open the file of the molecule again with Open File.
  4. Press Load State and choose the .json file. A message says State loaded.
  5. If an orbital was on show when you saved, it is drawn again after about one second.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What is kept

The colours and radii of the elements, the ball and bond radii, the three finish sliders, the two tessellation sliders, the contour values of the orbital, the density and the difference, the three opacities, the colour scheme, the choice of Quality for the orbitals, the mode Diffuse / Rydberg, the bonds, Find H-bonds, the orbital that was current, whether it was on show, and the position and orientation of the camera.

Open the molecule first

Load State applies the settings to the molecule that is open now. If the bonds in the file were saved from another molecule, because the number of atoms or their sequence of elements differs, the appearance is restored, the bonds are left as they are, and a message says State was saved for a different molecule — appearance restored, bonds left unchanged.

What is not kept

Loading a state does not bring back the density or the density difference that was on show, the state chosen for the density, the choice of Quality for the density and for the difference, the choices made in the two ALTEr sections, or the molecule itself. Files saved by older versions of OrbViz, under the name molcas_state_, still load.

Saving on an iPhone or iPad

Files are saved differently there; see Save files on iPhone and iPad.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Std. Sets gives four ready-made looks for the atoms and the bonds, so that you do not have to set the two radius sliders by hand. The four looks are fixed: OrbViz has no way to save a look of your own in this window.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press Std. Sets in the toolbar. A window titled Visualisation Standards opens, with four rows.
  2. Press Apply on the row you want:
    • Ball & Stick (default): ball scale 0.25, bond radius 0.09;
    • CPK / spacefill: ball scale 1.0, bond radius 0 (the bonds disappear inside the balls);
    • Large ball & stick: ball scale 0.45, bond radius 0.11;
    • Wireframe / sticks: ball scale 0.08, bond radius 0.06.
  3. The window closes by itself, and the two sliders Ball radius scale and Bond radius in the left panel move to the new values. The set is applied exactly, even where a value lies below the lowest mark of its slider (a bond radius of 0, a ball scale of 0.08): the slider then stands at its lowest mark.
  4. To leave the window without choosing, press Close or the Esc key.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Only two sliders change

A set changes the ball scale and the bond radius, and nothing else: the colours and the radii of single elements, the finish and the bonds themselves stay as they are.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The sections Surface Finish and Advanced of the right panel set how shiny the atoms, the bonds and the surfaces look, how much ambient light there is, and how smooth an orbital surface is made.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the right panel, find the section Surface Finish. It has three sliders:
    • Shininess (0 to 120, starting at 40): how sharp the highlight is;
    • Specular (0 to 255, starting at 80): how bright the highlight is;
    • Ambient (0 to 100, starting at 30): how much light falls on every part of the scene, even where the direct light does not reach.
  2. Move a slider. The atoms, the bonds and the surfaces change at once.
  3. For a smoother orbital surface, find the section Advanced and read its short text: it describes the way OrbViz divides each flat triangle of the surface into smaller ones and rounds them.
  4. Move Tess. level (1 to 5, starting at 2). The line under it gives the number of triangles: 1 is off, 2 gives four times as many, 3 nine times, 4 sixteen times, 5 twenty-five times.
  5. Move Curvature (0 to 1, starting at 0.60). At 0 the new triangles stay flat, at 1 they follow the full curvature.
  6. To see the effect, set Quality to High quality in the section Molecular Orbitals and show an orbital.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The two sections work on orbitals in High quality only

Tess. level is marked (HQ only): the section Advanced acts on orbital surfaces when Quality in Molecular Orbitals is High quality. With Fast (auto) the surface is not subdivided. The density and the density difference have their own Quality choice and do not follow these two sliders; see Electron density.

Saved with the state

The three finish sliders and the two tessellation sliders are kept by Save State; see Save and load a state.

items.title: What it is for
items.text:
PathVibViz shows the geometries that an OpenMolcas calculation passes through, and the vibrations of a frequency calculation. You load the file of a minimum search, a transition-state search, an IRC or MEP, a conical-intersection search or a frequency job. All the geometries of the run are drawn in one set of axes, so you can see what moves. You scrub through them, read the energy and the forces of each, plot how they converge, measure distances and angles along the run, and animate a vibration. For a run that searched for a conical intersection it also characterises the intersection.

Open PathVibViz. It runs in your browser and does not send your file anywhere.

items.title: Files it reads
items.text:
• The SLAPAF file of a run, .h5 or .hdf5: a minimum or transition-state search, an IRC or an MEP, or a search for a conical intersection. A file with symmetry shows all the atoms of the molecule.
  • The frequency file of a run, .freq.h5. You may give it together with the run's .scf.h5, which lets the tool recognise ghost atoms.
  • Molden files, .molden: the geometries of an optimisation, or the vibrations of a frequency job.

Load a file says what each kind gives you and what the tool does when a file holds less.

The page has these parts:

  • The toolbar, from the left: the back link, the version badge, Load File, Save State, Save XYZ, Save path XYZ, Save PNG, SVG (vector) with its choice of look, SVG (path) with the number of steps it draws, Load State, Conical intersection, the name of the loaded file, Theme and the ⓘ button, which opens a small window on how to cite OPAL.
  • The left panel, in three sections: Display, File and Measurements.
  • The view in the middle, with the scrubber along its bottom edge (‹, a slider, › and the frame count), a line that says how many atoms and which frame, and the ⌂ Reset button. Before a file is loaded it shows a welcome text.
  • The right panel, in up to six sections: Frame, Path, Conical intersection, Convergence, Vibrations and What is shown. Path and Conical intersection appear only for a file that has them.
  • The file bar along the bottom of the page, with the role of each loaded file, its name and its kind.
  • Three windows that open over the view: the enlarged plot, the conical-intersection window and the infrared spectrum.

Sections of the side panels fold. How that works is explained once, in Parts of a tool page.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The window Conical intersection characterises the intersection found in the last iteration of the file: a table of the numbers that describe it, a picture of the two energy surfaces round the intersection (the cones), and two curves, the gradient and the mixing angle, as you walk round the intersection. The method is that of J. Chem. Theory Comput. 12 (2016) 3636, which the window names.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the SLAPAF file of a conical-intersection search and make sure the button Conical intersection in the toolbar is on. See Conical intersections.
  2. Press Conical intersection in the toolbar, or Open window in the section of the same name of the right panel.
  3. Read the table. For the whole characterisation it holds the pitch δ, the asymmetry Δ, the relative tilt σ, the tilt heading θ, the quantities P and B, the type of the intersection, the heading and the mixing angle of this solution, and the direction of h. It also names the two states, gives their energies and the energy gap, and the iteration used, which is the last. A quantity that is not defined says so.
  4. Press Copy results as text to copy the table to the clipboard, one row to a line, with a tab between the label and the value.
  5. Look at the picture of the cones: the upper and the lower sheet over the branching plane, with x along g and y along h, coloured by the mixing angle. Drag to turn it. The wheel beside it shows the colour of each mixing angle; the two white marks are the wave functions at heading 0 and the red marks are those of this solution. Untick Branching plane to hide the grid at the intersection energy.
  6. Press Cones PNG to save the picture of the cones.
  7. Read the two curves under the table: Radial gradient (the average, the difference, the upper and the lower sheet) and Mixing angle, each against the heading in the branching plane, from 0 to 360 degrees. The dashed line in the second is the heading of this solution.
  8. To save a curve, choose Radial gradient or Mixing angle with Plot to export and press PNG, SVG or gnuplot ZIP.
  9. Close the window with ✕ Close, with Esc, or with a click outside it.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
When the file allows less

If the file gives the gradient difference but not the whole branching plane, the window says what is missing and shows the table with the text for g only. There is no cone and no curve, and the buttons that need them are off. See Conical intersections.

The search statements

The table can carry a row Search, which says whether the last geometry is at the intersection or the search stopped with the gap open, or was run at a fixed gap, and a row Coupling vector when the coupling is only approximate. Read them before you quote a number.

The mixing angle is the log's

The heading and the direction of h in the table are those OpenMolcas prints as the arbitrary values for this solution, so the numbers can be compared with the log.

A file with state tracking

With a root mapping in the file the table lists the energies in the order stored and notes that the mapping is not applied.

Saved curves

The saved curves are drawn dark on white. The pictures of the cones are saved as they are on the screen. See Export plots.

items.title: What it does
items.text: When SLAPAF searches for a conical intersection between two states, its file holds the gradient difference of the two states and, in the best case, the coupling vector between them. Together they span the branching plane, the two directions that lift the degeneracy. PathVibViz draws the two vectors, g and h, on the molecule, swings the molecule along each, and, when the file allows, characterises the intersection in a window of its own. This page is about the vectors on the molecule; the numbers, the cones and the curves are on The conical-intersection window.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the SLAPAF HDF5 file of a conical-intersection search. See Load a file.
  2. Look at the toolbar button Conical intersection. It is on when the file gives enough to show something. If it is off, hold the pointer over it: the tooltip gives the reason.
  3. Open the section Conical intersection in the right panel. The sentence at its top says what the file allows, in one of four cases (below). With the whole characterisation the sentence is empty.
  4. Press g to show the vector g on the molecule. The molecule swings along it and an arrow is drawn on each atom. Press h to do the same with h. The longest arrow is 1 Å long. They are the vectors of the last iteration of the file, and the molecule swings about the geometry of that iteration. The atom that moves most is displaced by 0.3 Å at the top of the swing.
  5. Change Amplitude (Å) and Speed in the section Vibrations to change the swing; they are the controls of the vibrations. See Vibrations.
  6. Press Stop in the section Vibrations to stop the swing: the molecule goes back to the geometry of the last iteration and the vector stays chosen. Press g or h again to leave the vector altogether and go back to the frame of the scrubber.
  7. Press Open window to see the numbers, the cones and the curves.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Four levels of data

What you get depends on the file, and the sentence in the section says which case it is:

  • None: the file has no gradient-difference or coupling data. The section is hidden and the toolbar button is off.
  • Refused: the file has data that the tool does not handle yet. This is the case when the two states come from two runs and a coupling vector is present, and when the file has symmetry. The section says so and the buttons are off.
  • g only: the gradient difference is there but the coupling is not, or it is approximate, or the file has no forces at its last iteration. The vector g can be shown and swung, and the window gives its text but no cone.
  • Full: the whole branching plane is known. g and h are shown, and the window has everything.

Why g and h are plain Cartesian

The two directions are not weighted by mass: they are the Cartesian vectors, rescaled so the real atom that moves most gets the full arrow. A ghost or dummy centre has no arrow. An arrow shorter than a twentieth of the longest is not drawn.

Is the last geometry at the intersection?

For a search at a fixed energy gap, or one that stopped with the gap still open, the tool adds a sentence in the section What is shown and in the window, because the last geometry is then not at the intersection. Read it before you trust the numbers.

A swing is not a path

While g or h is on show, the molecule is not a frame of the path. Save XYZ declines, and Save path XYZ writes the swing. See Save XYZ.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Convergence of the right panel draws three small plots that show how an optimisation converged: the Energy, the Gradient and the Step, each against the iteration. The frame you are on is marked on each plot, so you can read at a glance what a geometry was like in terms of energy, force and step.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load a file with several geometries. See Load a file.
  2. Open the section Convergence in the right panel. The three plots are one under the other.
  3. Read the Energy plot. The energy is drawn above the lowest value in the file, in kcal/mol, so that the end of the run is still readable. If the file stores the energy of several roots, every root is a line, and the one the optimisation follows is drawn thicker and named in the notes.
  4. Read the Gradient plot. For an HDF5 file it is computed from the forces of each iteration: the norm and the largest component, in Hartree/Bohr, for the real atoms. For a Molden file it shows the maximum and the root-mean-square force from the convergence block.
  5. Read the Step plot. It is the length of the displacement from one iteration to the next, in Å, over the real atoms, plotted at the first of the two iterations. Only an HDF5 file has it.
  6. Look for the vertical line and the rings on the plots: they mark the frame you are on. Scrub through the frames and they move. See Scrub through the frames.
  7. Click on a line of a plot to show the iteration nearest to the click. A click away from the lines opens the plot enlarged. See Enlarged plots.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A plot that cannot be drawn says why

Where a plot cannot be drawn, a sentence stands in its place: for example that the file has no energy for each iteration, or, for a Molden file, no step data. For a file with one geometry there is no history at all: the section shows the single sentence One geometry, no convergence history. and no plot. The three plots do not all exist for every file.

The restart of an IRC and the changes of state

In the run of an IRC, a dashed line marks the restart: the second branch starts from the starting geometry at that iteration, so the step into it is left out of the Step plot. In a run with state tracking, the same kind of mark shows where the states changed order. A file is never both.

The open marker

For a Molden file with a predicted last geometry, the energy plot draws that point as an open marker. Its energy is the predicted one, not a computed one. See What is shown.

Two states

For a run that names two states, the energy and the forces are the averages of the two states, and the titles of the plots say so.

The three plots can be saved

See Export plots.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Display of the left panel sets how the atoms and the bonds are drawn. The most important setting is how bonds are found: PathVibViz does not read bonds from the file, it finds them from the distances between atoms, and it does so again for every frame. That is how a bond that forms or breaks along a path appears and disappears as you scrub.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open the section Display in the left panel.
  2. Move Ball scale to make the atoms larger or smaller. It runs from 0.10 to 2.00 and starts at 0.50.
  3. Move Bond radius to make the bonds thicker or thinner. It runs from 0.03 to 0.40 and starts at 0.12.
  4. Move Bond detect tol. to change how readily two atoms count as bonded. It runs from 1.00 to 1.50 and starts at 1.20. Two atoms are bonded when the distance between them is smaller than the sum of their covalent radii times this number, and larger than 0.4 Å. A larger value finds longer bonds.
  5. Scrub through the frames and look at the bonds change. See Scrub through the frames.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The tolerance changes the marks on the path plot

For an IRC or MEP the plot of the section Path marks with a dashed line where the set of bonds changes. Those marks use the same tolerance, so they move when you move Bond detect tol.. See IRC and MEP paths.

Ghost centres

A ghost centre, which has no nuclear charge, is drawn see-through and never takes part in a bond.

The settings are not tied to a file

The three sliders keep their values when you load another file. Save State stores them and Load State puts them back. See Save and load a state.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The plots in the side panels are small. A click on one opens the same plot large, in a window over the view, with its legend beside the plot area and its own buttons to save it. It works for the three convergence plots, for the plot of a measurement and for the plot of the section Path.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Click a small plot, but not on one of its lines: on the empty part of the plot, or on its title. The window opens. A click on a line does something else: it shows the frame at that point and leaves the plot small.
  2. Read the plot. The frame you are on is marked on it, and the mark follows the frame when it changes. The title of the window names the plot.
  3. Click inside the plot area to show the frame nearest to the click. The window stays open.
  4. Save the plot with PNG, SVG or gnuplot ZIP under it. See Export plots. The enlarged plot of the section Path has no export buttons: that plot has no export of its own.
  5. Close the window with ✕ Close, with the key Esc, or with a click outside it.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Click on the line or beside it

A click that lands within a few pixels of a plotted line shows the frame; any other click on the small plot opens the window. On a touch screen, tap beside the line to enlarge.

The window closes when the plot goes away

Loading another file, or choosing another measurement that has no plot, closes the window: it shows a plot of what is no longer there.

Keyboard

Esc closes the top window and Tab stays inside it. See Windows.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The convergence plots and the plot of a measurement can be saved as a PNG image, as an SVG drawing, or as one ZIP file that holds the numbers and a gnuplot script to redraw the figure for a paper. The saved plots are always drawn dark on white, whatever the theme of the page.

items.title: How
items.text:
To save a convergence plot:

  1. Open the section Convergence in the right panel.
  2. Under the plots, choose which one with Plot to export: Energy, Gradient or Step. A plot that cannot be drawn for your file is greyed out in the list, and when none can be drawn the three buttons are off.
  3. Press PNG, SVG or gnuplot ZIP.

To save the plot of a measurement:

  1. Choose a measurement in the section Measurements by clicking its row. See Measurements.
  2. Press PNG, SVG or gnuplot ZIP under its plot. The buttons are off while the measurement has no plot.

To save a plot from the enlarged window, press the same three buttons under it. See Enlarged plots.

The files are named after the file you opened, without its ending, and the kind of plot. For a measurement the name carries the kind and the atoms, for example distance_C1-N2. The ZIP holds a folder with a table of numbers (.csv) and a script for gnuplot (.gp) that draws the figure as an EPS file.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Always on the print palette

An exported plot is drawn dark on white, with colours that stay readable on paper, even if the page is in the light or in the dark theme. The colours on the screen are not the ones saved.

A dihedral that wraps

A dihedral goes from 180 to -180 degrees. In its plot, the line is drawn in pieces, so that no line crosses the plot between the two ends. In the ZIP the pieces are columns whose name ends in _part2, _part3 and so on; each continues the column before it. The values are never shifted by 360 degrees.

What the table says about itself

The .csv file starts with lines that name the tool and its version, the file, what the plot is and how the values were made. If a measurement has no value at some iterations, they are left out of the plot and the lines say which.

On an iPhone or iPad

The files are passed to the share sheet of the system. See Save files on iPhone and iPad.

The picture of the molecule

The 3D view is saved with Save PNG, not from here. See Export images.

items.title: What it does
items.text: An IRC (intrinsic reaction coordinate) or MEP (minimum-energy path) run walks downhill from a transition state, step by step, and the optimiser takes several iterations between one converged point of the path and the next. The section Path of the right panel shows only the converged points, with the energy along them, and lets you walk from point to point. It appears for an HDF5 file that has path points, and is hidden otherwise.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the HDF5 file of an IRC or MEP run. See Load a file. The section Path appears in the right panel.
  2. Read the lines at the top of the section. For each branch they give the number of converged points and the iterations they cover, then the starting point.
  3. Look at the plot. It shows the energy above the lowest path point, in kcal/mol, against the path length from the starting point, in milli-Bohr. Dashed lines labelled bonds change show where the set of bonds changes. In an IRC the forward branch lies to the right of the starting point and the backward branch to the left, each as its own line.
  4. Press › or ‹ under the plot, or drag the slider between them, to go to the next or the previous path point. The molecule, the scrubber and the other plots follow. The line under the slider says where you are, for example Forward point 2 of 9 (iteration 14), path length 0.832 Bohr. or Starting point (iteration 1), path length 0 Bohr.
  5. Click on the line of the plot to show the path point nearest to the click. A click on the plot but away from its line opens the plot enlarged. See Enlarged plots.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Path points, not iterations

The slider walks the converged path points, not the optimiser iterations between them. If you move the scrubber to an iteration that is not a path point, the line under the slider says so.

Forward and backward

In an IRC, the branch OpenMolcas computed first is called forward and the other backward; the tool takes the names from the order in the file and never from the energies. A minimum-energy path has one branch and no label.

The path length

The path length is mass-weighted and measured along straight lines between the converged points, so it is slightly shorter than the length the run output gives where the path bends. If the file holds no atomic masses, the points are numbered instead and the plot says so.

The file does not say why a branch stopped

The file records the path points, not why a branch ended. The run output says that.

Molden files of an IRC

The geo.molden and mep.molden files hold the second branch only, and the Path section needs an HDF5 file. For the whole path, open the HDF5 file of the run.

items.title: What it does
items.text: You give PathVibViz the file of an OpenMolcas run, and it draws every geometry the file holds. The tool works out for itself what kind of file it is: a sequence of geometries, a single geometry, or a frequency file. The section File of the left panel then tells you what it found.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press Load File in the toolbar and choose a file, or drag the file onto the view. The picker offers .h5, .hdf5 and .molden files. Only one file is read, except in the case in the next step.
  2. To open a frequency file with the ghost atoms of its run marked, choose or drop two files together: the .freq.h5 file and the .scf.h5 file of the same run. The tool reads the frequency file and uses the SCF file only to find the ghost atoms. If you also give the .freq.molden file of the run, it is not read, because the frequency file holds the true masses and its own geometry.
  3. Wait a moment for the file to be read. A short message appears at the bottom: Loaded, the number of geometries and the number of atoms. The section What is shown adds, in words, what the tool found in the file.
  4. Open the section File in the left panel. It lists the Source (OpenMolcas HDF5 or Molden), the Kind (geometry sequence, single geometry or frequency file), the number of Atoms and of Frames. For the run of an IRC or MEP it adds the number of path points, the step, and the iteration at which the second branch restarts.
  5. Look at the file bar along the bottom of the page. It names the file with its role (Path file, Geometry file or Frequency file) and its kind. A name that is too long is shortened in the middle; hold the pointer over it, or tap it, to see the whole name.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Loading another file starts again

Loading a file clears the one before it: the measurements, the chosen vibration, the plots and any open window. Only the settings of the left panel stay as you set them.

The last frame of a Molden file

In a Molden geometry file written by SLAPAF the last frame is often not a computed geometry. The tool marks it. See What is shown and Scrub through the frames.

Which file for an IRC

The Molden files geo.molden and mep.molden of an IRC hold the second branch only. For the whole path, open the HDF5 file of the run, or irc.molden. The choice of file is yours, and the tool does not mark that the first branch is missing. For a Molden file whose name says IRC, the section What is shown adds a note on what such a file holds.

A file the tool cannot use

A file that is not HDF5, or that uses a feature the reader does not know, is refused with a plain message in red in the section What is shown, and the tool shows nothing. The file itself is not damaged.

What the HDF5 file must hold

The tool needs the geometry sequence of the run, which is what SLAPAF writes, with the charges of the atoms. A file without them is refused with a message that says what is missing.

items.title: What it does
items.text: You pick atoms in the view and PathVibViz measures a distance, an angle, a dihedral angle or an out-of-plane angle between them. The value is shown for the frame you are on and changes as you scrub, and a click on its row draws the value against the whole run. It is the quick way to see which bond stretches, which angle opens, or which torsion turns along a path.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load a file. See Load a file. The buttons of the section Measurements in the left panel are off until a file is open.
  2. Press Distance, Angle, Dihedral or Out-of-plane. The button stays pressed and a line under the buttons says what to click.
  3. Click the atoms in the view, in this order:
    • Distance: two atoms.
    • Angle: three atoms, with the vertex second.
    • Dihedral: four atoms in the order of the chain, 1-2-3-4.
    • Out-of-plane: four atoms. The bond runs from the first atom to the fourth; the second, third and fourth make the plane.

Each atom you pick is ringed and numbered in the view. The line under the buttons counts how many are still needed. When the last one is picked, the measurement is added to the list and the tool is ready for another of the same kind. 4. Read the list. Each row has a coloured swatch, the value, the kind, and the atoms with their symbol and their number in the file, for example C1 – N2. In the view the same colour draws the measurement on the atoms with its value. The value is in Å for a distance and in degrees for the other kinds. 5. Scrub through the frames. The values and the drawing follow the frame you are on. See Scrub through the frames. 6. Click a row to plot that measurement. The plot appears under the list, against the path length for an IRC or MEP, and against the iteration for any other run. The frame you are on is marked on it, and a click on its line shows the frame there. A click beside the line opens the plot enlarged. See Enlarged plots. 7. Press ✕ at the end of a row to remove that measurement. Press the button of the kind again to stop picking.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The sign of the dihedral and of the out-of-plane angle

The two have the sign that SLAPAF prints, so that you can compare the numbers with the output of the run. A dihedral runs from -180 degrees up to, but not including, 180.

Atoms are numbered as in the file

The numbers start at 1 and count ghost centres too, so a measurement keeps its atoms from frame to frame, and the number in the list is the number of the atom in the file.

A measurement without a value

If two of its atoms are at the same place, or three lie on a line so that the dihedral or the plane is not defined, the row shows a dash and says why, for the frame you are on. At such frames the plot leaves the point out and says which iterations it left out.

What can go wrong with a click

Picking needs a click, not a drag: turning the molecule never picks an atom. An atom cannot be picked twice for one measurement. The first thing under the pointer must be an atom: a bond in front of an atom hides it.

On the screen only

The lines and values are drawn on the screen. They are not in a recorded GIF, in Save PNG, or in the vector SVG.

Measurements are kept with the state

Save State stores the list, and Load State brings it back for the same file or the same molecule. See Save and load a state.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Save State writes the way you have set up the view to a small JSON file: how the molecule is turned and zoomed, the frame you are on, the settings of the left panel, the chosen vibration, the measurements, and which panels and sections are open. Load State puts it back later. It is how you come back to the same figure for a paper, or hand a colleague exactly what you saw. The file holds no geometry and no data from your calculation.

items.title: How
items.text:
To save:

  1. Set the view up as you want it: turn the molecule, go to the frame, make your measurements.
  2. Press Save State. The button is off until a file is open. The file is named after the file you opened, with _state and the ending .json.

To load:

  1. For the best result, open the same file first. See Load a file.
  2. Press Load State and choose the saved .json file.
  3. Read the message at the bottom. It says what was restored and what was not.

What comes back depends on what is open:

  • The same file: everything. The settings and the panels, the frame, the chosen vibration and its phase, the view and the measurements.
  • Another file of the same molecule: the settings and the panels, the view and the measurements. The frame and the chosen vibration are not restored.
  • A file of another molecule: only the settings and the panels.
  • No file open: only the settings and the panels.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The measurements need the same atoms

A measurement names atoms by their number in the file, so it comes back only for the same file or the same molecule. An entry that names an atom the file does not have is left out, and the message counts them.

What is not saved

The arrows of a vibration, the choice of g or h, the temperature and the pressure of the thermochemistry, the settings of the infrared spectrum and of the GIF, and the look of the vector SVG are not part of the state.

A file that is not a state

A file that is not valid JSON, or has no header from the OPAL suite, or is of another schema, is refused with a message and nothing changes.

On an iPhone or iPad

The state is passed to the share sheet of the system. See Save files on iPhone and iPad.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Two buttons of the toolbar write geometries to XYZ files, which almost any program reads. Save XYZ writes the step you are on. Save path XYZ writes the whole path as one file with a frame for every step, which a viewer can play as a movie. While a vibration, or g or h of a conical intersection, is on show, Save path XYZ writes one swing of it instead.

items.title: How
items.text:
To save one step:

  1. Move the scrubber to the step you want. See Scrub through the frames.
  2. Press Save XYZ. The file is named <name>.step<NN>.xyz, where <name> is the name of the file you opened without its ending and without the module part SLAPAF puts before it, and <NN> is the frame number the scrubber shows, with at least two digits.

To save the whole path:

  1. Press Save path XYZ with no vibration on show. The file is named <name>.path.xyz and holds every step of the file in its order, each exactly as Save XYZ would write it.

To save a swing:

  1. Choose a mode in the section Vibrations, or g or h of a conical intersection, so that the molecule swings.
  2. Press Save path XYZ. The file holds 24 frames, evenly spaced over one swing, at the amplitude on show. Its name is <name>.mode<N>.xyz for mode number N, or <name>.ci_g.xyz and <name>.ci_h.xyz.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The coordinates are the file's own

The coordinates are in Å, in the frame of reference of the file, and not in the principal axes in which the view draws the molecule. A ghost centre is written with the symbol X, so the atom numbers stay what they are in the file. Every atom of the file is written.

The comment line

The second line of each frame says the tool and its version, the file, and the step; for an IRC it also says whether the step is on the forward or the backward branch or is the starting point, and for a predicted last frame it says that the geometry was predicted and not computed. For a swing it gives the phase and the amplitude.

Save XYZ declines while a mode is on show

A swing is not a step of the path. If a vibration, or g or h, is on show, Save XYZ shows a message and writes nothing. Move the scrubber to go back to the path, then save.

On an iPhone or iPad

The files are passed to the share sheet of the system. See Save files on iPhone and iPad.

items.title: What it does
items.text: A frame is one geometry of the file, one iteration of the run. The scrubber at the bottom of the view moves from frame to frame, and the molecule, the plots and the read-outs follow. It is how you watch an optimisation go downhill.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load a file that holds several geometries. See Load a file.
  2. Drag the slider along the bottom of the view. The molecule changes with it. The text at the right of the slider reads the frame you are on and the number of frames, for example 3 / 12.
  3. Press › for the next frame and ‹ for the previous one. At the first or the last frame the matching button is off.
  4. Read the section Frame at the top of the right panel. It gives the frame number, the iteration, and, when the file has them, the energy in Eh and the energy relative to the lowest one in the file, in kcal/mol. For a Molden file with a convergence block it also gives the largest and the root-mean-square force.
  5. Look at the line at the bottom of the view: it says how many atoms the molecule has and which frame you are on.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A frame is shown as it is stored

Moving the scrubber, pressing ‹ or ›, or clicking a plot always shows the geometry as it is in the file, and ends the animation of a vibration or of g or h, if one was running.

The frame number is the position in the file

The scrubber counts the frames of the whole file, from 1. The Iteration line is the iteration number the file gives for that frame. In an IRC the two branches never share a frame number.

A frame with a stated prediction

For a frame that SLAPAF predicted and did not compute, the section Frame says Predicted for the next iteration, not a computed geometry and marks its energy as predicted. It gives no force for it.

A file with one frame

With a single geometry the slider is off and so are the two buttons: there is nothing to scrub.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Every frame of a run is drawn in the same set of axes, so that a molecule that moves along a path moves on the screen, and one that only turns in space does not. The axes are fixed once, when the file is loaded, from one frame: the last one, the converged geometry. You then turn, shift and zoom the picture as in the other tools of the suite.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load a file. See Load a file. The molecule is placed with its centre of mass at the centre of the view and its principal axes along the axes of the screen, and the camera is set so that every frame fits.
  2. Drag with the left mouse button, or with one finger, to turn the molecule.
  3. Drag with the right or the middle button, or with two fingers, to shift it. Scroll the wheel, or pinch with two fingers, to zoom. The page on Navigate the 3D view says how this works in all the tools.
  4. Press ⌂ Reset at the corner of the view to bring back the starting orientation, position and zoom.
  5. Move the scrubber, and watch the atoms move while the axes stay still. See Scrub through the frames.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Why the axes come from the last frame

A path may start far from where it ends, and a different set of axes for every frame would make the molecule seem to spin. One reference frame keeps the picture steady. A ghost centre carries no mass and does not shape the axes.

Measurements and arrows follow the atoms

The lines and values of a measurement, and the arrows of a vibration, are drawn on the atoms as you turn the molecule. They are drawn on the screen only. See Measurements.

The view comes back with a saved state

Save State keeps the turn, the shift and the zoom, and Load State restores them for the same file or the same molecule. See Save and load a state.

items.title: What it does
items.text: For a frequency file, the section Vibrations of the right panel lists the vibrational modes with their frequency and their infrared intensity, and animates any of them on the molecule. For a transition state, the mode with an imaginary frequency is the motion along the reaction coordinate, and watching it is the quickest check that the structure is the one you meant.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load the frequency file of a run: a Molden file with frequencies, or the .freq.h5 file, which you may give together with the run's .scf.h5. See Load a file.
  2. Open the section Vibrations. At its top, lines in words say what the file holds: how many modes it lists, whether that is all of them, whether there are intensities, and how many imaginary frequencies there are. For a transition state it says that one imaginary frequency is the usual sign of one.
  3. Look at the list. Each row gives the number of the mode in the file, its frequency in cm⁻¹, and its intensity in km/mol. An imaginary frequency is shown as its size followed by i. A frequency below 50 cm⁻¹ in size is marked near zero. The tool recognises the translations and rotations of the whole molecule from the modes themselves, and does not list them.
  4. Click a row. The molecule starts to swing along that mode, and a line under the list gives the number, the frequency, the intensity and the reduced mass of the mode.
  5. Move Amplitude (Å) to change how far it swings. It is the largest displacement of any atom at the top of the swing; it runs from 0.05 to 1.50 and starts at 0.40. Move Speed to make it faster or slower.
  6. Tick Arrows to draw an arrow on each atom, showing the direction in which it moves. The longest arrow is 1 Å long.
  7. Press Stop to stop the swing. The molecule goes back to its equilibrium geometry and the mode stays chosen. Press Play to start it again from the beginning.
  8. Click the chosen row again to leave the mode altogether and go back to the frame of the scrubber.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The arrows could point the other way

The sign of a mode is arbitrary. The arrows are drawn with the largest component positive, but the molecule moves both ways during the swing.

Modes marked as unreliable

For some files, OpenMolcas scales modes wrongly when a job with symmetry used analytic derivatives. The tool then marks the modes that are not orthogonal to another one as unreliable and says so under the list. Their frequencies are right, but their shapes should not be trusted.

An incomplete list

A job with symmetry can write only the totally symmetric modes. If the list holds fewer vibrations than the molecule has, a line says so, and the list is not the whole spectrum.

Which masses

A frequency file written as .freq.h5 has the true masses of the atoms. A Molden file has none: the tool uses the standard mass of each element, so an isotope is seen as the plain element. Ghost atoms and dummy centres have no mass.

A file without modes

If the file holds no vibrations, the section says so and the buttons are off. The HDF5 file of an optimisation, for example, has none.

Thermochemistry

For a .freq.h5 file a block Thermochemistry appears with boxes for the temperature in K and the pressure in atm and the corrections at those values. It is not given when the file cannot support it, and then it says why.

More buttons

IR spectrum, next to Arrows, opens a window with the simulated infrared spectrum; this page does not describe it. Further down, the section also has the controls of the animated GIF of the chosen mode, with Record & Download; they are described on Export an animated GIF.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Files differ in what they hold: some have an energy for every iteration, some only one geometry, some are frequency files. Instead of leaving you to wonder why a panel is empty, PathVibViz says in plain words, in the section What is shown of the right panel, what it found in your file and what it could not draw. A file that cannot be used is refused there, in red.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Load a file. See Load a file.
  2. Find the section What is shown at the bottom of the right panel and read the lines in it. Which lines you get depends on the file. The ones you meet most are:
    • Showing the geometry sequence with its energies. or Showing the geometry sequence only., for a file with several geometries.
    • One geometry, no sequence., for a file with one geometry. The convergence plots then say there is no history.
    • This file has no energy for each iteration: frames are shown without an energy line. for an HDF5 file with no energies, and a similar line for a Molden file. The frames are drawn, and the plots that need an energy say so.
    • This is a frequency file: showing its equilibrium geometry. for a Molden frequency file; its vibrations are in the section Vibrations.
    • For an HDF5 file with symmetry, a line that says the file stores the symmetry-unique atoms and that the others are generated from the file's own list. If that list cannot be used, the line says why and the atoms are shown as stored.
    • For a file with two states named, a line that says the energy and the forces are the averages of the two states.
    • For a run with state tracking, a line that says at which iterations the states changed order.
  3. Read the second paragraph of the section. It explains why the last frame of a Molden geometry file written by SLAPAF is not a computed geometry. See the tip below.
  4. If a line is red, the file was refused. Read it: it says what is wrong, for example that the file is not an HDF5 file, that it has no geometry sequence, or that it has no nuclear charges for its atoms.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The last frame of a SLAPAF Molden file is a prediction

SLAPAF writes one frame more than it computed: the geometry it has just worked out for the next iteration, with the energy it predicts for it and a force of zero, because none was computed. The HDF5 file does not hold that frame. PathVibViz recognises it by the zero force, says so on the frame line of the section Frame, and draws its point in the energy plot as an open marker. Do not call it a computed point.

Messages are about this file

The lines describe the file you loaded, not the tool. A plot or a button that is empty or off is explained here or in the plot itself.

items.title: What it is for
items.text:
RassiViz shows the result of a RASSI calculation done with OpenMolcas: the excited states of a molecule and the transitions from the ground state to each of them. For every transition it draws the transition dipole moment as an arrow on the molecule, lists the energy, the wavelength and the oscillator strength, and draws the absorption spectrum that follows from them. It can also draw the electron density that changes in a transition, as a surface in two colours.

Open RassiViz. It runs in your browser. It holds one file at a time: opening another file replaces the first.

items.title: Files it reads
items.text:
• The OpenMolcas .h5 or .hdf5 file written by the RASSI module. It holds the geometry, the energies of the states, the transition dipole moments and, usually, the transition densities.
  • An SCF, RASSCF or SLAPAF .h5 file is opened for its geometry only. A message says that the file holds no data on the states, and the Spectrum button stays off. To see the orbitals of an SCF or RASSCF file, open it in OrbViz.
  • A file without symmetry and a file with symmetry are both read. For a file with symmetry the atoms of the whole molecule are drawn.

The page has these parts:

  • The toolbar, from the left: the back link OPAL, the version badge, Open .h5, Spectrum, Save State, Load State, Export ▾ (the menu of the image formats), Spin, Tilt, Anim GIF, the progress of a density computation as a percentage, a line of status text, Theme and the ⓘ button, which opens a small window on how to cite OPAL and links to this tutorial.
  • The left panel, in three sections: Representation, Display and Surface Finish.
  • The view in the middle. Before a file is loaded it shows a welcome text. Afterwards it shows the molecule, the arrows of the transition dipole moments and the density surface.
  • The right panel, in three sections: Molecule Info (folded), States & TDM Vectors (open) and Electron Density (folded).
  • The file bar along the bottom of the page: the name of the loaded file and the kind of file.
  • Windows that open over the view: the spectrum, the details of the spectrum, and the two of the GIF export.

Short messages appear over the view when something succeeds or fails, and go away by themselves after a few seconds. The status text in the toolbar tells you what RassiViz is doing, for example that the density is being computed.

Sections of the side panels fold. How that works is explained once, in Parts of a tool page.

A usual order of work: open the file, read the table of states, switch on the arrows you want to see, look at the density of one transition, open the spectrum, and finally export an image or the spectrum.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The surface of a density is the set of points where the density has one chosen value, the isovalue. A small isovalue gives a large, bloated surface; a large one gives small caps around the places where the density is strongest. The controls of Electron Density that follow the computation set the isovalue and the transparency of the surface you already have, and they act at once, without computing again.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Compute a density as described in Electron density.
  2. In the section Electron Density, move Isovalue to change the value. The slider is logarithmic: each step of the slider multiplies the value by a constant factor. Its top is the largest value found on the grid, and it reaches four decades below.
  3. For a step of fixed size, press the buttons ◀ and ▶ on each side of the box: each press moves the slider by one hundredth of its length, which changes the isovalue by about 10 percent, to a smaller or a larger value.
  4. To give an exact value, type it in the box next to the slider and press Enter, or leave the box. On a touch screen the box can be read but not typed in; use the slider and the arrows.
  5. Move Opacity (0.1 to 1.0, starting at 0.65) to make the surface more or less transparent.
  6. Read the colours in the note above Transition: for the difference density blue is gain and red is loss, for the transition density blue and red are the two signs of the phase.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Where the starting isovalue comes from

When a density has been computed, the range of the slider and the starting isovalue follow what is on the grid. The first surface is drawn at the value whose surface holds 85 percent of the sum of the absolute values on the grid. A value you set yourself is kept when you compute the density of another transition.

The same value for both colours

The surface for the positive values and the one for the negative values use the same number: the isovalue is plus and minus the same number.

Opacity of 1

At an opacity of 1.0 the surface is drawn as a solid. Below that it is see-through, and RassiViz orders the parts of the surface for the turn you give the molecule.

A transparent surface and a transparent background

A see-through surface does not survive a GIF with a transparent background. The window of Anim GIF says so. See Export an animated GIF.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The sections Display and Surface Finish of the left panel set the size of the atoms and the bonds, the distance that decides which atoms are bonded, whether the hydrogens are drawn, and how shiny the surfaces look against which background.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the section Display, move Ball scale (0.05 to 1.0, starting at 0.25) to make all the balls larger or smaller.
  2. Move Bond radius (0.02 to 0.20, starting at 0.090) for the thickness of the sticks.
  3. Move Bond cutoff (0.8 to 1.3, starting at 1.20). Two atoms are bonded when their distance is smaller than the sum of their covalent radii times this number. The bonds change as you move the slider.
  4. Untick Show H to hide the hydrogen atoms and the bonds to them. It is ticked when a file is opened.
  5. In the section Surface Finish, move Matte ↔ Shiny (0 to 120, starting at 40) for the sharpness of the highlights, Specular (0 to 100, starting at 30) for their strength and Ambient (0 to 1.5, starting at 0.30) for the light that falls on every side.
  6. Click the colour box of Background to choose the colour of the view. It starts as a dark blue.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
The surface finish acts on the surfaces too

Matte ↔ Shiny, Specular and Ambient change the look of the atoms, the bonds, the arrows and the density surface together.

The background is part of the picture

The colour of Background is the colour behind the molecule in a PNG or SVG image when the option Transparent background of the menu Export ▾ is off. See Export images.

Bond radius of zero

The slider Bond radius stops at 0.02, and at that value the sticks are thin but still drawn. The style CPK of Representation sets the radius to zero: the number beside the slider then reads 0.000, the slider sits at its left end, and no bond is drawn.

The view is fitted again

Each change of Ball scale, Bond radius, Bond cutoff or Show H builds the molecule again and fits it to the view, so the zoom and the shift you set with the mouse are lost.
