items.title: What it does
items.text: RassiViz draws what changes in the electrons when the molecule goes from the ground state to an excited state. You can draw the difference density, the density of the excited state minus the density of the ground state: where it is positive the electrons gather, where it is negative they leave. Or you can draw the transition density, which links the two states and is the quantity behind the transition dipole moment. The surface is computed from the densities stored in the RASSI file, on a grid around the molecule.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open a RASSI file. When it holds the transition densities, RassiViz computes the difference density of the first transition by itself. The percentage in the toolbar shows the progress, the status text names the step (for example Computing density…), and when it is done the status text says Density surface ready with the number of triangles and the time.
  2. To look at another quantity, fold out the section Electron Density in the right panel. Under Transition, choose the transition, for example S₀→S1 ΔE=3.12 eV (397 nm).
  3. Choose Δρ (difference) or ρTD (transition). The note under the choice gives the colours.
  4. Under Grid, choose Fast (N=30) or High (N=50). The line under the button Compute says how long the computation is expected to take on a laptop, with the number of grid points and of basis functions.
  5. Press Compute. The button is off while the computation runs. The surface replaces the earlier one.
  6. Tick or untick Show surface to show or hide the surface without computing again.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A change of choice needs Compute

Changing Transition, the choice between Δρ and ρTD, or Grid does not draw anything new. Press Compute after you change them. Only the isovalue and the opacity act at once, see Density isosurface.

Colours

For the difference density, blue is where the density increases (the electrons go there) and red is where it decreases. For the transition density, blue and red are the two signs of the phase; the transition density is not a probability density, and the note under the choice says so.

A large molecule is not computed by itself

For a large molecule, or a large basis set, the computation can take minutes. Above a size limit RassiViz does not start it when the file is opened. A message says that the density was not computed, and why, and the line under Compute gives the estimate. Press Compute when you are ready. The Fast grid takes less time than High.

No density in this file

When the file holds no transition densities, Compute stays off and there is no density to draw; the arrows and the spectrum work as usual. A file written with symmetry is read through its symmetry; if RassiViz cannot do that for your file, a message says so, and for some transitions of such a file the difference density is available while the transition density is not.

A new file starts again

Opening another file stops a computation in progress and clears the surface.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Molecule Info of the right panel gives a short summary of what the file holds: the formula, where the centre of the transition dipole arrows lies, the number of atoms and states, and, for a file written without symmetry, how many electrons the wavefunction holds against the nuclear charge.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open a file, then fold out the section Molecule Info in the right panel. It is folded when the page starts.
  2. Read the formula at the top. Carbon comes first, then hydrogen, then the other elements in alphabetical order; a number after the symbol is the number of atoms of that element.
  3. The row Coord. frame says how the coordinates of the file were converted: from Bohr to Å, with the factor used (0.529177210903 Å for one Bohr).
  4. The rows CoM X, CoM Y and CoM Z give, in Å, the point where the arrows of the transition dipole moments start.
  5. The row Atoms is the number of atoms drawn, and SFS states the number of spin-free states in the file.
  6. When the file has no symmetry, a line below gives Electrons, nuclear charge and net charge. When the densities in the file are all zero, the line reads Electrons: not stored in this file and gives only the nuclear charge.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
What the centre is

OpenMolcas sets the origin of the multipole operators to the centre of mass unless the input gives another point, and RassiViz takes the origin from the file. The rows are labelled CoM for that reason. If your input named another origin, the arrows start there.

A message instead of the centre

A file that has no multipole origin, or too few values for it, gives a message in this section and over the view: the arrows are then drawn from the origin of the coordinate system of the file, not from the centre of mass.

A net charge far from zero

When the number of electrons differs from the nuclear charge by more than 2, a warning in the section says so and advises to check INACtive and NACTel in the RASSCF input. A charged molecule gives a net charge that is not zero without any error, so read the number before you take it for a mistake.

Files with symmetry

For a file written with symmetry, or a file that has no densities, the electron line is not shown.

items.title: What it does
items.text: RassiViz reads the .h5 file that the RASSI module of OpenMolcas writes. It draws the molecule, lists the states and their transitions from the ground state, and prepares the transition densities and the spectrum. The page holds one file at a time.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Press Open .h5 in the toolbar and choose the file. You can also click the box in the welcome text, or drag the file onto the view. If you drop several files, only the first one is read.
  2. While the file is read, the status text says Loading and the name of the file. When the file is ready, the status text says the name, the number of atoms and the number of states, for example name.h5 — 24 atoms, 5 states. When the file has transition densities, RassiViz starts to compute the first one a moment later (step 5) and the status text then shows the progress of that computation; the numbers of atoms and states stay in Molecule Info.
  3. Look at the file bar along the bottom of the page. It shows the name of the file and, in its right part, the kind of file: OpenMolcas HDF5 (RASSI). A long name is shortened in the middle so that its ending stays visible; point at it, or tap it, to see the whole name.
  4. The molecule appears in the view. The right panel lists the states, and the button Spectrum is on.
  5. For a file that has the transition densities, RassiViz starts to compute the density of the first transition by itself. The percentage in the toolbar shows the progress. See Electron density.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A file that holds no states

An SCF, RASSCF or SLAPAF file is opened for its geometry. The molecule is drawn, a message over the view and the status text say Showing the geometry only and name the kind of file, the table of states reads No TDM data. and Spectrum stays off. The file bar names the kind, for example OpenMolcas HDF5 (RASSCF).

A file that is not usable

A file that holds neither states nor a geometry, and a file that is not HDF5, is not opened. The status text starts with a cross and says why, for example This file contains no state-interaction data, so RassiViz cannot display it. The molecule that was on show before is gone: opening a file, even one that fails, clears the previous one first. The right panel is not redrawn, though: Molecule Info, the table of states and the list of transitions keep what the earlier file showed, and Spectrum stays on. Open a good file to start again.

Only .h5 and .hdf5

The file chooser offers .h5 and .hdf5 files (on an iPhone or iPad it offers every file). A file dropped on the view must end in .h5 or .hdf5; another name gives the status text Please drop an .h5 or .hdf5 file.

Symmetry

A RASSI file written with symmetry shows all the atoms of the molecule. When RassiViz cannot tell how the densities of such a file map onto the whole molecule, a message says that it does not draw them; the molecule, the arrows and the spectrum are still there.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section Representation of the left panel chooses how the molecule is drawn: ball and stick, space-filling, large balls or thin sticks. It also chooses whether the bonds are all drawn as single lines or are given an order (double, triple) from the distances. The bonds are only a picture: they are found from the geometry and they do not change the arrows, the densities or the spectrum.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. In the section Representation, press one of the four buttons: Ball & Stick, CPK, Large B&S or Sticks. The button of the style in use is highlighted. Ball & Stick is on when a file is opened.
  2. Under Bond order, press Single to draw every bond as one line, or Auto to let RassiViz find double, triple and partial bonds from the distances. Single is on when a file is opened.
  3. When Auto is on, a row Aromatic appears. Tick it to draw the bonds of aromatic rings as aromatic bonds. It is ticked when it first appears.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
A button sets two numbers

Each style button sets Ball scale and Bond radius in the section Display to fixed values, and the two sliders move to them. You can move the sliders afterwards, see Display settings. The highlight of the style button stays where it was until you press another one.

CPK draws no bonds

CPK sets the bond radius to zero, and with a bond radius of zero no bond is drawn at all. The balls fill the space instead.

The view is fitted again

Each change of this section, and of Display, builds the molecule again and fits it to the view, so the zoom and the shift you set with the mouse are lost. The turn of the molecule is kept.

items.title: What it does
items.text: Save State writes the way the page looks now to a small JSON file: the sizes and the colours, which arrows are on show, the settings of the density, and the point of view. Load State puts these back later, on the same molecule, so that you can return to a picture you made or make the same picture of another file.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open a RASSI file and set the page as you want it.
  2. Press Save State in the toolbar. The file is named after the file you opened, with .json in place of its ending, for example name.json. The status text says State saved.
  3. Later, open the same RASSI file first, then press Load State and choose the JSON file. The status text says State loaded.
  4. If the state was saved for another file than the one that is open, RassiViz still applies it, and a message says which file the state was saved for. The transitions are matched by their number only, so check the result.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Load the molecule first

A state is applied to a molecule that is already loaded. With no file open, Save State says that there is nothing to save, and Load State says that you must open the .h5 file first.

What is kept

The sizes of the balls and the bonds, the bond cutoff, the choice Single or Auto, Aromatic and Show H; the three settings of the surface finish and the background; the scale, the radius and the choice of Scale by of the arrows; the colour and the visibility of each transition; the settings of the density (Transition, the kind of density, Grid, the isovalue and Opacity); and the position of the camera and the turn of the molecule.

What is not kept

The density itself is not stored: after loading a state, press Compute to draw the density with the settings that were loaded. The settings of the spectrum window are not stored either. The highlight of the style button in Representation stays where it was, although the sizes it set are loaded.

A file that you can read

The state is a text file in the JSON format. Near its top, a line names the tool and its version, followed by the DOI of the OPAL reference once the reference has one.

On an iPhone or iPad

The file is passed to the share sheet of the system. See Save files on iPhone and iPad.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The window Absorption Spectrum can save the spectrum you see as a PNG image, as an SVG drawing, or as a set of files for Gnuplot that you can edit and run to make a figure for a paper.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open the spectrum and set it as you want it: profile, width, range, sticks, peak labels and mode. See The spectrum. What you export is what these controls show.
  2. Press PNG in the toolbar of the window to save an image of 1600 × 900 pixels.
  3. Press SVG to save a drawing of 800 × 450 points. Its text and lines can be edited in a vector program.
  4. Press Gnuplot to save one ZIP file. It holds a folder with two files: a data file, .dat, with the energy, the wavelength, the normalised absorbance and the molar extinction coefficient for every point of the curve, and a script, .gp, that draws the figure from it as an EPS file.
  5. The files are named after the file you opened, with _abs_spectrum added: for example name_abs_spectrum.png, name_abs_spectrum.svg and name_abs_spectrum_gnuplot.zip.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Always dark on white

The exported files are drawn dark on a white background, whatever the theme of the page, and a colour that would be too light on white is darkened. The colours you chose in the table of states are kept as far as the contrast allows; the colours of the table itself do not change.

What the Gnuplot files hold

The data file starts with a line that names the tool and its version, then the name of the file, the profile and the width, and the position of each absorption maximum. A line with the DOI of the OPAL reference is added after the first line once the reference has one. The script holds the axes, the range you set and one arrow and label for each transition whose oscillator strength is not too small. The .dat file covers the eV range you set, so widen the range first if you want more.

On an iPhone or iPad

The files are passed to the share sheet of the system. If sharing is refused, a message says so. See Save files on iPhone and iPad.

The picture of the molecule

The image of the molecule, with the arrows and the density, is exported with the menu Export ▾ of the toolbar, not from this window. See Export images.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The button Spectrum opens a window with the absorption spectrum that follows from the transitions of the ground state: each transition, with its energy and its oscillator strength, is spread into a Gaussian or a Lorentzian curve, and the curves are added. The energy is on the bottom axis in eV and the wavelength on the top axis in nm.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open a RASSI file and press Spectrum in the toolbar. The button is off for a file that holds no states.
  2. Choose the shape under Profile: Gaussian or Lorentzian. Gaussian is on at the start.
  3. Move Width (eV) (0.01 to 0.5, starting at 0.10) to change the width of each curve.
  4. Move the two sliders of eV range to choose the part of the spectrum to show. They start a little outside the lowest and the highest transition, and they cannot cross.
  5. Tick or untick Sticks to show or hide a vertical line at each transition, with a dot at its top and its wavelength in nm. The line has the colour of the transition in the table of states.
  6. Tick or untick Peak labels to label the maxima of the curve with their wavelength.
  7. Under Mode, choose Norm. for a curve whose highest point is 1, or ε for the molar extinction coefficient in L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. Norm. is on at the start.
  8. Press ℹ for the details: the parameters in use, the formulas of the two kinds of spectrum and a short Python script that makes the same curve.
  9. Close the window with the cross at the right of its toolbar, with Esc, or by clicking outside it.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
All the transitions are used

The spectrum is made from every transition in the table of states, whether its arrow is on show or not. A transition with an oscillator strength of zero adds nothing to the curve.

The curve is a model

The curve is the stick spectrum of the calculation spread with the width you choose. The width is not read from the file, and nothing in the curve describes a real line shape. In ε mode the height follows from the oscillator strengths with a constant given in the window of details.

Sticks and peak labels

A peak label that falls on the line of a stick is not drawn twice: when Sticks is on, the sticks carry the wavelengths.

The window follows the theme

On screen the spectrum is drawn on a dark or a light background, following the Theme button. The files you export are always drawn dark on white; see Export the spectrum.

items.title: What it does
items.text: The section States & TDM Vectors of the right panel lists the transitions from the ground state to each excited state: the energy, the wavelength and the oscillator strength. For each transition it can draw the transition dipole moment as an arrow on the molecule. The direction of the arrow tells you along which axis of the molecule the light moves the electrons, and its length tells you how strong the transition is.

items.title: How
items.text:
1. Open a RASSI file. The section States & TDM Vectors is open when the page starts.
  2. Read the table. The first row, S₀, is the ground state. RassiViz takes the state of lowest energy as the ground state and numbers the others S₁, S₂ and so on in order of energy. Each further row gives the energy difference to the ground state in the column ΔE/eV, the wavelength in λ/nm, and the oscillator strength in f.
  3. The arrow of the first transition, S₀→S₁, is on show when a file is opened. Tick the box in the column Vis of a row to show the arrow of that transition, or untick it to hide it. Show all switches all the arrows on or off together.
  4. Click the colour box in the column Col to change the colour of a transition. The arrow, its label and the stick of the spectrum take the new colour.
  5. Move Vec. scale (0.1 to 5.0, starting at 1.0) to make all the arrows longer or shorter, and Vec. radius (0.3 to 3.0, starting at 1.0) to make them thicker or thinner.
  6. Under Scale by, choose what sets the length of an arrow: |TDM|, the length of the transition dipole moment as stored in the file, or √f osc., the square root of the oscillator strength. The default is |TDM|.

items.title: Tips and pitfalls
items.text:
Where the arrow starts and what it shows

Each arrow starts at the centre given in Molecule information and is labelled with its transition, for example S₀→S₁. It has a head at both ends: it shows the axis of the transition dipole moment, not which way it points.

No arrow for a forbidden transition

When the quantity that sets the length is zero, that transition has no arrow. The row stays in the table.

The table feeds the spectrum

The spectrum is made from all the transitions in the table, whether their arrows are on show or not. See The spectrum.

The colours repeat

There are six starting colours, used in turn. With more than six transitions the colours repeat; change them with the boxes in the column Col if you need to tell them apart.
